content.source_text: From hastily installed sheds and tents to more intricate structures with signage and considered design, author Penny Hardy highlights the absurdity, delight and ingenuity of dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic . Collected in Hardy's recently announced book, Pandemic Architecture: NYC Dining Sheds 2020-2024 , the sheds represent a very specific time in the landscape of the city, when restaurants tried to operate during indoor dining restrictions. Many have since been deconstructed, as the city tries to implement a standardised shed programme to keep the seating while maintaining safety and sanitation standards. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani recently cleared the legal way for year-round installation . Hardy took photos of the sheds in Downtown Manhattan on walks during the height of the pandemic and afterwards, as many remained up for years after the 2020 to 2021 lockdowns. Though many of the restaurants have since closed or moved, Hardy believes that it's clear that the impact of the structures has changed the way we view the streetscape. Penny Hardy's new book looks at the range of impromptu dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic "These structures created a new typology for building in public space and have forever changed the way we use the street," she told Dezeen. "Before this new typology, the street was aggressively preserved as a place of transit by the city. Now, in addition to transit, it offers a place for people to connect and socialise." She added that the recent city legislation opens up room for a return to the creativity that has been limited by the high costs of storage and assembly of the structures during the winter months. "The restaurant owners' resourcefulness, humour, and wildly different tastes made the streets more varied and alive," said Hardy. "The structures were raw, inventive, funny, and as varied as New York itself. They brought an old-school punk, DIY spirit back into an increasingly polished city." The book contains dozens of examples taken by Hardy, as well as essays by New York writers such as Michael Bullock and Fred Bernstein . Read on for a selection of images from the book and Hardy's commentary. "Suburban design via Home Depot" in Greenwich Village "'We need to get something up quick. Go to Home Depot. Improvise'. I imagine this was the directive given to an employee or self-imposed by the owner. "Ubiquitous 'colonial moulded interior door' with handle and lock, surrounded by vibrant magenta plastic panelling, taped heart detailing and painted soft pink plywood. Why didn’t they paint the door?" "Less is enough" in West Village "Use structures that already exist. They provide privacy, protection, and shelter from the weather. Why make things more complicated? "The neighbourhood institution, Julius, kept it simple. Perhaps the owner was a camper – bring in a tent from the country, order a few more, and they were done." "Learning from Las Vegas" in Little Italy "If only Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown had been able to see these sheds: one a decorated shed, the other architecture becoming the sign itself. "Baby John created a dining structure fit for his namesake. A curved vinyl banquette pulled from deep storage, a monumental crown, and signage visible from blocks away combined to create a VIP experience that drew long lines and gave the place instant cachet. Venturi and Scott Brown would surely have joined the queue." "An imposing mash-up of classical architecture" in Little Italy "Down the street, a fellow, longtime restaurateur created an imposing mash-up of classical architecture and gothic detailing. "Its sense of grandeur, in direct contrast to the temporality of the sheds, creates a playful contradiction. Venturi and Brown would have appreciated the 'complexity and contradiction'." "The wild west" in Chinatown "Almost overnight, the street became a space of radical improvisation, where rigid building restrictions of the city were tossed aside, as restaurants fought for survival. "Exposed electrical wires brought air conditioners and fans into the sheds. Practical and terrifying at the same time." "Take me away" in SoHo "Perhaps we can transport them somewhere tropical, offering a brief respite from the city. If they can't get on an aeroplane, maybe the dining shed can take them there. "A thatched roof, white curtains tied with rope tassels, and tropical plants conjure a beachfront cabana." "Co-existing" in West Village "The interweaving of street signs and structures with the dining sheds created humorous juxtapositions. "Why extend the structure to enclose the postal relay box? Rather than stopping short of it, the shed carefully absorbs it into the design, even carving out space for the neighbouring tree. Existing street infrastructure becomes part of the architecture." "Living in the street" in NoHo "Owners looked for ways to make street dining feel comfortable, creating environments that helped diners forget they were sitting in a place never meant for a meal. "The dark-stained wood panelling and curated selection of framed paintings evoke the atmosphere of farm life, creating the feeling of dining in the countryside." "Architecture, design and construction professionals enter the fray" in Flatiron "Whether these were designed by an architect, interior designer or contractor, they all had the visible sign of a professional being involved. Material choices, lighting, and built-in seating suggest a level of planning beyond improvisation. "A classic gable roof, clapboard siding, and exposed stud framing suggest the work of a general contractor with spare materials from their last project?" "Even the heaters have been carefully considered" in Nolita "The minimal, modular design suggests the involvement of an architect. "Even the heaters have been carefully considered, integrated beneath the seating." The post Ten pandemic-era dining sheds that show "wildly different tastes" of New Yorkers appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Mexico City -based Mariel Lozano Studio has designed interiors and furniture for a hospitality project in Mexico City, organising the compact space to create "tranquillity" and reduce clutter. San Luis is the debut property for Stays, a concept from music and design practice Mad Monk Studios that will eventually encompass multiple rentable residences. San Luis Stays is a one-bedroom apartment within a new building Mariel Lozano Studio was brought on to design the interiors of the 50-square-metre apartment, located inside a newly constructed building in the Roma Norte neighbourhood. "The initial interior suffered from an overwhelming combination of builder-grade finishes, requiring a conceptual reset to create a harmonious, high-end guest experience," said the design team. Mariel Lozano Studio added a variety of bespoke teak wood furniture pieces to warm the concrete interior To inject warmth and personality into the one-bedroom abode, Lozano wrapped portions of the exposed concrete walls in teak panelling. The same wood variety was used for several items of custom furniture, which were designed by Mariel Lozano Studio and fabricated by carpenters on site. A dining table that extends from a shelving unit is among the custom pieces "To optimise the compact layout, custom-designed fixed furniture was prioritized to hide clutter and maintain a tranquil feel," said the team. "Key elements, such as a custom bed frame featuring concealed luggage storage, keep the visual space clear, allowing guests to experience stillness inside the apartment." The bedroom is separated from the living area by a sliding slatted screen These custom pieces include a built-in L-shaped sofa and a wall-mounted TV cabinet in the living room, and a storage unit and table in the dining area. The bed headboard, which runs the full length of the room, also features an integrated sound system. The headboard features an integrated sound system "Because Mad Monk Studios is fundamentally a music studio, sound is an essential part of the hospitality concept," said the team. "With this in mind, the custom bed frame incorporates integrated audio speakers, paired with curated playlists by Mad Monk Studios for guests to listen while living in the space to get a glimpse of what the space is intended to feel like." Read: PPAA designs "discreet yet powerful" Mexico City hotel Lamartine The bedroom is divided from the living area by a slatted wood partition that slides open and closed, and both rooms have access to a small balcony. In the kitchen, white cabinetry and square backsplash tiles, black countertops and stainless steel appliances create a simple, minimalist aesthetic that contrasts the dark wood elsewhere. The boutique hospitality concept was created by Mad Monk Studios Grey floor tiles also differentiate the kitchen from the oak flooring in the rest of the apartment. Simple lighting includes an almost spherical Nelson Ball Bubble Pendant by Herman Miller above the dining table, a semi-cylindrical sconce over the sofa and a pair of burgundy Flowerpot VP1 Pendants by Verner Panton either side of the bed. The bespoke furniture and efficient spatial layout are designed to maximise the compact footprint A vintage stackable ashtray by Isamu Kenmochi and drinking glasses by En La Superficie were also chosen as decor accessories. "Subtle pops of colour were added through specific curated objects to make the space feel vibrant," the team said. The black and white kitchen provides a contrast with the rich wood furniture elsewhere Mexico City has surged in popularity with tourists and expats in recent years, and a variety of boutique accommodation options have opened as a result. Others include Hotel San Fernando in Condesa, minimalist Lamartine in Polanco, and the Shaker-inspired Círculo Mexicano hotel. The photography is by Fabián Martínez . content.source_text: From mouldable wax lampshades that can be melted and remade to a desk lamp that packs flat inside an A4 envelope, this roundup celebrates a series of unusual lighting designs. Photo courtesy of City Girls Lamps by City Girls City Girls is the studio and alias of two unnamed London artists who create Frankenstein lamps from everything and anything they find on eBay, Facebook Marketplace and the side of the road. So far, the duo's scavenger hunting has seen them create lighting out of a fibreglass model boat, old sequins and dishevelled butterflies extracted from a smashed up toy. Once each lamp is complete, it is affectionately given a name like Pamela, Lola or Jean. Among the collection is the elegant Virginia, a swan-like lamp with an arched green head, a metal body made of old chair legs and a wire decorated with oversized glass beads. Find out more about these lamps › Photo courtesy of Baguette Studio Le Labo 1.0 by Baguette Studio Paris-based Baguette Studio developed a range of pure wax lampshades that can be melted down and endlessly remade without any loss of material. Called Le Labo 1.0, the collection brings together a wall lamp, pendant lamp and table lamps in two sizes. The studio created a custom rotational moulding machine, normally used to shape plastic parts, to sculpt the wax components. "One of the questions we're raising with this project is about ownership of objects," explained Philippe Gaud, who co-founded the studio with Emma Lohner. "Instead of owning an object you basically own 400 or 800 grams of wax that can be melted down and reused." Find out more about Le Labo 1.0 › Photo by Chris Mottalini Floor lamp by Wretched Flowers Wretched Flowers is the brainchild of New York designers Loney Abrams and Johnny Stanish, whose practice includes weaving stainless steel chainmail to create armour-like wallhangings and lighting. This floor lamp is among the pieces in their eclectic collection. Shaped like an elongated version of Verner Panton's iconic 1968 Flowerpot lamp, the lighting was sheathed in a striking chainmail cloak, tapestried with a delicate selection of hand-beaded glass and gemstones. Find out more about this floor lamp › Photo courtesy of Billy Easter Gel Lamp by Billy Easter London designer Billy Easter released the candy cube-like Gel Lamp through her studio, Public Parts . The lamp is made of a hollow cube of silicone –measuring approximately 11.5-by-11.5-by-11.5 centimetres. Its base contains a dimmable LED. At the bottom of the cube sits a slim opening, into which slices of transparent coloured gels can be slid, subsequently changing the colour of the lamp. Find out more about Gel Lamp › Photo courtesy of Seletti Bic Lamp by Mario Paroli and Seletti Bic Lamp is a pendant light shaped like the iconic Bic Cristal ballpoint – the world's bestselling pen, informally known as a Biro. Measuring 12 times the size of the standard pen, the lamp was designed with three different "lid" iterations in classic black, blue and red. The lamp's hexagonal body, which represents the portion of the pen filled with ink, was created out of a large LED light fixture. Bic Lamp was conceived by designer Mario Paroli and Italian brand Seletti . Find out more about Bic Lamp › Photo by Audra Grays and Maxim Lester Fused by Audra Grays and Maxim Lester London designers Audra Grays and Maxim Lester joined forces to conceive this desk lamp out of waste material from their respective design practices. Called Fused, the project is the culmination of offcuts from Grays' glassmaking activities and scraps from Lester's metalwork, fused together to create this geometric utilitarian lamp. The emerging designers combined their material leftovers to consciously cut their making costs. Find out more about Fused › Photo courtesy of Unit.d A4 Lamp by Andu Masebo Also based in London, designer Andu Masebo crafted this lamp out of three pieces of galvanised sheet steel that can fit inside an A4 envelope. Masebo rolled and folded the metal by hand to create a series of round and rectilinear components that, when assembled, are held together with neat incisions. The lamp was debuted earlier this year at Unit.d , an emerging design gallery in Haggerston that was founded to platform collectible design at affordable prices. Find out more about A4 Lamp › Photo by Gustav Almestål Buké Lamps by Simon Skinner Swedish designer Simon Skinner scoured charity shops and flea markets for second-hand bowls, ashtrays and tiny cat figurines, which he stacked on top of each other to create 20 kitschy table lamps. Each piece of glassware was sandblasted to create a unified whole, simultaneously covering the internal bulb, creating lamps that look as if they are made of objects suspended in ice. Skinner has likened his playful process to messing around with Lego or arranging flowers. Find out more about Buké Lamps › The post Eight unconventional lighting designs that tear up the rulebook appeared first on Dezeen .

title: Freitag Turns Used Truck Tarps Into a New Kind of Luxury
summary: The new Reference collection pairs one-of-a-kind patina with streamlined silhouettes, unexpected industrial details, and repair kits designed to extend each bag’s life

content.source_text: When talking about luxury fashion, there are certain conventions that consumers have come to expect: sumptuous materials, opulent detailing, and conceptual—if not impractical—design. Fortunately, Freitag designer Anne Bachmann doesn’t dabble in conventions. Photography courtesy of Freitag “I am fascinated by the effortless beauty of objects that were never designed to please,” she says, referring to the used truck tarps repurposed to create Freitag’s newest collection of high-end bags. The Reference collection launched Oct. 8 with four new bag designs that blend artistic upcycling and luxury. With an “elevated, minimalist aesthetic,” the Reference collection highlights what Freitag does best: tell a story through sustainable, unconventional, one-of-a-kind materials. Photography by Timothy Schaumburg; courtesy of Freitag When conceiving the design, Bachmann imagined a collection that transcended the typical bag experience. She aimed to create something practical, but elegant; one-of-a-kind, yet ever-evolving. When she was presented with used truck tarps, one of the company’s famed upcycled materials, she knew she had found the key component of the collection. Tarps repurposed for the Reference collection. Photography courtesy of Freitag. “Because we cut our bags from used truck tarps, every one-of-a-kind piece already starts out with its own history, character, and unique patina,” Bachmann explains. “And as you take it out into the world, it picks up your own daily scuffs, and becomes a real companion.” It also doesn’t hurt that the sturdy tarpaulins make for a bag that is as durable as it is stylish. Photography by Timothy Schaumburg; courtesy of Freitag Each of the collection’s four bags is designed with a trapezoidal silhouette, creating a light, dynamic flow without compromising its sculptural elegance. While there are core colorways—white, silver, red, blue, and a limited-edition black—the variation from bag to bag means each purchase is a unique work of art. Sourced across Europe and hand-selected by the production and sourcing teams based in Zurich, the tarp “patina,” or markings that uniquely adorn each bag, was a pivotal consideration when building each piece. Photography courtesy of Freitag “Every tarp ages differently on the road, creating subtle variations in color and character before they reach us. Hand-picking the variations in patina, meaning the beautiful marks that weather, environment, and even tree branches leave behind on the tarp during their first life, became equally as important as the colorways,” Bachmann adds. Photography courtesy of Freitag Of course, as the cliché goes, the devil is in the details. That is especially true for a streamlined design like the four featured in the Reference collection. To further elevate the design, each bag features a new label and magnetic clasp unique to the collection. To say Bachmann’s inspiration for the distinct clasp was serendipitous would be to discredit the thoughtfulness of the design; the idea came to her in Freitag’s Zurich factory when she noticed a peculiar hook mechanism on heavy-duty shelving. Photography by Timothy Schaumburg; courtesy of Freitag “I would describe it as opportunistic wandering,” she says of the moment. “Strolling through a space or an urban environment without a specific destination, keeping yourself completely open and receptive so you actually catch a spark of inspiration when it hits.” The intersection of form and function creates a luxury experience that Bachmann hopes will naturally build an attachment that transcends typical fashion. “Emotional attachment prevents waste,” she says. “What we love and share a history with, we rarely throw away.” Photography courtesy of Freitag True to Freitag, the Reference collection extends the brand’s circular approach without sacrificing style or craftsmanship. To further encourage a long relationship between bag and owner, each bag comes with a detachable repair kit that can be taken apart and used to repair the bag with its original tarp material. If there is one tried-and-true element of luxury, it’s exclusivity—the knowledge that the piece you own is the only one in the world like it. The Reference collection promises that every bag created is built to grow and evolve with every use.

title: Friday Five with Veronica Mishaan: Inside the Making of a Bogotá Penthouse
summary: The designer draws on 30 years of family memories, a personal art collection, and the surrounding Andes to reimagine a longtime home for its next chapter

content.source_text: Veronica Mishaan grew up with a love of design. Sure, it helps that her mother, Susana Mishaan de Millán, was also a successful designer in Bogotá and Cartagena, Colombia. She credits her mother with her lifelong passion for painting and fine art. “We have different styles, but she has taught me about confidence, layering, and proportions,” Mishaan says. After graduating from Tufts University, where she studied quantitative economics and international relations, Mishaan wanted to pursue painting as a career. Her father, however, encouraged her to direct her art and design skills toward helping her mother with her interior design practice. “I realized interior design is just another art form,” Mishaan recalls. “And something that was supposed to be six months has turned into 16 years of work.” Alongside her mother, Mishaan helped build M De M Designs, where the pair designed bespoke interiors and handcrafted furnishings in Bogotá and Cartagena. After six years, Mishaan assumed sole leadership of the firm and evolved the business into Veronica Mishaan Design House , where she began developing her own creative vision and international ambitions. Now with offices in New York City, Bogotá, and Bermuda, Mishaan oversees residential, hospitality, commercial, and product design projects worldwide. On a clear day, the Andes Mountains in the background become part of the main living room’s interior decor, which prominently features artwork by Peter Halley. A custom sofa upholstered in Lee Jofa wool pairs with marble-top tables and a cast-bronze water lily table, arranged in a circle to encourage connection. “A successful space generates conversation,” Mishaan says. Photography by Max Burkhalter. Mishaan’s artistic foundation and analytical mind inform her design philosophy. She approaches every interior as she would a canvas, “thoughtfully layering color, texture, geometry, and materiality to create spaces with depth, movement, and meaning,” she says. “When I’m designing a space, I try to balance the materials, the proportions, and the flow of a space. It changes with every client. I don’t like using the same style in every project I create. I use every project as an opportunity to learn more.” Veronica Mishaan joins us for today’s Friday Five . We spent five minutes catching up with her to learn more about a 6,250-square-foot Bogotá penthouse she recently designed and the ideas that inspired it. In the family room, dark blue grasscloth walls, a parchment-wrapped custom bookcase, blue leopard Stark carpeting, Lee Jofa mohair upholstery, and animal-print drapery create a layered yet inviting gathering space. Photography by Max Burkhalter. Bogotá Penthouse “This project in Bogotá reflects our core philosophy: spaces that evolve with time, embody personal narratives, and harmonize past and present,” Mishaan says. This apartment—which has been in the owner’s family for more than 30 years—blends art, treasured objects, and furniture collected over decades with contemporary pieces designed by the firm. Guests are welcomed by a custom Rug & Kilim rug paired with a bronze sculpture from the family’s art collection. An Elsa Foulon porcelain pendant hangs above, while a striking cast bronze staircase railing—created from molds taken from an actual tree branch—extends through the home’s vertical circulation. Photography by Max Burkhalter. What Inspired the Bogotá Penthouse 30 Years of Family Memories The layout was reimagined for the owners’ current lifestyle while honoring the past. The renovation introduces custom tinted wide-plank oak flooring, a mix of recessed and decorative lighting, and walls finished in smooth plaster. The highly personalized primary suite was relocated and enveloped in a rich navy wallcovering, with a bed upholstered in paisley wool, Kelly Wearstler bouclé chaise and bench, and custom brass, wood, and glass shelving. The primary bath features pink marble floors that continue up the walls and transition into blue-and-white waterjet marble. A “dream dressing room” comprises mirrored walls, a custom parchment vanity, and a curved bench upholstered in Pierre Frey velvet. Guest rooms were tailored to the family, including custom bunk beds for the grandchildren. Custom-built bunk beds maximize functionality while Temple Studio wallpaper introduces playful character for visiting grandchildren. Photography by Max Burkhalter. “The client wanted this home to be updated to the new stage of life, but did not want to erase all the memories that were lived in that space for 30-plus years,” Mishaan says. Furniture and artwork were reused and placed in new locations; the desk in the primary bedroom, for example, once sat in the living room. Bogotá’s Greenery and the Andes Mountains The apartment’s views of the Andes Mountains also influenced the design. “The view of the mountains of Bogotá is not a view you get in many metropolitan cities, so I thought it was something worth using as an inspiration,” Mishaan says. Photography by Max Burkhalter That landscape inspired the playroom’s sage green millwork, honey oak floors, dark wood doors and baseboards, and natural marmorino plaster walls. Earthy tones throughout reference the surrounding terrain, while wood and botanical motifs reinforce the connection to the landscape. The dark blue blossom wallpaper by Phillip Jeffries in the primary bedroom creates a serene, transportive atmosphere reminiscent of a peaceful garden. Marmorino plaster walls provide a refined backdrop for a sage silk Rug & Kilim rug in the secondary living room. Existing furnishings were preserved, while the game table chairs were refreshed in Nobilis fabric to seamlessly blend heritage with contemporary comfort. The client’s personal art, including Flow Followers , 2011, by Patrick Tschudi. Photography by Max Burkhalter. The Owners’ Art Collection and Material Palette The art collection anchors the space with cultural and emotional significance, featuring works by Peter Halley, Sophia Vari, Pedro Ruiz, and Larraz. However, Mishaan explains that the selection of materials ultimately drove much of the project. “There was no clear storyline,” she notes. “It became a balanced combination of the materials that felt right to the client and myself.” Original built-in bookcases and wall paneling in the home office were lacquered in deep blue, extending onto the ceiling for a dramatic monochromatic effect. Existing furnishings were reconfigured, while a blue leopard Stark carpet introduces texture and personality. Photography by Max Burkhalter. The thoughtful conglomeration of materials, textures, and patterns includes leopard Stark carpets, printed linen window treatments, a reused antique Aubusson rug, a wool bouclé sofa, and dark brown velvet window treatments. Custom furnishings, millwork, bronze hardware, and architectural details add a personal touch, while honey-toned wood flooring, dark wood accents, bespoke doors, and a custom family room bookcase wrapped in white parchment add warmth. “Extensive use of marmorino plaster throughout the common areas [creates] warmth and softness,” Mishaan adds. Artisan workshops throughout Colombia produced much of the custom furniture and millwork, giving the apartment another connection to the place it calls home.

content.source_text: Local practice Formant Studio created custom furniture and fixtures while designing Mexico City restaurant Nota Tavern, taking references from classic Chicago taverns in the fit-out of a former residence. Located in the city's Escandón I neighbourhood, Nota Tavern is a two-storey Italian-American restaurant. It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that was converted into an apartment building, with the owner preserving half of the original house. The restaurant sits in this portion. Formant Studio designed the interiors and most of the furniture at Nota Tavern in Mexico City Formant Studio was tasked with translating the design of classic Chicago taverns into a contemporary mode. "The main request was to create a faithful interpretation of the neighbourhood taverns of Chicago – the kind of places built less around spectacle and more around familiarity," Formant Studio co-founder Alejandro Valencia told Dezeen. "The design translates the character of a classic tavern into a contemporary architectural language." The two-storey restaurant serves Italian-American cuisine Valencia also said the studio took other cues from Chicago and integrated the clean minimalism of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and the warmer modernism of Frank Lloyd Wright , both architects known for their work in the US city. Also in the tradition of the 20th-century modern architects, Formant Studio designed most of the furniture, from the black-stained oak tables to the steel bar stools and sleek metal sconces. The space was once a hacienda-style residence and its original columns were preserved and restored The majority of the dining room was clad in Mexican rosewood panels, which also form the custom banquettes upholstered in black Kvadrat textiles. Formant Studio said that the previous space defined how it organised the restaurant. Mexican rosewood covers the walls and forms banquette seating The current space still has ornate stone pillars that once framed an entrance portico. The team removed the paint from the pillars, turning them into a centrepiece of the main dining space. An entrance vestibule holds a host stand and a door leads to a metal spiral staircase painted in a rich brown. This staircase leads to a private dining room upstairs. Past the host stand, the main dining room opens up. Visitors walk into a front area with a large banquette and a seating bar that looks out of an operable window onto the street. The design was drawn from classic Chicago taverns "The shape of the existing space largely determined the furniture layout," said Valencia. "We used the longer walls to accommodate the built-in booths, establishing a clear spatial rhythm while keeping the central area flexible and allowing the dining room to adapt to different group sizes and configurations." Read: Gjergji Shkurti integrates bar, retail and hi-fi at Million Goods in Brooklyn Past the columns, the room has an array of tables arranged under the double-height ceiling. The rafters of the former space were painted white and a mezzanine from the private dining space juts out over a row of banquette seating. This mezzanine has a high boundary that provides privacy from below. At the back of the space is the bar, with a mirror backsplash and rosewood millwork above. Steel contrasts with wood and minimalist decor A sound system by Paxwave was installed in the space. The tablescapes were styled with sheer white cloths, which contrast with the stained-black chairs and the polished grey terrazzo flooring. The kitchen space sits under the private dining room and is hidden from the main space. More mirrors line the wall that divides the kitchen, while the windows opposite have metal grating. Street-facing windows bring light into the space, where mirrors were used to further diffuse the light Art and antiques were curated by Galería Córdoba . Formant Studio also designed its own studio in Mexico City , which it shares with photographer Fabián Martinez . Dezeen included Formant Studio in a list of notable Mexico designers earlier this year. The photography is by Fabián Martinez. content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: from a zip-up sofa bed to a chair that appears to wear a leather corset, the following seats have recently been published in our Showroom section. Modular seating systems, design-forward task chairs , amorphous lounge seats, and chairs shaped like leaves are also included. The following seats come from a variety of international design brands and manufacturers. Read on to discover a selection of our latest chairs. Nina lounge chair by Patricia Urquiola for Andreu World A glossy, hammered shell meets an amorphous upholstered seat in this 1970s-informed seat by designer Patricia Urquiola for furniture brand Andreu World . The Nina lounge chair has a compact yet expressive form also inspired by a 1656 portrait, where the subjects wear oversized, puffy skirts. Find out more about Nina › Vipp453 Swivel chair by Vipp A futuristic frame made from aluminium characterises this chic task chair by Danish brand Vipp . Vipp453 Swivel is available in a selection of seat and backrest upholstery options, and is intended for use in both workplaces and home offices. Find out more about Vipp453 Swivel › Cattle armchair by Gibson Karlo for Design By Them Sturdily stuffed cushions drape over a metal frame in this series of hard-meets-soft armchairs by design duo Gibson Karlo for furniture brand Design By Them . The Cattle armchair takes cues from makeshift agricultural structures found in rural Australia. Users can select between a glossy camel or wine-red coloured frame with matching upholstery fabric. Find out more about Cattle › Khoy sofa bed by Khoy Finnish company Khoy has developed king-, queen-, double- and single-sized beds that zip-up into correspondingly sized seats. The Khoy sofa bed comes in a selection of upholstery fabrics, each united by a round-cornered, bolster-like aesthetic designed to be comfortable in any style of interior. Find out more about Khoy › Ginkgo lounge chair by Anne-mette Bartholin and Morten Ernst for Cozmo The leaves of the ginkgo tree were referenced in the shape of the seat of this chair, as designed by Anne-Mette Bartholin and Morten Ernst for furniture brand Cozmo . The tri-legged Ginkgo lounge chair has a sculptural backrest comprising two lobes that meet in the centre, joining in the middle to create the bottom of the seat itself. Find out more about Ginkgo › Camelot seating system by Antonio Citterio for Flexform Architect Antonio Citterio worked with Italian brand Flexform on a seating system that comprises upholstered seats, cushions and backrests supported by a wood-and-metal frame. Camelot 's abundance of cushions make it distinctive, with contrasting or matching piping creating further texture. title: Victoria Beckham designs first homeware collection for Westwing

"Home is where some of life's most meaningful moments happen, and this collaboration felt The post Victoria Beckham designs first homeware collection for

content.source_text: Fashion designer Victoria Beckham has today unveiled her debut homeware collection for online platform Westwing, which includes shell-shaped butter dishes and shimmering cutlery. The Westwing collaboration is the first homeware project by Beckham , who founded her eponymous fashion label in 2008. Victoria Beckham has unveiled her debut homeware collection for Westwing "Home is where some of life's most meaningful moments happen, and this collaboration felt like a natural way to explore that world through the same lens of design, craftsmanship and attention to detail that defines everything we do as a brand," she said. According to Westwing, Beckham looked to the 19th-century Arts and Crafts movement when creating the collection of tableware, textiles and decorative objects characterised by organic forms and minimalist materials. Stainless-steel salt cellars are among the designs in the collection Among the pieces are stainless-steel butter dishes and salt cellars with a subtle seashell shape, as well as ribbed butter knives and hammered cutlery. A selection of plates and serving dishes were patterned with scale-like embossed elements, finished in porcelain and glass. A series of glasses features in the collection Textured glass was also used to create a series of wine glasses, champagne coupes and tumblers, as well as petite candle holders and amorphous vases for one or two stems. Crisp white napkins and coasters and shiny napkin rings follow a similar design. Read: David Beckham designs pair of Maseratis informed by his "passion for classic cars" "Signature details inspired by Victoria Beckham's ready-to-wear and accessories collections, including elegant chain motifs and jewellery-inspired accents, lend the pieces a sense of sophistication, while subtle shell elements introduce a touch of playfulness," said Westwing. The collection comes in bespoke green packaging that was conceived to reflect Beckham and Westwing's individual styles. The line has bespoke green packaging Partnerships between household designers and major brands have been in no short supply over the last few years. Last December, designer Gustaf Westman created a selection of Christmas tableware for IKEA , while glassware brand Iittala released mugs, bowls and plates designed in collaboration with media company Pokémon in April. The photography is courtesy of Westwing and Victoria Beckham. The post Victoria Beckham designs first homeware collection for Westwing appeared first on Dezeen .

title: Aesop explores scent and storytelling through fragrance installations around the world
summary: Skincare and fragrance brand Aesop has transformed its stores around the world into temporary perfumeries, using suspended paper and books to reference the fables behind its fragrances, as shown in this video carousel produced by Dezeen. content.source_text: Skincare and fragrance brand Aesop has transformed its stores around the world into temporary perfumeries , using suspended paper and books to reference the fables behind its fragrances, as shown in this video carousel produced by Dezeen. The Fragrant Fables campaign spanned more than 15 locations across 10 countries, showcasing Aesop 's collection of 12 perfumes , each developed around the idea of connecting fragrance with storytelling. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dezeen (@dezeen) Aesop combined scent and storytelling for its global fragrance installations As part of the campaign, Aesop created an exhibition at Tokyo National Museum's Hyokeikan, working with Japanese papermaker Hiroko Tanino and her studio Tesuki Washi Tanino to create bespoke washi paper installations. Based in a valley beside the Tokigawa River, the studio produces handmade washi paper from natural materials such as paper mulberry. Tanino is one of 11 artisans officially certified in traditional handmade papermaking in Japan. Paper, books and printed pages recur across the installations For the exhibition, Tanino's studio produced three different finishes of washi, each incorporating botanical ingredients or aromatic characteristics associated with one of the featured fragrances. The washi was formed into large hanging sheets, labyrinth-like structures and cascading shapes, which were suspended between the museum's marble columns and set against its geometric mosaic floors. Custom-made washi paper was folded into scroll-like forms Elsewhere, custom-made sheets were folded into scroll-like forms that undulated within timber frames. The Tokyo exhibition focused on three fragrances, separating their individual olfactory elements so visitors could smell the ingredients in isolation. Large scrolls displayed the fables as oversized, poem-like texts within the installations One display explored Aesop's newest fragrance Unforeseen Aer , using a large scroll made from bespoke washi that was held in a simple timber frame and surrounded by draped sheets of paper. Nutmeg, one of the fragrance's key ingredients, was incorporated directly into the paper to give its surface a textured finish. The experience concluded in a library displaying the written fables. Individual ingredients were displayed in isolation to smell individual components The wider Fragrant Fables campaign translated the fragrances and their ingredients into physical displays, using materials, objects and photography associated with each scent alongside the perfumes themselves. Each scent was given a fable-like name, with a story inspired by its ingredients printed on packaging designed to resemble the spines of books. Aromatics and raw ingredients were incorporated into the paper The fragrances were presented through three stages, starting with its ingredients in their raw form, followed by an interpretation of how those ingredients might smell in nature and finally the finished perfume. Across the locations, hundreds of printed paper sheets were suspended from ceilings, with some curled into loose, wave-like forms and others arranged in dense layers. The campaign marks the launch of the newest fragrance Unforeseen Aer Large scrolls displayed the fables as oversized, poem-like texts within the spaces, while stacks of white paper were used as plinths for the signature amber perfume bottles. In New York, live readings of the Fragrant Fables accompanied the installation, bringing the written stories into the spaces alongside the fragrance displays. The packaging was designed to resemble the spines of books A separate exhibition in Taiwan featured a wooden bookcase displaying books alongside isolated fragrance ingredients, while materials were presented in vessels around the installation. While the individual settings differ, paper, books, raw ingredients and amber bottles recurred throughout the campaign. In some locations, live readings brought the written fables into the perfumeries Aesop was established in Melbourne in 1987 and regularly works with local artisans, architects and designers on its stores and installations. Other Aesop projects featured on Dezeen include its Madrid store where four original cast-iron columns were retained as part of the interior, as well as its Knightsbridge store in London , which features a floor-to-ceiling installation made from gridded bars of cream-coloured soap. Earlier this year, the brand released its Aposē lamps with The Factory of Light installation at Milan design week, to mark the launch of its first-ever lighting designs. Partnership content This video carousel was produced for Aesop as part of a partnership. Find out more about our partnership content here . title: Garage Italia Gives the Fiat 500 an Electric Makeover
summary: The custom shop reimagines the Italian icon as an open-air electric runabout with woven seating, marine-grade materials, and nearly endless ways to make it your own

content.source_text: For yacht owners arriving in a Mediterranean port, finding a way to explore the surrounding town presents a different sort of transportation challenge. Zipping around on a Vespa might sound charming, but not everyone is made for the scooter life. Italian auto custom shop Garage Italia has created its own take on the classic Fiat 500 Spiaggina to give the yachting crowd a stylish alternative for getting around town. Photography courtesy of Garage Italia At its core, the Spiaggina is a humble Fiat 500. The “Cinquecento,” as it’s called in Italian, was created to be to Italy what the Mini Cooper was to Britain and the VW Beetle to Germany: small, basic transportation to bring mobility to the masses in the post-WWII era. The original Fiat 500 Jolly, also known as the Spiaggina, transformed that practical foundation into a doorless, open-air vehicle designed for leisurely drives along the Mediterranean coast. With its distinctive woven seating and removable canopy, it became a fixture of Italian resort culture. Photography courtesy of Garage Italia The Garage Italia remake distinguishes itself from its forebears by using electric power, with a rear-mounted motor delivering 13 horsepower and 60 lb-ft of torque. Hardly muscle-car statistics, but it’s enough to get the convertible up to more than 45 miles per hour. The 11 kWh battery gives it 87 miles of range on the WLTP test cycle. That should be more than enough for short trips around coastal towns, while electric power eliminates the need to carry additional gasoline aboard a yacht. Photography courtesy of Garage Italia But the other way this Jolly stands out is a bit more obvious: it’s extensively customizable. The sheet metal comes in 18 shades (off-menu colors are also an option), and the weather-resistant roof, cushions, and other components are available in dozens of fabric patterns from Italian textile company Mariaflora . The seats are handcrafted by Bonacina , an Italian furniture maker specializing in woven designs since 1889, and are available in natural or tinted rattan or Polycore, a composite material designed to withstand sun and salt exposure. Even the flooring takes its cues from the marine world, using durable, waterproof EVA material from ItalDek . And as with Porsches, Ferraris, and all sorts of other exotic machinery these days, you can configure your ideal version on its maker’s website . Photography courtesy of Garage Italia At €85,000 (around $97,000) before options and taxes, this electric runabout costs roughly as much as a BMW 7-Series. It’s a considerable departure from the Fiat 500’s affordable origins, but practicality has never been the point of the Spiaggina. With its open-air design, handcrafted materials, and seemingly endless customization options, Garage Italia has transformed a humble Italian icon into something closer to a bespoke design object on wheels. Photography courtesy of Garage Italia
content.original_title: Garage Italia Gives the Fiat 500 an Electric Makeover

title: A 5-Year-Old Kitchen Finds a New Home on Copenhagen’s Paper Island
summary: Garde Hvalsøe relocates an ash-and-zinc kitchen from Josephine Yaa Akuamoa’s studio to her waterfront home, where familiar materials take on a new context

content.source_text: The kitchen in Josephine Yaa Akuamoa’s new home on Copenhagen’s Paper Island spent its first five years in a workspace. Danish kitchen design company Garde Hvalsøe created it for Akuamoa’s studio , File Under Pop, before moving it into her home as the space’s central element . Photography by Heid Lerkenfeldt Built in ash on a zinc frame, the kitchen is Garde Hvalsøe’s Solid model. Long, wide planks run across the finger-jointed drawer fronts to show off the grain. Each drawer has chamfered sides, allowing them to sit close together and read as a single plank. The upper cabinets use the brand’s Koshi-do fronts, developed with Copenhagen-based OEO Studio to combine Japanese aesthetics with Danish craftsmanship. Photography by Heid Lerkenfeldt Søren Lundh Aagaard, partner and CEO of Garde Hvalsøe, had previously worked with Akuamoa on another home. “Bringing something previously used and lived in into a newly built space was both a challenge and a statement,” he says. Akuamoa points to the zinc framing, the lava sink, and the pale ash. “The three materials complement each other beautifully and age with grace,” she says. Photography by Heid Lerkenfeldt Before the kitchen went in, the team stripped the house back, demolishing the existing kitchen and its electrical installations, the bathroom, the wooden wall panels, and the staircase connecting all three floors. The kitchen and dining area now take up the ground floor, with bedrooms on the middle level and an adaptable room at the top. One side of the house looks out over the sea and sky, and the other onto a shared garden. Garde Hvalsøe also made the bespoke ash wardrobes. Photography by Heid Lerkenfeldt Paper Island served as an armory for the Danish navy under Christian IV and later as a paper warehouse for the national newspapers. The new building’s contemporary architecture draws on the island’s historic harbor warehouses. Wooden maritime gates frame the structure, and a diagonal element in the roof references Copenhagen’s harbor architecture. Akuamoa’s interior takes its cues from the water and open sky on every side of the island. The house uses nearly equal parts wood, raw stone, and ceramics. Ash runs throughout, and the limestone echoes the sandstone harbor walls and the yellow brick of the neighboring buildings. Photography by Heid Lerkenfeldt
content.original_title: A 5-Year-Old Kitchen Finds a New Home on Copenhagen’s Paper Island

content.source_text: Restaurateur Josh Greenspan and furniture company USM have created VV's Cocktail Room in Manhattan, a small space wrapped almost entirely in Steel Blue USM Haller modular shelving and informed by Greenspan's visits to Japan and Hong Kong . Named after Greenspan 's daughter Vivienne, VV's Cocktail Room (VV's) is located in Chelsea and contains just 18 seats to mimic the intimacy of an omakase cocktail experience, where bartenders lead a multi-course tasting or cocktail menu. Josh Greenspan and USM have completed Manhattan cocktail bar VV's Cocktail Room The project stems from Greenspan's ongoing conversations with USM, which frequently collaborates with designers to outfit spaces and create installations from the flexible panelling system. "I started imagining something a little wild – a space built entirely from the USM system, pushing its modularity in unexpected ways," Greenspan told Dezeen. "I'm thrilled that the USM team embraced the idea and came along for the ride." The space is wrapped in a dark blue USM Haller System Visitors to the bar pass a glass block wall partition to enter the space. Inside, navy blue USM panels form the walls that surround the space and wrap behind the bar, where they jut out into shelving. A dark walnut wood was used for the bar top and tables, which is offset by bar seats upholstered in a burgundy fabric and banquette seating built by Greenspan's father, Michael Greenspan, covered in a similar hue. Read: Norwegian designers use reclaimed materials to customise USM Haller furniture Other details include a wavy pendant light by New York lighting studio Studio Kawabi that spans the length of the bar and a painting by Japanese artist Keita Morimoto affixed to the back wall. The space was informed by the "visual language" of Tokyo and Hong Kong, according to the team, and aims for the futuristic aesthetic between the 1960s and 1990s of the two metropolises. The panels expand into shelves behind the bar Greenspan worked with USM's director of architectural development, Ian Mutschelkanus, to create an interior where the USM Haller System serves as "the architectural framework of the space" rather than simply being inserted. "Rather than furnishing the interiors, USM defines them," said the team. "Each composition of the modular system demonstrates its remarkable versatility beyond furniture and into the realm of spatial design." It was informed by the "futuristic aesthetic" of Tokyo and Hong Kong between the 1960s and 1990s Greenspan partnered with James Beard Award-winning bartender Neal Bodenheimer and longtime friend Vincent Favela for the omakase cocktail program, while his mother, five-time James Beard Award winner Dorie Greenspan , created a bar snack menu. Past spaces that used USM panels for walls include retail space for Coperni in Paris . Other recently completed bars in New York include Odd Ball by House Under Magic and a second Brooklyn location for concept shop and wine bar Million Goods designed by Gjergji Shkurti . content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: Australian workplace brand Zenith has designed the expressive Profondo seating collection, informed by the spirit of 1970s Italian furniture. The Profondo collection includes a sofa and a standalone armchair, with sculptural forms that take cues from the "generous proportions and unapologetic sense of style" synonymous with Italian furniture created during the 1970s. The Profondo collection includes a sofa and a standalone armchair Each piece is characterised by a pillowy seat and flanged edges, and can be upholstered in a selection of Zenith textiles and leather. Alternatively, customers can request their own materials to be used to upholster the seating. Each piece is characterised by a pillowy seat and flanged edges "Profondo is more than a place to sit," said Zenith. "It is a statement piece designed to shape the character of a space, creating warmth, presence and a lasting impression – it is comfort elevated, presence amplified, a bold expression of contemporary design inspired by one of furniture's most iconic design eras." content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: Australian studio Gibson Karlo has created an all- metal iteration of its Twill chair for furniture brand Design By Them , maintaining the seat's plasticine-like aesthetic. Designers Sarah Gibson and Nicholas Karlovasitis of Gibson Karlo looked to the nostalgic appearance of a fresh pack of plasticine when designing the original timber version of the chair , which launched in 2022. Aluminium containing at least 30 per cent recycled content was used for the chair The new all-aluminium iteration shares the visual language and stackability of its wooden forerunner, while its uncoated, hand-burnished raw aluminium finish gives it added dimension. The designers envisage inevitable marks and scratches inflicted during day-to-day use to become part of the finish over time, gradually developing a natural and distinctive patina. The lack of a top coat means that the surface cannot be chipped or scratched through, allowing the chair to be easily maintained and restored. An optional seat pad can be added for enhanced comfort across long periods of sitting "As industrial designers, we got super geeky detailing the metal version of Twill to match the timber version," said Gibson Karlo. "There are custom extrusions in places you wouldn't expect, and introducing metal also opened up a new world of colour, functionality and playfulness – the range was inspired by plasticine strips, after all." Design By Them used aluminium containing a minimum of 30 per cent recycled content for the chairs, which are produced in a 100 per cent solar-powered facility and carry a five-year warranty. content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: designer Piergiorgio Cazzaniga and furniture brand Andreu World have added extra cushioning to one of their successful seating designs to make Capri Comfort – a minimalist executive chair that can now support longer periods of sitting. Capri Comfort is an evolution of the Capri line of lounge and executive chairs, which have a light and pure expression defined by a slim upholstered back and seat and minimal visible mechanisms. The Capri Comfort chairs are enhanced with extra cushioning For Capri Comfort, Cazzaniga and Andreu World built out the seat and backrest with next-generation high-density foams, providing ergonomic support for modern executive offices, meeting rooms and home workspaces. "Without altering the minimalist silhouette of the classic model, this design conveys a sense of understated luxury that invites long meetings or moments of reflection," said Andreu World. The chairs have a minimalist form The Capri Comfort chair is available with a choice of three backrest heights – low, medium or high – and three swivel bases, either with gliders or casters. All versions include a tilting mechanism and pneumatic height adjustment to support dynamic sitting and enable a healthy recline, and come in a huge choice of fabrics including options from leading textile brands Kvadrat and Camira. content.source_text: Anonymous London design duo City Girls creates one-off lighting out of reclaimed lace, coat hangers and scale models scavenged from eBay, Facebook Marketplace and the side of the road. City Girls (stylised as city.girls.xp) is the studio and alias of two unnamed artists, who started making lamps together two years ago after bonding over a shared love of old knickknacks. London-based City Girls creates one-off lighting out of reclaimed materials The north London duo are making a name for themselves by crafting one-of-a-kind pieces out of everything from discarded sequins to chains and feathers sourced second-hand on the internet or in real life, which at one point left them rooting through the debris of a smashed-up toy on the street. Once each lamp is complete, it is affectionately named something like Pamela, Jean or Allegra, to give it a distinct identity. Zoe is a tall, feathered floor lamp Among the duo's growing collection is Zoe , a tall floor lamp characterised by a gridded metal frame wrapped in old jersey fabric, and embellished with goose feathers extracted from a hat. Sabine , the pair's first working lamp, features a base crafted out of a fragment of an old chrome chair, topped with a translucent shade made of a fibreglass model boat. City Girls deliberately work with a mishmash of materials Lola and Nina are a pair of boxy lamps cloaked with Glomesh sequins, a material that was also draped over the metallic Raquel . City Girls has previously described the process of cobbling together its lighting as akin to the act of getting dressed, throwing together a mismatched outfit. This visual style is especially clear in curving Virginia , made from old metal chair legs and crowned with a swan-like arched green head. The duo has been anonymously making lamps together for two years The duo also has a penchant for objects that show signs of fabrication through welds and seams, or anything else that nods to their former purpose. City Girls named themselves after a Victorian novel by radical author Margaret Harkness called A City Girl, which details vivid descriptions of 1880s London streets. Read: Billy Easter's Gel Lamp shifts colour using transposable slides The studio has been steadily growing its presence in the UK capital. Over the summer, local interior designer Jermaine Gallacher curated the exhibition Ten Lamps by City Girls at the Ragged School, London Bridge. City Girls named themselves after a Victorian novel by Margaret Harkness During this month's London Design Festival, a wealth of other collectible design was on display in various city-wide exhibitions. Among them was the second-ever Studio Iron show in South Kensington, curated by artist Isamaya Ffrench and featuring pieces by designers including Andu Masebo, Barnaby Lewis and Jane Wright. The photography is courtesy of City Girls. The post City Girls lamps are designed to look like outfits casually thrown together appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: a radiator with interchangeable accessories informed by workbench pegboards is among seven new products featured on Dezeen Showroom. Grid radiator by Elisa Ossino for Tubes Pegboards found in garages and workshops informed the appearance and functionality of this modular radiator by designer Elisa Ossina for Italian brand Tubes . Grid comprises a recycled aluminium board pocked with circular holes, into which hooks, pegs, rails, small shelves and mirrors can be slotted. The radiator was recently featured on Dezeen Showroom alongside an undulating wall panel made from cork and a XXX. Read on to see more of the latest products: Geocode collection by VitrA Tiles Naturally quarried varieties of stone from around the world inform the appearance of tiles in this collection by surfaces brand VitrA Tiles . The Geocode collection is made from porcelain and comes in eight patterns and three size formats. Find out more about Geocode › CorkVector Panel by Gencork Portuguese brand GenCork has released a wall panel made from cork that features a three-dimensional design made using the Corkvectors algorithm, created by the brand's creative director Le Brimet. The CorkVector Panel aims to create visual interest in interiors as well as providing sound dampening properties thanks to its absorbent solid cork material. Find out more about CorkVector Panel › Nyla leather chair by Omidi Furniture brand Omidi has released a task chair elevated by its leather upholstery. The Nyla leather chair sits on an aluminium alloy base, with users able to select base types, backrest heights and colours. Find out more about Nyla › Metacode tiles by VitrA Tiles Surfaces brand VitrA Tiles' Metacode tile series unites the visual qualities of concrete and rusted metal. Wall and floor tiles comprise the collection, and their slip resistance makes them suitable for diverse interiors. Find out more about Metacode › ReSKU 2.0 fabric by Camira British textile brand Camira has released a new fabric named ReSKU 2.0 that contains 66 per cent recycled wool, 21 per cent flax and 13 per cent recycled polyamide. The material was originally released in 2024 to mark the brand's 50th anniversary, and was informed by its 1998 ReSKU fabric, made from recycled army jumpers. Find out more about ReSKU 2.0 › Laminex Colour Collection 2027 by Laminex Australian surface brand Laminex has released its 2027 Colour Collection , which comprises ten new finishes that recall various aspects of the nation's natural landscapes. The range is made up of four wood grains and six block colours, which can be used for various applications throughout interiors. content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: ITO Design let function drive form when creating this task chair , which features a distinctive sculptural back, for office brand Narbutas . The Silora chair features a striking backrest, with two petals that wrap around from the front, continuing the organic curve of the seating design's adaptive dual lumbar support. The Silora task chair has a sculptural back The chair is intended to combine aesthetics and ergonomics, in response to demand for workspaces that are cosier and less formal than their predecessors. "The Silora chair's design is driven by function – its asymmetric lumbar support frame becomes the basis for its distinctive form," said ITO Design . "By wrapping the mesh around the structure, the design conceals technical complexity while maintaining visual interest, resulting in a unique, refined 3D backrest shape." The chair is intended to combine ergonomics and aesthetics In addition to the heigh-adjustable lumbar support, the Silora chair includes a synchronous mechanism with five locking positions for the seat and backrest, a forward tilt mechanism that encourages more active sitting, and 2D or 3D adjustable armrests. The seat and backrest are available in a range of fabric options, including Narbutas' new 3D Rhythm mesh, which has a soft, three-dimensional texture and comes in a sophisticated palette of darker colours. content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: surfaces brand VitrA Tiles has developed V-Flex, a method of installation that aims to meet evolving architectural expectations by being simple and adhesive-free. The company's V-Flex system provides a quick and simple installation option for projects that seek efficiency, the flexibility to make changes over time, or the ability to preserve the existing floor beneath. V-Flex allows for quick, adhesive-free installation The system uses Välinge’s Ceraloc locking technology, with tongue-and-groove edges that allow tiles to slot into place, enabling precise alignment and even grout lines with reduced drying time. In addition, the installation method provides good acoustic performance. The V-Flex method provides flexibility VitrA Tiles recommends this method for use when installing tiles in interiors spanning retail spaces, showrooms, offices, hotels, education facilities and commercial spaces. content.source_text: Scottish design studio Filament has developed a financial learning platform for children based around a toy egg that reintroduces physical interaction to the process of saving and spending money . The conceptual project is Filament 's response to the increasing digitisation of money, which can make it harder for parents to teach children important financial lessons. Filament has developed a modern version of a piggy bank for kids "When money becomes invisible, the core lessons attached to it disappear, too," the Glasgow-based studio explained. "We are losing the physical friction that used to teach us the value of earning and saving. Nest Egg is designed to replace that missing friction with a physical platform that literally grows up alongside the child." The system is based around a toy egg and an accompanying app Filament set out to develop a hardware solution that evolves over time, providing tactile forms of interaction that gamify the process of saving money and move it away from a purely screen-based activity. According to the studio's co-founder Craig Lynn, Nest Egg takes its name from an expression commonly used to refer to financial savings, while its playful form makes it easier for children to engage with. "We noticed that physical, tangible objects are important when educating children," Lynn told Dezeen. "The shift to digital transactions is robbing them of that piggy bank smash moment enjoyed by previous generations." Children can earn stars by completing tasks The product acts as a smart alternative to the traditional refrigerator star chart, where kids gain stars for good behaviour or completing tasks. The main element is a physical egg that opens to release a character hidden inside once the child has collected a set number of digital stars. Stars can be earned by undertaking chores or achieving developmental milestones set out by parents using a companion app. Read: Wing-See Yau designs Tamagotchi-like toy to help make reading fun This process helps build anticipation and teaches children the benefits of delayed gratification, which is important when trying to understand saving. The fracturing egg evokes familiar toys like Hatchimals, but rather than becoming redundant once it hatches, the hidden toy then transitions into a tangible user interface. The toy figure incorporates NFC technology that allows children to access an accrued allowance when tapped against the parent's smartphone, as well as unlocking narrative animations relating to good financial habits. The egg opens to release a hidden toy once the child has collected a set number of digital stars The egg remains with the child until they reach a stage of financial maturity set by parents in the app, at which point it undergoes a final mechanical crack that reveals their own real-world debit card. "The final crack represents a physical graduation from a simulated environment into the real banking ecosystem," claimed Filament. "It is the modern design equivalent of smashing the porcelain piggy bank. But instead of loose pennies spilling out, it hands young adults the tools for true financial independence." The toy character incorporates NFC technology that allows children to access an accrued allowance Lynn pointed out that, while some financial providers in the UK like Starling and GoHenry offer prepaid bank cards for teenagers, there was nothing aimed at helping younger users take their first steps into financial literacy. The project uses behavioural economics to subtly introduce lessons such as the benefits of saving, while also levelling up over time to retain the child's interest and reward consistent good habits. The system was designed to teach financial literacy The studio is looking to partner with a suitable bank to support further development of the Nest Egg concept, which would require accompanying infrastructure to transform it into a fully functioning product. Filament was founded in 2014 by Lynn, alongside fellow Glasgow School of Art graduates Gregor Aikman and Danny Kane. The studio aims to help businesses turn ideas into commercially ready products that align with genuine human needs. Other technology-aided education toys that have recently been featured on Dezeen include a Tamagotchi-style reading helper and Yoto's screen-free audio player . title: Harvard University transforms waste wool into cladding for retrofits
summary: Grinham Research Group at Harvard University has developed an insulating cladding tile made from waste wool, which was presented at this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale. content.source_text: Grinham Research Group at Harvard University has developed an insulating cladding tile made from waste wool , which was presented at this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale . In an installation named Upcycling Wool Ecologies, Grinham Research Group showcased its tiles on a timber frame in Oslo 's Sofienberg Church as part of the triennale's main exhibition, which takes place from 17 September to 1 October. Grinham Research Group saw the potential in wool's insulative, fire-resistant and antibacterial properties, and wanted to save it from being discarded as a residual material in the agricultural and textile industries. Harvard University's Grinham Research Group has developed a wall tile made from waste wool The group also wanted to develop a material that could help facilitate building reuse. Their solution was a tile with a multi-layer design that can be applied to the exterior of buildings, avoiding the costly work of digging into a wall to upgrade its insulation. Made from recycled wool, the tiles have a low-density back panel that acts as an insulating board and a denser outer panel with greater durability and weather resistance. The cladding tiles were showcased at Oslo Architecture Triennale "We need pluralistic solutions that reflect the complexity of nature," Grinham Research Group founder Jonathan Grinham told Dezeen. "Architecture can actively design these new industrial ecologies that retain the value of materials, skilled labour, and existing industries while creating scalable retrofit solutions," he continued. "By transforming waste wool into durable exterior cladding, biogenic carbon captured through grass, sheep, and wool can be retained in the built environment, while the same material improves the performance and extends the useful life of existing buildings." Read: Finnish company launches "world's most carbon-storing building material" To make the tiles, wool is treated with an alkaline solution that partially breaks down its keratin proteins, before a mechanical process further separates the material into a liquid. Citric acid is then added, which, when heated with the wool-derived keratin, binds residual and unprocessed wool fibres into a rigid composite without the need for a petrochemical resin. According to the group, around 1.95 billion kilograms of raw wool are produced each year, with approximately 60 per cent used for wool clothing manufacturing. Unused wool is typically stockpiled, burned or buried. A dense, durable layer is placed over an insulating panel "The decline of domestic textile manufacturing, competition from synthetics, and selective grading have left enormous quantities of wool without a viable market," said Grinham. "Wool has lost its economic value, but not its material properties," he continued. "We're developing new chemistries that transform this overlooked natural polymer into a useful biocomposite for building insulation and cladding." Grinham Research Group pressed the tiles into a fluted design For the Oslo Architecture Triennale installation, Grinham Research Group sourced preconsumer waste wool from the American Woolen Company in Connecticut. It used a mixture of naturally coloured and dyed fibres, which resulted in the variations in tile colours. The tiles showcased at the event featured a fluted surface design, but the material could be pressed into different shapes and designs. Other material innovations that have recently featured on Dezeen include a wall surface made from forestry industry offcuts that is almost pure carbon, and a dress made from living mycelium that can repair itself . The photography and video are courtesy of Grinham Research Group. Oslo Architecture Triennale takes place from 17 September to 1 October at Sofienberg Church in Oslo, Norway. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. The post Harvard University transforms waste wool into cladding for retrofits appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: After Dyson recently hit headlines with its tech-driven toothbrush , we revisit eight projects from the Dezeen archives that add polish to the everyday dental tool. Accessories by Landor & Fitch Accessories is a collection of toothbrush add-ons, designed specifically for people with dexterity challenges. It has more than 142 designs, including handles with chunky grips and ridged edges, which make them easier to hold. They also come in a range of textures and colours, which lend them a decorative, homeware-like appearance. The designer said the project was sparked by accessible design research that had found "users hacking toothbrushes in functional but extremely uncomfortable ways". Find out more about Accessories › Sustainable Sonic Toothbrush by Suri One of the most recognisable toothbrush brands on the market today, Suri was launched to tackle global dependence on plastic toothbrushes. In 2022, it released the Sustainable Sonic Toothbrush, with an aluminium body and plant-based brush head that are both recyclable . More recently, it updated its design with Suri 2.0 , which has features such as a pressure sensor and wireless induction charging. "We wanted to create a brush that champions design, performance and sustainability without compromise," Suri told Dezeen. Find out more about Sustainable Sonic Toothbrush › Benjamin Brush by BleepBleeps and MAP Designed to make brushing teeth more enticing for children , the Benjamin Brush featured an integrated speaker that played music for the recommended two-minute brushing time. The prototype product had a blue silicone body, designed to be easily held, and interchangeable "pom pom" brush heads that added a playful look. Find out more about Benjamin Brush › Dyson CameraJet by Dyson Dyson 's first dental hygiene product is an electric, tech-driven toothbrush with an integrated mouthwash jet. Named the Dyson CameraJet, the product has a camera set near the oscillating brush head, which identifies gaps between teeth and negates the need for flossing. "By combining a camera, machine learning, precision fluid dynamics, advanced brushing technologies, connectivity and WiFi, Dyson CameraJet introduces an entirely new way to keep your mouth healthy," said founder James Dyson. Find out more about Dyson CameraJet › Misoka by Kosho Ueshima The Misoka toothbrush is designed to clean teeth without toothpaste. Instead, users just need to dip the brush in water. This is because the bristles are coated in nano-sized mineral ions that, after being loosened by water, are transferred to the teeth. These ions are then able to remove stains and form a protective coating on the enamel, according to its creator, Kosho Ueshima. Find out more about Misoka › Ara by Kolibree The Ara toothbrush was launched in 2017 with integrated artificial intelligence , intended to help users improve their oral health. A low-energy Bluetooth connection linked it to an app, which displayed brushing data including frequency, duration and areas covered. Find out more about Ara › The post Six designs that freshen up the humble toothbrush appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: wallpapers, tiles and surfaces are all among recent wall and floor coverings published on Dezeen Showroom . The selection includes wallpapers based on designs by William Morris , marbles with dramatic and unusual blue veining, and square-format tiles designed to look handmade. A spectrum of international design brands and companies have listed their products on our Dezeen Showroom section. Read on to find out more. Omogenea surface collection by Dimore Surfaces The texture and appearance of volcanic rock is the bedrock of this moody surface collection by Italian brand Dimore Surfaces . The Omogenea surface collection has a matt, fine-grained appearance that comes in a variety of neutral colourways. Find out more about Omogenea › The Unfinished Works by Morris & Co Heritage English brand Morris & Co has released a new range of fabrics and wallpapers based on designs by William Morris and his collaborator John Henry Dearle, which are kept at The Huntington museum, USA. Morris' trademark botanical motifs spread across the surfaces of the pieces in The Unfinished Works , faithfully recreated by the brand's enduring Chiswick studio. Find out more about The Unfinished Works › Grace tiles by Ceramiche Keope Limestone is mimicked in Italian brand Ceramiche Keope 's light, neutral Grace tiles . Stone quarried in Saint Antoine d'Auberoche in France was the specific reference, due to its cloudy aesthetic and use in the construction of historic buildings. Find out more about Grace › Pangea Blue marble by Antolini Italian stone brand Antolini has released a distinctive variety of marble named Pangea Blue , featuring vivid areas of striking blue veining. Its dynamic and eye-catching surface makes it appropriate for use in main bedrooms and bathrooms. Find out more about Pangea Blue › Breccia Rosa 4D slab tile by Iris Ceramica Italian manufacturer Iris Ceramica Group 's Breccia Rosa 4D slab tile replicates the dusty rose-coloured nature of a natural marble quarried near Verona, Italy. A background of light pink is streaked with beige and white striations, while its porcelain materiality makes it versatile in application. Find out more about Breccia Rosa 4D › Eterna Nouveau wallpapers by Astek Oversized botanical motifs create a distinctive aesthetic in this series of wallpapers by US brand Astek . Eterna Nouveau wallpapers comprise prints based on aquatic, carnivorous and garden flowers, each available in a choice of colourways. Find out more about Eterna Nouveau › Lume tiles by Marazzi Italian tile manufacturer Marazzi 's Lume tiles now feature a square format, while exhibiting the same handmade style appearance as the rest of the range. Users can select between Bone, Caramel, Emerald, Ocean, White, Blue, Green, Turquoise colours, and either the usual square or one featuring a subtle leaf-shaped motif. Find out more about Lume › Milano Impressions surfaces by PoliLam US brand PoliLam looked to Italian stone types and terrazzo to inform its Milano Impressions surfaces . These can be used to line rooms or in the production of furniture, with its selection of neutral colourways and styles allowing it further versatility. Find out more about Milano Impressions › Laminex Colour Collection 2027 by Laminex Ten new colours and patterns comprise Australian surface brand Laminex 's 2027 Colour Collection , with each informed by the country's varied landscapes. Four wood grains and six block colours make up the newly released range, from dusty Red Centre to moody Smoked Bluegum. Find out more about Laminex Colour Collection 2027 › Dezeen Showroom Dezeen Showroom offers an affordable space for brands to launch new products and showcase their designers and projects to Dezeen's huge global audience. For more details email showroom@dezeen.com . Dezeen Showroom is an example of partnership content on Dezeen. Find out more about partnership content here . content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: Australian surface brand Laminex has released its 2027 Colour Collection, adding 10 new designs inspired by the country's landscape to its laminate range. Six solid colours and four wood grains make up the Laminex Colour Collection 2027 , ranging from the alpine white of High Country to the deep ochre of Red Centre, and from moody Smoked Bluegum to gentle Raw Spotted Gum. The Laminex Colour Collection 2027 adds four wood grains and six solid colours. Photo by Bunston Architecture The wood grains are reproduced using Laminex 's AbsoluteGrain technology to capture the tactile authenticity of timber as well as its TrueScale technology to eliminate repeats. Laminex's surface collection is made up of low-pressure melamine and high-pressure laminate, which it has been manufacturing in Australia for over 90 years. The colours are drawn from the Australian landscape. Photo by Bunston Architecture The brand says the Colour Collection 2027 balances nuance, warmth and depth, bringing together a curated palette that works in harmony in either residential or commercial settings. "The most enduring interiors aren't built around a single hero colour or material," said Laminex. "They're created through palettes that work together effortlessly." "Colour Collection 2027 was designed with exactly that in mind – giving designers, makers and homeowners the confidence to create spaces that feel considered today while remaining timeless for years to come." title: Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style AI agent
