content.source_text: Meta is creating a tiny, portable Muse Charm device for carrying around the company's AI agent, chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has announced. Produced by Meta's new design team, led by former Apple design chief Alan Dye, the device resembles an Apple Watch but with a small lanyard instead of a strap. Meta is set to launch the Muse Charm AI device A customisable cartoon character occupies the entire two-inch screen, prompting comparisons to an AI-powered Tamagotchi . This avatar acts as the cutesy embodiment of the Muse AI agent the company launched earlier this month, billed as a "personal assistant" that can automate daily admin such as writing emails and booking appointments, rather than just answering questions. The Muse Charm features a fingerprint sensor in the corner that users can tap to start talking to the AI, with a built-in 5G modem for Wi-Fi-less internet access. There also appears to be a small camera, allowing the agent to take in information about the user's surroundings. Read: Sweekar is world's "first emotionally intelligent" pocket-sized pet Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg teased the product, set to go on sale ahead of the Christmas holidays, during the company's annual Meta Connect showcase, which also saw the launch of two new smart glasses . "We've packed a lot of technology into this little guy," Zuckerberg said in his keynote. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you." It houses the company's Muse AI agent The avatar can be set to a menagerie of characters, from a Muse mascot known as "Jolly" to an anthropomorphic mango, a labradoodle and a piece of toast wearing sunglasses. Combined with playing into Gen Z's love for bag charms and Labubu-style plushies , the device seems to be pitched at a younger demographic, who are already more likely to see AI bots as companions rather than mere helpers . Meta's Muse AI has been downloaded more than 2.5 million times since its launch in early September, according to Sensor Tower data, and is set to be added to Meta smart glasses over the coming months. The company does not have the best track record when it comes to handling private and sensitive information. Read: Meta unveils lightweight VR glasses and camera-free AI glasses at Connect 2026 Meta Glasses have faced backlash for being used to film people – especially women – without their consent, and for sharing private videos captured by users with subcontractors in Kenya as part of training Muse AI. These issues may be compounded by adding an AI agent into the mix and giving it eyes and ears. In the two weeks since its launch, Muse AI has already been accused of reading users' private messages , attempting to hack their Gmail and nudging them to share their passport information and bank account details . Using cuteness as a way to encourage users to adopt a product they might otherwise be sceptical of is not new . Robotics companies have been following a similar playbook in recent years, with launches including fluffy robots that clip onto a handbag and emotionally intelligent AI pets . The post Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style AI agent appeared first on Dezeen .

title: ReSKU 2.0 fabric by Camira

content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: recycled wool and renewable flax come together in a warm melange of colour in British textile brand Camira 's ReSKU 2.0 fabric . ReSKU 2.0 was launched to celebrate Camira 's 50th anniversary in 2024 and inspired by the brand's original 1998 ReSKU fabric, made from recycled army jumpers. ReSKU 2.0 combines recycled wool with flax For ReSKU 2.0, the brand combined recycled wool and polyamide generated from its own manufacturing waste with harvested flax, a renewable, low-carbon crop that grows with little water. The process is conducted through Camira's textile recycling arm, iinouiio, which makes use of advanced textile reprocessing techniques, and the fabric it yields has a rich, tweedy look that showcases the natural colour variation of recycled materials. The fabric shows off the beauty of recycled materials ReSKU 2.0 is available in a choice of 24 shades. Camira says it is suitable for applications such as seating, curtains and panels, in settings including modern workplaces and hospitality venues. "More than a fabric, ReSKU 2.0 represents a commitment to circular thinking and responsible manufacturing," said Camira. "By turning production waste into a valuable resource, it demonstrates how heritage, innovation and sustainability can work together to create a textile that is recycled, renewable and ready for the future." Product details: Product: ReSKU 2.0 Brand: Camira Contact: victoria.kulczycki@camirafabrics.com Materials: 66 per cent recycled wool, 21 per cent flax, 13 per cent recycled polyamide Colours/finishes: 24 colours Dimensions: 1400 millimetres Dezeen Showroom Dezeen Showroom offers an affordable space for brands to launch new products and showcase their designers and projects to Dezeen's huge global audience. For more details email showroom@dezeen.com . Dezeen Showroom is an example of partnership content on Dezeen. Find out more about partnership content here . title: Lasvit suspends chandelier of flowers preserved in glass in Napa Valley home
summary: Czech lighting brand Lasvit has preserved the forms of dried flowers inside hand-blown glass to create a large chandelier in a home in Napa Valley, California, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen for the brand. Called Herbarium, the installation was made from dozens of individually crafted glass pieces suspended at different heights above The post Lasvit suspends chandelier of flowers preserved in glass in Napa Valley home appeared first on

content.source_text: Czech lighting brand Lasvit has preserved the forms of dried flowers inside hand-blown glass to create a large chandelier in a home in Napa Valley, California, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen for the brand. Called Herbarium, the installation was made from dozens of individually crafted glass pieces suspended at different heights above the home's main living area. Lasvit installed its Herbarium chandelier in a Napa Valley residence Some of the glass pieces are long and slender, while others form rounded, teardrop-like shapes, creating a loose cascade that extends towards the floor. Each piece was made by placing dried flowers and plants beneath molten glass. The heat consumes the organic material while leaving its impression embedded in the crystal. The glass pieces preserve impressions of dried flowers and plants "Our glassworks are surrounded by wild nature," said Lasvit chief designer Mária Čulenová, who led the creative team behind the installation. "With Herbarium, we wanted to capture this wilderness so that anyone could take home a piece of this landscape – a piece of the meadow, preserved in glass." The chandelier echoes the vegetation surrounding the Napa Valley home The chandelier occupies the centre of the double-height living room, where it hangs in front of a large window overlooking the surrounding landscape. Its clear and amber-toned pieces catch both daylight and artificial illumination, casting irregular shadows across the pale walls. The glass pieces cast irregular shadows across the living room walls The residence sits in Napa Valley, surrounded by vineyards, wildflowers and a stream running through the property. Inside, the Herbarium installation echoes the vegetation visible through the windows, preserving its forms in glass. Dozens of individually crafted glass pieces create the cascading chandelier Herbarium is part of Lasvit Icons, a collection of the Czech glassmaker's designs adapted into modular systems. Rather than producing every installation entirely from scratch, the system uses individually handcrafted components that can be configured for different interiors, from private homes to larger architectural projects. Herbarium forms part of Lasvit's modular Icons collection Founded in 2007 by Leon Jakimič, Lasvit specialises in bespoke lighting, glass installations and architectural glass, combining traditional Bohemian glassmaking with contemporary design. Other projects by Lasvit featured on Dezeen include its 2025 Soaked in Light exhibition , which featured a splash-shaped installation and glass light imprinted with a tree branch. Partnership content This video was produced for Lasvit as part of a partnership. Find out more about our partnership content here . title: Jesse Butterfield marries paper and metal in A Veiled Boundary exhibition
summary: Sewn paper and hand-hammered steel sit side by side in these lighting pieces and stools by designer Jesse Butterfield, displayed during London Design Festival 2026. The aptly named Sew Paper Lighting and Stool Des Pois series premiered during Butterfield's A Veil Boundary exhibition, curated by Alex Tieghi-Walker, in the city-wide festival's Brompton Design District. The paper lanterns The post Jesse Butterfield marries paper and metal in A Veile

content.source_text: Sewn paper and hand-hammered steel sit side by side in these lighting pieces and stools by designer Jesse Butterfield, displayed during London Design Festival 2026. The aptly named Sew Paper Lighting and Stool Des Pois series premiered during Butterfield 's A Veil Boundary exhibition, curated by Alex Tieghi-Walker , in the city-wide festival's Brompton Design District . A series of stools and paper lighting comprised the exhibition The paper lanterns continue the centuries-old tradition of using the material to make lampshades, as a result of its physical lightness as well as its translucency. To realise the Sew Paper Lighting series, Butterfield teamed up with The Paper Foundation , a Lake District-based paper mill, founded by sixth-generation papermaker Mark Cropper. Light shades are stitched together "We got to visit The Paper Foundation and see their process, then select six or seven different papers," said Butterfield. "We went through their archive and chose what we thought would have nice drapage and lighting effects, as well as selecting different papers for different applications." The paper used in the lamps is handmade in the Lake District Slim stainless steel frames dictate each piece's general form and purpose: from pendants and wall lights to floor and table lamps. Beyond this, the lanterns strewn around the space comprise folded, draped and otherwise physically manipulated handmade paper, hand-stitched into amorphous shapes. Read: RCA design students exercise restraint in One Tool One Stool exhibition In dialogue with the paper lamps, Butterfield's Stool Des Pois series explores the sheet metal's capacity to behave in a similar way to paper. A paper model was the natural starting point for the stool, which was then scaled up and recreated in steel, heated and hammered by hand until a thinness and lightness akin to paper was achieved. The stools are decorated with a hammered texture and singed spots The stools are based on the same initial model and dimensions, with natural variations owing to their handmade nature, ensuring that no two are entirely alike. Further distinction is made through the polka dot patterning, a result of intentional blackening of the metal which introduces further visual interest while telling the story of their manufacturing process. Both items feature elements made from or informed by paper and metal "This is the first time where I'm leaving the dots on the surface," said Butterfield. "They come from the making process – in the past I've sanded them away, but I wanted to bring them in now as they fit with the theme of things being perfectly imperfect," he added, nodding to the leitmotif of this year's Brompton Design District programme. Elsewhere in the district, RCA students exhibited a series of stools created with a single tool and Isamaya French launched her second-ever Studio Iron show . The photography is by Andy Stagg . A Veil Boundary was on show from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival . See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. title: MSCHF twists Lexus electric cars into absurd shapes in New York
summary: Brooklyn creative studio MSCHF has created two twisted and bent versions of Lexus electric cars for New York City's fall art week, which the studio said is a play on the automotive industry's concept car prototypes. The Motomorphosis sculptures, called Circle Car and Twisted Car, were installed at Hudson Yards event space Chelsea Industrial next The post MSCHF twists Lexus electric cars into absurd shapes in New York appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Brooklyn creative studio MSCHF has created two twisted and bent versions of Lexus electric cars for New York City's fall art week, which the studio said is a play on the automotive industry's concept car prototypes. The Motomorphosis sculptures, called Circle Car and Twisted Car, were installed at Hudson Yards event space Chelsea Industrial next to their functional counterparts, a Lexus RZ450e and Lexus RX450h+. MSCHF has created two sculptures that look like morphed Lexus EVs for New York Armory Week Circle Car is an elongated Lexus RZ450e turned around on itself, while Twisted Car looks like a Lexus RX450h+ that has been twisted and wrung out like a giant mechanical towel. The team said Motomorphosis plays on the idea of a concept car, a prototype vehicle presented by car companies to showcase innovations in technology and style as an indicator of the company's direction. The sculptures resemble two electric Lexus vehicles "We had this idea of inverting the idea of a concept car and taking a purely formalist approach to the object," MSCHF chief creative officer Kevin Wiesner told Dezeen. The forms were based around the impossible 3D formulations in digital design software. "In this case, operations like twisting, stretching, and bending are part of a standard 3D program language that results in impossible objects; native digitally, but absurd physically," said Wiesner. Read: MSCHF creates furniture collection from "pile of car parts" "Circle Car also taps into a specifically implied absurdity of movement; no matter how much it drives, it remains in one place chasing its own tail," he continued. "Twist Car is one of those shapes that is taken directly from 3D software operations, though this degree of twist usually shows up as a visually compelling mistake." The sculptures are made from a steel armature, with "thousands of individual pieces joined together like LEGOs to form the skin". While they incorporate some Lexus car parts, they are non-functioning and do not turn on, according to the studio. The installation plays on the 'concept car' format Previously, MSCHF created furniture from Mercedes-AMG vehicle parts and cut a Gufram Pratone chair into little bits . The photography is courtesy of MSCHF. Motomorphosis is on display at Chelsea Industrial from 25 to 26 September. title: Meta unveils lightweight VR glasses and camera-free AI glasses at Connect 2026
summary: Meta has revealed slimline VR glasses for immersive entertainment on the go and an audio-only, camera-free version of its Ray-Ban glasses as the latest additions to its expanding product portfolio. Announced by CEO Mark Zuckerberg last night at the technology company's annual Connect conference, the Meta VR Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses expand its The post Meta unveils lightweight VR glasses and camera-free AI glasses at Connect 2026 app

content.source_text: Meta has revealed slimline VR glasses for immersive entertainment on the go and an audio-only, camera-free version of its Ray-Ban glasses as the latest additions to its expanding product portfolio. Announced by CEO Mark Zuckerberg last night at the technology company's annual Connect conference, the Meta VR Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses expand its market-leading range of eyewear and headsets. The Meta VR Glasses represent the bigger breakthrough, bringing virtual-reality gaming, 3D movies and other immersive digital experiences into a form factor only slightly larger than an ordinary pair of glasses. Meta's VR Glasses are slimmed down from previous headset form factors This allows them to be worn for longer than current headsets and carried on the daily commute, as people might do with a pair of over-ear headphones. Meta says it achieved the lightweight construction by splitting the architecture into two: the glasses, weighing about 100 grams, plus an attached "puck" that clips onto a pocket or bag and handles the processing. Also key are the glasses' ultra-compact pancake lenses, which are about the size of a Scrabble tile and are fixed within a soft mesh structure on the inside of the frames. They have a two-part architecture with an attached puck The wearer manually shifts these lenses to sit directly in front of their eye, filling everything but their peripheral view with a 5K display. This micro-OLED display offers angular resolution of 37 pixels per degree – more than Meta's current market-leading Quest VR headsets and enough to deliver crisp text and rich imagery. The Meta VR Glasses can be used to play games or watch entertainment from the Meta Quest platform, including movies recorded in or converted to 3D. There are also new immersive formats that Meta is pioneering, like "immersive sports" streamed in ultra-high definition from the edge of the playing field at live events. Ultra-compact lenses deliver high-resolution viewing Users navigate the operating system using their eyes, voice and natural hand gestures like swiping and pinching, without having to use controllers – in some cases even to play entire games. Meta also envisions the VR Glasses being used for work. Using full-colour passthrough – the view of the world in front of the glasses that's captured through its outward-facing cameras – wearers can turn any table surface into a keyboard and touchpad and surround themselves with multiple virtual screens from their Mac or PC. The VR Glasses will deliver up to three hours of continuous media playback from the battery on the puck. Meta expects to put the device on sale in spring 2027. The VR Glasses are for work as well as play Unlike the rest of Meta's eyewear offering, the VR glasses are not intended to be worn all the time or to be used primarily for AI assistance, although the company's new Muse AI will be built-in. The use of Meta's AI glasses out on the street has earned them the nickname of "pervert glasses" , due to various documented incidents of men using the barely visible camera to covertly film women. Surveillance concerns were also amplified after a Swedish news investigation revealed that videos captured by wearers' cameras – including highly sensitive ones where they were nude or having sex – were being streamed to subcontractors in Kenya . Read: "Big Tech is using design philosophy as a smokescreen" The pushback against these aspects of the technology may be a driver behind Meta's other key new product launch at Connect, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses. Developed with long-term partners EssilorLuxottica, these glasses lack the controversial camera of other Meta models, as well as the small screen of the Meta Ray-Ban Displays , launched this time last year. Their functionality is more limited, letting users listen to audio through small open‑ear directional speakers built into the frame and interact by voice with Meta's AI assistant. Audio-only AI glasses are also in the new lineup The slimmer feature set has allowed Meta to introduce new slimmer styles like the partially wire-frame Ray-Ban Clubmaster. The glasses' 12-hour battery life and 43-gram weight also mean they can more easily be worn all day. In addition to the new products, Meta revealed the Gen 3 version of its Ray-Ban Meta glasses, with three new frame silhouettes, and several new versions of the cheaper Meta Glasses , launched just three months ago, including one with pop star Lisa, whose influence is partly responsible for the Labubu craze. The VR Glasses are designed for portability and comfortable wear The keynote presentation also detailed the expanding capabilities of its Muse "personal AI agent", which was first revealed two weeks ago and which the company will be adding to all of its glasses. At the end, there was a quick sneak peek at a new Tamagotchi-like Muse Charm gadget. Meta has established itself as the dominant player in the small but growing market for AI glasses, accounting for 94 per cent of display-less AI glasses shipped in the first half of 2026, according to tracking by Counterpoint Research . By the end of the year, it will have more than 100 different styles available in its Ray-Ban, Oakley and own-brand collections. content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: textural concrete meets the aesthetic of oxidised metal in this series of tiles , designed by surfaces brand VitrA Tiles . Combining modern and industrial influences, Metacode is a series of wall and floor tiles that emulates the look of concrete, with a metallic update. The Metacode tiles blend the look of concrete and metal Gold, Copper or Iron finishes make the slab tiles resemble the patina of oxidised metal, with the mottled tonal variation and visual depth that entails. VitrA Tiles ' Metacode Tiles are made with the brand's advanced surface technologies, which give the products a tactile surface that enhances the material expression. There are three metallic finishes The tiles have R10 slip resistance and are suitable for both residential and commercial spaces. The Metacode tiles are part of VitrA's Code series, which is dedicated to reimagining familiar materials like stone and concrete through innovative surface design. content.source_text: The latest edition of Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project , curated by Christian + Jade, features pieces ranging from a pedestal constructed out of leftover shipping industry steel to a pagoda-like sculpture made from wooden trays. This year's edition of the annual exhibition, which launched in 2008 to showcase Danish design, is currently taking place in the historic Charlottenborg Palace in central Copenhagen. Here, curators Christian Hammer Juhl and Jade Chan of Christian + Jade have displayed works by ten Denmark-based designers in a fresco-covered room with a bare wooden floor that makes the pieces resemble artworks themselves. The Mindcraft Project 2026 is shown at Charlottenborg Palace While there are no specific parameters for which designers take part in The Mindcraft Project , the curators said that this year, it was quickly apparent that their picks all had something in common. "We wanted to include designers at different stages of the career from different parts of Denmark, but also international designers who have been a part of shaping the Danish design scene," Chan told Dezeen. "As our list grew, a very obvious red thread started to appear – there is a strong commitment to a special material or technique." It shows works by ten Danish or Denmark-based designers While Danish design is very well-known globally, the curators hope that The Mindcraft Project can help spotlight its less commercial side and give more of a focus on craft. "We've always admired the platform and seen it as very important in Danish design culture because it gives a stage to more experimental and less commercially driven works," Juhl added. "It gives a platform to people who are diving into craft and sort of lies in-between the craft and the design." Freya Dalsjø showed a delicate woven basket All the Mindcraft Project designers this year have a strong focus on their chosen material, with some choosing to show existing pieces and others creating entirely new work for this year's edition. Among the latter were fashion designer Freya Dalsjø , whose Basket and Match Seat were painstakingly constructed from thin strands of leather, woven together to create a sculptural yet functional basket and seat or pillow. "I was really honoured that they asked me; it's first and foremost an interior-focused exhibition, so it's super nice to be a part of it," Dalsjø told Dezeen. "[Christian and Jade's] idea to ask me for these pieces was really good because the material worked – you can really see it in this context, in something other than fashion." The light within unfinished buildings inspired these pewter lamps Designer Sigurd Nils Schelde also created new work for the exhibition, designing three pewter lamps that draw on architectural lighting. "These works focus on different observations of architectural lighting from unfinished buildings; I was interested in how you see the light within a building," Schelde told Dezeen. "It's like you're looking into the belly of the beast, and I was trying to adopt that into a more industrial language." The Untitled sculpture was made from oak and quartzite Schelde and Dalsjø's pieces are among some of this year's contributions that have a more polished, designed finish that clearly shows the work that went into refining the material, while other designers chose instead to highlight the raw materials. Among them was Hans Severin Jacobsen , whose Untitled sculpture was made from oak and quartzite that the designer sourced from a gravel pit next to his studio in Jutland. Jacobsen placed a rough-hewn 90-kilogram stone from the pit on a sleek oak base, cutting and squaring the sides of the stone to give it its final shape. "I usually work with found stones where I leave some or all of the stone untouched, but with this piece I've worked to impose geometry on this natural stone," he told Dezeen. "So this is man-made geometry." Daito Takefusa's ceramic sculpture resembles stone This focus on materiality was also evident in designer Daito Takefusa 's piece Fragmented Signs (Double Touch B), which at first glance also appeared to be made from stone. But the sculpture was made from ceramic, which Takefusa shaped with a rock to create its surface pattern before experimenting with different glazes, multiple layers of clay and oxides, to create an unusual, rough texture. Read: RCA design students exercise restraint in One Tool One Stool exhibition "What's interesting for me is the process of firing and coming up with the final product – it resembles archaeology," he told Dezeen. "I cover [the clay] with a material that doesn't melt, and after the firing, I brush it off," Takefusa continued. "It's akin to archaeological research; I never know what it's going to look like after the firing." The products in The Mindraft Project exhibition flank a central piece by FOS , a room divider made from cast bronze with an organic design pattern made using hand tools. Leftover steel from a superyacht was made into a pedestal In contrast, designer Anton Hendrik Denys ' console and pedestal were made from readymade, leftover stainless steel from the furniture and shipping industry, which he combined using his knowledge of creating custom-made pieces for art galleries. "The small chunky piece [in the pedestal] was for a bar stool for a super yacht, where they just needed a very thin piece of chunky stainless steel, and these pieces were disregarded afterwards," he told Dezeen. "I asked what they had left and how we could put that together, and then the shape and the thickness of the material defined the end result. I haven't changed the shape of the leftover pieces; I only put them together." The Well, in front, took months to make Another notable piece was made by Lene Bødker , whose The Well design took months to make. Using glass that she melts in a kiln before shaping it through a lost wax casting process, Bødker came up with an end design that was inspired by the wells of Rome as well as the healing powers of nature. "This specific work is called The Well," Bødker told Dezeen. "It has no bottom; you can imagine it goes deep, deep down into the ground, and you can pull up this magical, healing holy water." Near Bødker's piece is another design with a focus on water, designer Thomas Woltmann 's ceramic-clad water fountain Helligkilden that features beautifully glossy tiles dyed with natural ochres. As well as metal, stone, glass and leather, The Mindcraft Project also presented works in wood, including designer Anna Søgaard 's functional products made from elm. Anna Søgaard's boxes resemble a pagoda Her Curved Work, a set of trays and boxes, was made using a table saw to create a curved profile and then stacked to showcase their geometric shapes. The boxes ended up resembling a pagoda, with the pattern of the grain showcasing Søgaard's attention to detail. "I like boxes, storage that can contain things, but for me, it's about the sculptural way of working – I actually don't work with what you're putting inside, just the form of the box," she explained. "It nearly looks like architecture, but this pagoda is actually just a single box and you can continue stacking it." The Trio of Stools were stacked to form a sculpture The final designer of this year's project, Nicholas Shurey, also worked with wood for his joyful Trio of Stools, Ziggy Pattern. Partly inspired by designer Kansai Yamamoto's jumpsuit made for David Bowie, these sculptural seats bridge the gap between the sculptural and the functional, craft and design, neatly encompassing the theme of this year's exhibition. Other recent design shows with a focus on materials include Hanging Baskets and One Tool One Stool at London Design Festival. The photography is by Benjamin Lund . The Mindcraft Project 2026 takes place at Charlottenborg Palace, Nyhavn 1, 1051 København K from 23 to 27 September. title: Seven savvy pieces from London Design Festival made of material offcuts
summary: On the heels of London Design Festival, we have rounded up a selection of furniture and products presented during the city-wide event made of scraps that would otherwise have gone to waste. content.source_text: On the heels of London Design Festival , we have rounded up a selection of furniture and products presented during the city-wide event made of scraps that would otherwise have gone to waste. London Design Festival (LDF) concluded on Sunday, after a week of product launches, exhibitions and installations that showed the best of the capital's design scene. Throughout the event, a slew of designers unveiled projects using materials leftover from manufacturing, whether as an attempt to slash costs, preserve resources or simply experiment visually. Here are seven examples of the trend spotted during London's biggest design week: Top: photo by Lewis Duckworth. Above: photo by Carmel King Dagwood Bench by Lewis Duckworth Lewis Duckworth is one of London's many emerging talents. As the co-founder of guerrilla collective Design Everything , he is always looking for ways to create furniture with the inevitable limitations that come with being a young, independent designer. Dagwood Bench is one such project, made from timber end pieces leftover from furniture production, which are often too narrow or short to be reused and would normally go to waste. Duckworth created the bench from a single laminated plank, sandwiched between two timber faces. The designer explained that offcuts were arranged within these pieces of wood to create a form that "appears visually thick while remaining lightweight and structurally capable". "This project explores ways to re-evaluate these 'un-usable' elements by incorporating them into a larger, cohesive material system," he said. "Given that they started as an industrial byproduct, it felt most appropriate to reprocess them in a standardised format". Duckworth's Dagwood Bench is among the 34-strong shortlist of buildings, furniture and objects nominated for a 2026 Wood Award . A selection of these designs was on display at the Material Matters exhibition during LDF. Second Song by Spared Second Song is a selection of bird-shaped collectible objects by Brighton-based design studio Spared . The studio is known for transforming waste generated by its varied clients into furniture and products, such as tables made from old coffee grounds developed for the Corner cafe at London's Tate Modern museum. Cast using a selection of bio-based binders, the collectible birds were made of offcuts ranging from shell and stone to workshop sawdust and thin scrapings from the surfaces of plastic chopping boards used in industrial kitchens. Second Song was another project presented at Material Matters. Photo courtesy of Out of Worky Tissue box by Tom Golland This statement tissue box was part of Out of Worky , an exhibition of bespoke pieces made using scrap materials that the participants had collected over years of taking on myriad jobs as emerging designers. Tom Golland combined offcuts of walnut and white oak to form the unusually tall tissue dispenser, which is held together with two zinc-plated steel bolts. The show was presented by The Worky , a collective founded by Marley Wellings, Jake Robertson, Kieran Slater and Milo Tonry-Brown. Photo courtesy of Design Everything Chair by Oscar Warman Dubbed "everything I could find in my shed", this timber chair by emerging designer Oscar Warman is a Frankenstein-like hodgepodge of old pieces of furniture that were partially damaged. The chair features a duo of rotten and frayed front legs, which had to be cut and altered. This meant that Warman needed to source a strong piece of timber for the back legs, which he found in the form of part of a shelf that he "cannibalised" by taking it off the wall and using it alongside its brackets. "By designing in this way I spent time mocking up and offering each part to one another to try and resemble a chair shape," said Warman. "I like how few processes were used in the making of this piece and the time was spent problem solving how to make them function as a chair." The chair is still on display as part of Design Everything's With Limitations show at Aram Gallery, which runs until 10 October. Photo courtesy of Design Everything Fused by Audra Grays and Maxim Lester Fused is one of a handful of lamps made by emerging designers Audra Grays and Maxim Lester , who, quite literally, fused together different material offcuts from their respective practices to create lighting. After Lester came across Grays's decorative glass experiments on Instagram, the designers combined the glass offcuts with scrap metal and electrical back boxes found in Lester's workshop. LED strips were pulled from old lamps to illuminate the pieces. Also displayed at Aram Gallery, the rectilinear sconce lights are not the only pieces the duo made from offcuts that were on show during LDF. The pair also presented a chunky desk lamp as part of the Kiln Shift exhibition by Clink Street Ceramics. Photo courtesy of Max Radford Gallery Graywacke OffCut Chair by Carsten in der Elst Based in Cologne, designer Carsten in der Elst has spent the last six years utilising "the full potential of industrial by-product material" when crafting pieces of furniture. Central to In der Elst's portfolio is his Graywacke Offcut series – monolithic tables and chairs made from rough-hewn lumps of stone salvaged from a quarry in Lindlar, western Germany. One of these ancient-looking chairs was presented as part of the Progressive Permanence exhibition by Max Radford Gallery at the Christopher Farr showroom in Shoreditch. Photo courtesy of Design Everything Coat rack by Duy Huynh Emerging designer Duy Huynh is another exhibitor showing as part of With Limitations, who is presenting a timber coat rack made from offcuts salvaged from a stand he crafted to show work at his recent degree show. The size of each piece of wood, reassembled by the designer, was determined by where the previous joints had been cut to create the stand. "This piece is a bit smaller than a conventional coat rack, but I wanted to keep that acknowledgement of where it came from to show the idea that if we treat our materials right, they can serve us for a long time," said Huynh. London Design Festival 2026 took place at various locations around the city from 12 to 20 September. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. title: Bentley's first fully electric car embraces heritage in a "progressive way"
summary: Car brand Bentley has revealed the Torcal, its first fully electric car. content.source_text: Car brand Bentley has revealed the Torcal, its first fully electric car . Ahead of its unveiling, we spoke to design director Robin Page about how the car balances an electric future with the brand's heritage. Unveiled today at a launch event in London, the Torcal is a fully electric SUV – the first fully electric vehicle by the luxury car company. Unlike other luxury car brands – most notably Ferrari and Jaguar – Bentley has not radically overhauled the shape for its first electric vehicle. The Torcal is Bentley's first electric car According to Page, this was to create an electric car that was clearly modern, but also recognisable as a Bentley. Page told Dezeen his team began talking about direction four years ago. "That was when we asked, 'Are we doing a car dedicated to an electric language, or should we do another great Bentley with a more modern language – not directly focused on electrification?'" "We decided that our best route would be to embrace our heritage and DNA, but in a modern, progressive way." Dezeen spoke to Bentley design director Robin Page ahead of the launch The Torcal has a long wheelbase with a form that evokes previous Bentleys. Page explained that this form stemmed from Bentley's design principles rather than aerodynamic concerns related to electrification. "With electrification, what mainly drives the form's language is the aerodynamics and the package proportion – aerodynamics directly relates to range," he said. "The laws of aerodynamics start to give you quite a moulded form and a certain tail, b ut we decided that aerodynamics shouldn't lead the design. What's dominated the shape is our design principles, and they are based on our DNA and heritage." The Torcal was unveiled today in London The Torcal takes stylistic cues from previous Bentleys, including a continuous bonnet line, expressed rear arches and a prominent grill. "Outright elegance, the iconic g rill, the endless bonnet line, the resting beast – they're our principles, and we've let them dominate the design rather than aerodynamics," said Page. Although aerodynamics didn't drive the design, Page highlighted the vehicle's range of 600 kilometres. The car aims to be modern while evoking the brand's heritage The grill, inessential in an electric car, is still clearly expressed. As with the overall design of the car, Bentley nodded to the past. It referenced the grill of the Continental T, but with a modern twist – it can be illuminated in a diamond pattern. Page said the team decided it needed a grill and that closing it off would feel "like a hand over a mouth", opting for what it considers an art piece. "[We] decided to celebrate it, to do a piece of art with light," said Paige. It has an illuminated grill At the launch, the Torcal was presented in a light, yellowy green, another modern update to the brand's heritage. "The Bentley green is a much darker, solid green," said Page. "W e wanted a colour that showed the form, something a bit lighter, this colour works pretty well." Inside, the car has a wing-shaped dash and natural materials including timber and Merino wool. It has a modestly sized screen – for a high-end car – and numerous physical dials. "We didn't want to go down the clinical, super modern material route, because you end up with this quite stark, cold feeling inside," said Page. "It really captures a place you want to be, rather than something you look at and think, 'that's modern'. It needs to be something that feels fresh, but feels comfortable." The interior includes Merino wool seats Bentley said its choice to make its first electric car an SUV will open up a new market and offer something that other luxury car brands are not doing. "The reason we're all doing SUVs is that it's a growing market," he said. "We've had a lot of comments from customers who say they could use this Bentley every day." When it goes on sale later this year, the Torcal will be the first Bentley to feature the brand's redesigned logo , which was revealed last year. content.source_text: Alaska-based artist Nicholas Galanin has created a metal sculpture resembling a stretched animal hide in front of the St Louis Gateway Arch to challenge "narratives of westward expansion" for art festival Counterpublic. Land is Never a Gateway (Sightline/Lifeline) is located in front of the Eero Saarinen -designed monument, on a small sidewalk plot. From there, visitors can crouch down and look up at the piece, which is meant to create an optical illusion with the gateway. Nicholas Galanin has created a sculpture at the St Louis Gateway Arch When viewed from below, the sculpture resembles animal hide stretched across the arch, transforming it visually from a monument into a hide-processing frame. Galanin created the piece to challenge the narratives surrounding the ideologies of Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny, movements under which colonial settlers, ranchers and the US government began to migrate past the Mississippi River and into the western United States beginning in the early 1800s. The piece seeks to challenge narratives of Westward expansion Eero Saarinen's Gateway Arch, a grand, 630-foot-tall ( 94-metre-tall) swooping structure located on the banks of the Mississippi River, was designed as a monument to Westward expansion and is referred to as "The Gateway to the West" in popular culture. "The work developed through thinking about the Gateway Arch and the narratives of westward expansion it monumentalizes," Galanin told Dezeen. "I wanted to interrupt that sightline." "That alignment is both a sightline and a lifeline: a reminder that perspective determines which histories are visible and which have been obscured." Read: Torkwase Dyson fuses sound and architecture for St Louis installation Galanin, who is based in Sitka, Alaska and is of local Lingit and Unangax̂ descent, was informed by visits to St Louis for the piece, where he researched local history as part of the commission for Counterpublic . Specifically, he examined "the histories held in the land itself" and "Indigenous dispossession, racial capitalism, segregation, and extraction," he told Dezeen. Processing a hide, or animal skin, is a traditional art practised by many Native American and First Nations people. One step in the lengthy process involves tying the hide to a frame to stretch and cure it, which is pictured in Galanin's sculpture. It aligns perfectly with the arch when viewed from below, transforming the structure into a hide-processing frame Galanin often explores " adaptation, resilience, survival, active cultural amnesia, dream, memory, cultural resurgence, connection to and disconnection from the land" through his work, according to his artist statement. The third edition of the Counterpublic brings together local and global artists to create commissioned pieces and works around the city. This year's festival, Coyote Time , invited artists to explore the history, present and future of St Louis, and included installations by artists such as Oglála Lakȟóta artist Kite and Los Angeles-based artist Alice Bucknell among fifty others. It is led by executive director James McAnally and assistant curator Charlie Farrell, with guest curation by Jordan Carterm, Rapheal Fonesca, Stefanie Hessler, Nora N Khan and Wanda Nandibush. In 2023, New York artist Torkwase Dyson designed a monolithic black structure that highlighted the ragtime music of American composer Scott Joplin for the event. The photography is by Jon Gitchoff, courtesy of Counterpublic Counterpublic runs from 10 September to 12 December. For more architecture, design and art events across the world, visit Dezeen Events Guide . content.source_text: Mexican lighting designer Federico Stefanovich has worked with local interiors firm Nama Studio to renovate his studio in a hotel-turned-arts building in Mexico City 's Centro neighbourhood. Known for his expressive metal lighting, Federico Stefanovich renovated the interior of the balcony-clad Edificio Humboldt, a historic building designed by Canadian architect Thomas Sinclair Gore and completed in 1922. Today it holds dozens of art and design studios and workshops. Federico Stefanovich worked with Nama Studio to create his studio in Mexico City Stefanovich and Nama Studio carefully preserved the historic details while adding rich colours and textures to showcase Stefanovich's designs and provide working space. It serves as a studio, showroom and production workshop. "The balconies were one of the elements I immediately fell in love with when I first saw the space," Stefanovich told Dezeen. "The large original windows, which open completely onto the balconies, had already been carefully restored before our intervention, preserving details from the 1920s, including their handles and iron latches." It is located in Edificio Humboldt, a historic building in the city's centre Visitors enter the studio area via a seating area with showcase shelving that leads out into the long, main space with a lounge area at one end and a long table for displaying goods on the other. In this primary showroom area, Edificio Humboldt's windows bring in plenty of natural light – which can present a problem for showcasing lighting designs. The team created custom panelling to create backdrops for the lights To get around this and take full advantage of the light-filled rooms, panels were added to create backdrops for the lights, including a custom-designed modular panel system with metal poles interspersed with wooden blocks supporting them on the edges. The panel's blue colour was created by layering tones almost like a limewash. An entrance nook has seating "I would describe it as a muted mineral blue, with a slightly weathered quality," said Stefanovich. "We wanted the colour to have depth and variation rather than read as a completely flat or uniform surface." "The perimeter panel system is interrupted by the windows, creating a rhythm between the new architectural elements and the historic structure." Layered blue paints were used to create the custom panels In the main space, this "muted mineral blue" is complemented by chocolate-toned plaster and brown-stained wood in the furniture, pedestals and wainscotting. Aged flooring hints at the age of the building. Sliding fibreglass panels hide the workshop The lounge area, completely lined by the blue panel system, features a semi-circular sofa custom-made by Stefanovich's team. Running along the elongated showroom is another panelling system. Instead of blue, the team opted for fibreglass that is yellowy and opaque but translucent enough to let light through, reminiscent of Japanese washi paper. The studio created a custom sofa for the space These fibreglass panels are part of a sliding door system that reveals the workshop area with utilitarian elements such as plywood furniture, MDF panels and steel storage racks. Overall, Stefanovich said that the space was meant to reference his design style directly, which he described as ornate but not overly so. Read: JSa transforms Mexican factory for its own architecture studio "There is a subtle mid-century quality to the space, combined with handmade processes and certain more expressive, almost baroque gestures," he said. "The intention was to bring these references together in a contemporary way, creating an environment that feels sophisticated but not overly formal, and that allows the architecture and my pieces to exist as part of the same language." A central table displays work and process For the opening of the studio, Stefanovich collaborated with gallery Ago Projects to display his Salina Collection. The designer said the fibreglass in the studio space references the fibreglass of the collection. Other self-designed studios include Jasmine Fisher's atmospheric studio in London and Victoria Yakusha's studio with a "living island" in Miami . The photography is by Alejandro Ramirez Orozco . content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: carefully tailored leather upholstery takes centre stage in the Nyla executive chair , produced by furniture brand Omidi . Bringing the feeling of a private office wherever it sits, the Nyla leather chair combines a high back, leather upholstery and advanced adjustment controls smoothly integrated into its aluminium alloy base. The Nyla executive chair is upholstered in leather Omidi created the Nyla leather chair out of the belief that true luxury lies not in excess but in refinement, striving to reduce the chair to a clean and balanced silhouette while centring the capability of leather to develop unique character and make an item feel more personal over time. "Omidi's leather executive chair collection focuses on combining refined craftsmanship with modern comfort, offering designs suitable for both professional offices and luxury home workspaces," said the company. The brand's chair's are designed for ergonomic comfort as well as quiet luxury A Gold winner in the MUSE Design Awards, the chair includes integrated armrests to support a natural body position and a sculpted seat made from high-density foam that provides firmness and resilience. The adjustment mechanisms include a gas lift system certified for up to 136 kilograms, 135-degree multi-angle tilt and a sliding seat, while lumbar support supports the natural curve of the spine and reduced pressure on the back over prolonged periods of sitting. Taking the form of a thin panel of perforated aluminium, Grid combines "tidiness, aesthetic modularity and minimal rigour", according to Tubes. Its geometric surface turns the radiator into an architectural The post Grid radiator by Elisa Ossino for Tubes appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: Italian brand Tubes and designer Elisa Ossino bring an echo of the workshop tool board to heating design with their electric Grid radiator. Taking the form of a thin panel of perforated aluminium, Grid combines "tidiness, aesthetic modularity and minimal rigour", according to Tubes. The Grid radiator is a thin panel with smooth circular perforations Its geometric surface turns the radiator into an architectural element while serving as an attachment point for optional accessories like shelves or hooks – a feature that is particularly practical in the bathroom. "The object is a reinvented everyday ritual, where warmth meets geometric elegance," said Ossino . "Minimalism, functionality and personality coexist in a project designed for those seeking distinctive contemporary design." The cut-outs accommodate optional accessories and decoration Grid's deceptively simple design involved the creation of new manufacturing equipment that could achieve the softened, controlled indentation of the cut-out circles. The radiator is made of recycled and recyclable aluminium, entirely from an Italian supply chain, and is available in a choice of 140 RAL colours. Grid's catalogue of accessories includes hooks, shelves, towel rails and, for the first time, a small mirror. content.source_text: Tech brand Apple has revealed the 600-seat Apple Music Hall, its first live music venue, which sits alongside its offices within London's Battersea Power Station . Set to open later this year, the venue overlooks the power station's Turbine A at the northern end of the huge brick building. It will be Apple 's first permanent performance venue. Apple has unveiled Apple Music Hall within Battersea Power Station Designed by Apple's in-house team led by Apple Places vice president Kristina Raspe, the venue takes its industrial language directly from the Giles Gilbert Scott-designed power station. The venue is flanked by brick walls, while the building's huge structural steel joists are exposed at the rear of the performance space. Read: Apple reveals Battersea Power Station store as latest "evolution of the Apple Store" As a nod to the art deco design of the original power station, a series of four illuminated, streamline-styled arches span the venue. Bronze, art deco balconies were placed between the arches, as box-like areas overlooking the main venue space. The venue has an industrial aesthetic According to Apple, the flexible venue was designed to give artists an "unprecedented level of creative control". The venue has an 11.5-metre-wide stage and can be arranged in multiple configurations as either an all-seated or all-standing venue, or a combination of the two. Music will be played through a 48-speaker spatial sound system, while 16 hardwired cameras can capture performances to be broadcast. "In short, an artist can perform an intimate live show for fans at Apple Music Hall and walk out with a finished Spatial Audio recording, a broadcast-ready mix, and multicamera video — all from a single show," said Apple. Apple Music Radio has also been relocated to the building Alongside the main venue space is what Apple describes as a "full production facility" that contains a pair of professional-standard recording and mix studios. The venue also includes a dedicated space for Apple's radio station – Apple Music Radio, which will now broadcast from inside the building. The radio station will now broadcast from the former power station Apple Music Hall was built alongside Apple's Foster + Partners-designed European HQ , which occupies the centre of Battersea Power Station. One of London's best-known buildings, the power station was refurbished in 2022 by architecture studio WilkinsonEyre after being derelict for 40 years . It now contains apartments on the upper floors, with restaurants and shops, including an Apple Store in the former turbine halls. The photography is courtesy of Apple. The post Apple unveils music venue within Battersea Power Station appeared first on Dezeen .

title: I IN contrasts concrete architecture with bright colours in Andersson Bell Tokyo store
summary: Local studio I IN drew on the existing architecture when creating fashion brand Andersson Bell's flagship store in Japan, which is filled with glossy, reflective surfaces and warm red and yellow hues. content.source_text: Local studio I IN drew on the existing architecture when creating fashion brand Andersson Bell's flagship store in Japan , which is filled with glossy, reflective surfaces and warm red and yellow hues. Located in Tokyo's Aoyama neighbourhood, the original building from 1993 has an exposed concrete interior that heavily influenced I IN 's design for the store. The interior of Andersson Bell has a brutalist feel "It is quite rare to find such a magnificent space in Tokyo, and we were fortunate to have the freedom to take a bold and radical approach to the design," I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen. "Especially, the building's strong composition of mass and void became a major source of inspiration and guided us throughout the spatial planning." Warm yellow hues decorate the space The studio aimed for the interior to be contrasting but not competing with the architecture. "The idea was to translate the brand's identity of 'contrast' into space design," Terui continued. "The existing architecture, built in Tokyo in the 90s, already had a very strong character and presence, so rather than competing with it, we wanted to introduce a strong modern layer that would create a beautiful contrast with the existing architecture." The different floors have different colours To do so, I IN, which Terui founded with Hiromu Yuyama, introduced warm, saturated colours across the building's three storeys. Bright red, orange and yellow hues contrast against the boardmarked concrete walls throughout the space, with the red section also visible through the store's large front window. I IN custom-made all the furniture for the interior "The red comes from the brand's signature colour and became the introduction of the store," Terui said. "As guests move through the space and step upstairs, they experience a gradual transition from red to orange and then to yellow," he continued. "Rather than simply applying colour to each floor, we wanted this transition to become part of the spatial experience, giving each level a different atmosphere and creating a sense of progression as guests move through the building." Read: I IN uses glossy surfaces and Edo purple to create "new form of Japanese luxury" for Ginza Lounge Terui and Yuyama also added pipes that "extend through the existing architecture as if piercing its structure", the studio said. As well as contrasting the concrete's grey hue with more colourful details, I IN juxtaposed its raw tactility with plenty of glossy and mirrored details, including a glass floor, steel pipes and tables and display cases with shiny, lacquered surfaces. Steel pipes add shiny details to the interiors The furniture pieces used in the 309-square-metre store were tailor-made by the studio and designed to feel like a part of the existing architecture. "All of the furniture was custom-made for the store," Terui said. "We followed the same idea of creating a bold presence, taking inspiration from the powerful character and scale of the existing architecture," he continued. "Rather than treating the furniture as separate elements placed within the space, we designed each piece as a part of the architecture, as if it had always been there, so that the furniture and the space ultimately merge into one." The top floor has yellow colours I IN has previously also designed a tile-clad store for designer Nigo's Human Made brand and a glossy purple lounge for department store Matsuya Ginza . The photography is by Tomooki Kengaku . The post I IN contrasts concrete architecture with bright colours in Andersson Bell Tokyo store appeared first on Dezeen .

title: "Too often, neurodiverse design is a marketing ploy"

content.source_text: Lazy attempts to frame interiors products as more inclusive for neurodivergent people are becoming too common, writes Ellie Foster . Most of us would agree that increasing awareness around neurodiversity is important and overdue, with 15-20 per cent of the global population demonstrating traits of ADHD, autism, dyslexia and the like. It makes sense that interior designers pursuing a more inclusively built world are following the conversation closely, asking themselves to better accommodate those who interpret and experience space differently. For better or worse, product manufacturers have been following along too. However, too often, neurodiverse design is merely a marketing ploy. Is neurodiverse design just another gap in the market to exploit, similar to greenwashing before it? Naturally, some contract furnishers will bristle at that accusation, and for specifiers aiming to envelope people up and down the spectrum it may also rankle. But recent industry events and product launches make it difficult for me to come to any other conclusion. In the past three years, there has been no shortage of events championing "designing for difference" in my inbox; no lack of press releases pulling on the terms hypo- and hypersensitivity to explain that a task chair comes in both brights and neutrals. More recently, the sheer volume of these kinds of emails has raised questions for me about honest intentions. Do this many manufacturers really care about making products that improve the wellbeing of all? Read: "Many of our everyday spaces are doing us harm" Or, is neurodiverse design just another gap in the market to exploit, similar to greenwashing before it? Having a heightened awareness of space myself, these are the same questions that have started to gnaw at my conscience in a big way. For more than a few brands, the plan of attack has been to showcase how updated furniture collections soothe individuals overstimulated by clashing patterns and loud colours, and energise those rendered lethargic by muted tones and minimalism. At last year's Clerkenwell Design Week , one commercial name hosted a showroom installation addressing the acute sensory needs associated with certain diagnoses. Once attendees had marvelled at the work, the structure doubled as a backdrop for a talks programme on how we can be kinder to neurodivergent employees and service users through the use of design. The focus on colour overlooks the psychological and physiological impact that objects have on neurodiverse brains The activation then linked to a new luxury vinyl tile collection – one that looked similar to the brand's previous lines, but professed to ease mental anguish nonetheless. All that is to say, the event was good; well-intentioned, well-received. The tenuously linked PVC planks in Herringbone, Chevron and Checkerboard? Not so much. The fanfare around ever-so-slightly tweaked product ranges rarely ventures beyond those two "H" words (hyposensitivity and hypersensitivity), which are almost exclusively used in the context of colour. The main outcome – for me, at least – is a subtle repositioning of said brand as the ethical choice, alongside an excuse to mass produce its current portfolio in a range of new and "progressive" hues. Read: First autistic Barbie allows "more children to see themselves" in doll The focus on colour overlooks the psychological and physiological impact that objects have on neurodiverse brains in other ways. Low-hanging light fixtures leading to feelings of claustrophobia; castor-mounted furniture causing emotional instability; chairs with too many components creating distraction or obsessive compulsions. These are just a few topics that could broaden the conversation around neurodiversity in product design – and the fact that we're still accepting that additional Cobalt and Stone colourways are enough to prevent meltdowns only proves that the area remains chronically understudied. I want to urge interior designers not to take things at face value From where I'm sitting (and that's in a central Manchester co-working space revamped just a year ago), it seems obvious that often it's just a rebranding of the same old products. Neurodiverse-friendly lounge chairs come in the same kaleidoscopic fabrics that were once flogged in the name of "design versatility"; those with stripped-back aesthetics – at one time marketed to fans of wabi-sabi or biophilic design trends – are now prime for people overwhelmed by pattern complexity and vibrance. Repackaging collections that already exist shows a significant lack of care for people whose entire worldview can be skewed by spatial discordance, as manufacturers continue to cash in on industry-wide conversations around diverse perspectives. Read: "Space that is exclusionary does not live up to its full potential" I want to urge interior designers not to take things at face value. To read between the lines on brands pushing a "designing for difference" rhetoric, to uncover whether these same brands championed neurodiversity before it became a global talking point. It's also worth investigating whether neurodiverse individuals have been involved in the product design process at all or if, at the very least, the process was informed by talking to them directly. It goes without saying that product and interior designers mutually aspiring for more inclusive interior settings is a positive thing, but the problem lies in the recent surge of stuff that overpromises and under-delivers. The risk is that marketing products in this way leaves neurodiverse occupants failed, and designers mis-sold. Ellie Foster is an architecture and design journalist based in Manchester. title: Isabel + Helen showcase their "obsession with movement" with kinetic models at The Conran Shop
summary: British designer duo Isabel Gibson and Helen Chesner have filled The Conran Shop's gallery with colourful, kinetic models for their London Design Festival exhibition, Motion Sickness. Spinning orbs, flapping wings and wheeled devices all feature in the exhibition, which marks 10 years since the founding of their London-based art and design studio, Isabel + Helen. content.source_text: British designer duo Isabel Gibson and Helen Chesner have filled The Conran Shop 's gallery with colourful, kinetic models for their London Design Festival exhibition, Motion Sickness. Spinning orbs, flapping wings and wheeled devices all feature in the exhibition, which marks 10 years since the founding of their London-based art and design studio, Isabel + Helen . The show explores the creative process of design duo Isabel + Helen Many of the models are prototypes, created for collaborations with brands such as Hermès and Burberry, or for installations at venues ranging from the V&A museum to the Coachella festival. The duo wanted to give insight into the creative process behind their projects, which typically centres around model-making. The gallery is filled with kinetic model prototypes "We saw it as an opportunity to showcase the behind-the-scenes of what we do and what we make," explained Gibson, as she and Chesner gave Dezeen a tour of the show. "The way we work, we usually jump to prototypes quite quickly," she said. "Because you can imagine how something will move and you can sketch it, but you need to get hands-on to see how it works in real life." Spinning orbs, flapping wings and wheeled devices all feature Movement has been a recurring theme in Isabel + Helen's work since they founded the studio in 2015, three years after graduating from Chelsea College of Arts, which is where they met. "We've had this obsession with movement and kinetic sculpture," Gibson told Dezeen. Read: Is London having a design renaissance? "Usually the movement has some form of transformation, or a reveal moment; that's something we're always interested in," added Chesner. "The way things move also affects how you see them," she continued. "You can have so many different emotions too; something can feel really joyful or quite sinister." The backdrop is a series of limited-edition motion paintings The backdrop to Motion Sickness is a series of limited-edition paintings, each depicting a colourful wheel. The designers produced these artworks with movement, using a kinetic machine they built themselves. It allows them to spin a paintbrush, forming a motif of concentric circles. Other focal points in the show include a toy train carrying half a dozen eggs, which wobble in time with one another as the device is wheeled along the table, and a series of 15 paper spheres that spin when you pull a string. One model is a toy train carrying half a dozen eggs Chesner said these projects develop through "trying stuff out and not being too precious about anything". "A lot of the time stuff doesn't work, but you have to just constantly build on it," she said. Simple labels encourage visitors to interact The exhibition also marks a decade of on-and-off collaboration between Isabel + Helen and The Conran Shop . One of the duo's first commissions was the store's LDF exhibition, A Load Of Jargon, presented in 2016 in collaboration with design website It's Nice That. "They saw us at the beginning, when we started out, so marking 10 years with them was really nice," added Chesner. It is among the first exhibitions that The Conran Shop has staged in the basement gallery of its store on London's Sloane Square, which has been the flagship since the closure of its previous locations on Fulham Road and Marylebone High Street. The exhibition was on show at The Conran Shop for LDF It comes a time of reinvention for the retailer, which was founded by Sir Terence Conran in 1973. Since 2023, it has shifted its business model to focus more on its own collections rather than selling pieces by other brands. Other recent milestones include the launch of a furniture collection with Francis Sultana , which was unveiled during last year's LDF. Motion Sickness was on show at The Conran Shop from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival . See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. title: Fritz Hansen Sound Club invites visitors to enjoy music in Bauhaus-inspired listening spaces
summary: Danish design brand Fritz Hansen has teamed up with audio specialist Technics to transform its Farringdon showroom into a series of domestic listening scenes for London Design Festival. As part of the Fritz Hansen Sound Club, the showroom has been organised into four domestic scenes where guests are invited to listen to a curated selection The post Fritz Hansen Sound Club invites visitors to enjoy music in Bauhaus-inspired listening spaces appear

content.source_text: Danish design brand Fritz Hansen has teamed up with audio specialist Technics to transform its Farringdon showroom into a series of domestic listening scenes for London Design Festival . As part of the Fritz Hansen Sound Club, the showroom has been organised into four domestic scenes where guests are invited to listen to a curated selection of vinyl records. Fritz Hansen Sound Club held its latest edition during London Design Festival The installation combines Fritz Hansen's furniture and lighting products with turntables, headphones and speakers from Japanese firm Technics . A 90th anniversary limited edition of the Kaiser Idell Luxus table lamp and Technics' SL 40CBT turntable form the centrepiece of the various settings, both reimagined in a matching burgundy hue. The installation invited visitors to listen to a selection of vinyl records In reference to the table lamp's modernist origins, the interior styling evokes the Bauhaus movement and combines 1930s furniture with pieces from Fritz Hansen's catalogue. Fritz Hansen Sound Club originally debuted during 3 Days of Design in Copenhagen, with the aim to explore how sound informs the way users experience interior settings. It featured a special burgundy edition of the Kaiser Idell Luxus table lamp "Sound plays a direct role in how we experience space," said Fritz Hansen creative director, Els Van Hoorebeeck. "It shapes how we move, where we pause, and how we relate to furniture, light and materials." "With Fritz Hansen Sound Club, we explore how these elements work together to define the character of a space, and how this way of thinking continues to shape our design today." Read: London design "an international success story" says Sadiq Khan The Study area pairs steel-framed desks with Arne Jacobsen's Ant Chair in a cherry veneer finish, while the designer's iconic Egg Chair provides a cosy spot for relaxing in the nearby Reading Corner. Downstairs, the Living Room provides a setting for socialising, with a turntable and speakers oriented towards the guests. A matching version of Technics' SL 40CBT turntable completed the setup Furniture including Poul Kjærholm's PK31 sofa and PK80 daybed creates a relaxed, lounge-like feel, while a 1930s drinks trolley and PK61 coffee tables encourage conversation and interaction. Fritz Hansen was founded in 1872 and is known for working with famous architects and designers, including Jacobsen and Kjærholm, as well as Hans J Wegner, Børge Mogensen and Verner Panton. The exhibition also featured a selection of other Fritz Hansen furniture More recently, the brand has collaborated with contemporary talents such as Piero Lissoni, Jamie Hayon and Cecilie Manz, who created a compact and comfortable plywood chair that can be used in a variety of contexts. A new version of Manz's Monolit chair forms part of the presentation, alongside a more compact, wall-mounted take on the Kaiser Idell lamp and an upholstered version of Japanese studio Nendo's N02 Recycle chair. A new version of Cecilie Manz's Monolit chair forms part of the presentation Other highlights from this year's London Design Festival include the debut show of design platform Collate Lobby and a bamboo pavilion covered in traditional Indian police shields . Fritz Hansen Sound Club is open daily to the public until 20 September at 78 Cowcross Street as part of London Design Festival . title: Victoria Yakusha crafts sculptural jewellery boutique in New York
summary: Ukrainian designer Victoria Yakusha has created a sculptural, almost monochromatic interior for a jewellery brand's flagship boutique in New York City. Also from Ukraine, the brand Guzema's store in SoHo is its first US flagship and occupies a 1,100-square-foot (102-square-metre) space on Wooster Street. content.source_text: Ukrainian designer Victoria Yakusha has created a sculptural, almost monochromatic interior for a jewellery brand's flagship boutique in New York City. Also from Ukraine, the brand Guzema 's store in SoHo is its first US flagship and occupies a 1,100-square-foot (102-square-metre) space on Wooster Street. Almost all of the Guzema boutique is coloured in a warm beige tone for a cohesive appearance Victoria Yakusha Studio used her signature minimalist style to design a space that feels calming and curated. "My work here was closer to that of a sculptor," said founder Victoria Yakusha. "We didn't want the feeling of traditional retail. We wanted something more intimate." Centrally positioned vitrines have rounded edges and are upholstered in grey suede The long, narrow interior is laid out with products presented in recessed niches on both sides, and inside a series of sculptural vitrines running back through the centre. These monolithic islands are upholstered in dove-grey suede and "rounded like a river stone" to create a soft, serene statement. Mineral-toned plaster creates texture across portions of the walls and ceiling The remainder of the decor is slightly lighter in colour, with mineral-toned plaster and matching storage units creating the impression of a single cohesive surface. In the store window, a series of white hand-sculpted vessels with textured skins and bowl-like tops are used to present Guzema's jewellery in a novel way. Read: Victoria Yakusha opens Miami gallery with plant-covered "living island" These pieces follow the same visual language as the Sonaih floor lamp from Yakusha's own design brand Faina , which produces furniture, lighting and decor. "We wanted the jewelry to feel discovered, not just displayed. That's how we came to the idea of the installation," Yakusha said. "Each vessel is hand-sculpted, layer by layer. It's an artwork in itself. It becomes part of the experience, a way of revealing something precious." A consultation area in the back of the boutique is furnished with pieces from Faina At the back of the store is a semi-private consultation area for one-on-one appointments, screened from the main space by a glass-block partition. Several more Faina designs feature in this salon, including a curved sofa, ottoman and sconce, along with a burnished-metal table and silver tableware by Natalia Criado . A window installation featuring hand-sculpted vessels faces SoHo's Wooster Street A former fashion editor, Yakusha has opened galleries for her furniture line in both Antwerp and Miami , and earlier designed the interior for Kyiv eatery Istetyka that balances rough and smooth surfaces. Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, she has designed a furniture collection as an homage to her homeland and proposed a museum to preserve threatened Ukrainian cultural heritage. The photography is by Matthew Williams . The post Victoria Yakusha crafts sculptural jewellery boutique in New York appeared first on Dezeen .

summary: Local designer Veronica Mishaan has revamped a penthouse apartment with bursts of colour and animal prints in Bogotá, Colombia.
