"We aimed to preserve the essence of the space The post Veronica Mishaan carries out "successful juxtaposition" of patterns in Bogotá penthou

content.source_text: Local designer Veronica Mishaan has revamped a penthouse apartment with bursts of colour and animal prints in Bogotá , Colombia. The 580-square-metre apartment was redesigned to balance the needs of the family with the ability to host, while preserving and displaying the clients' art and antiques collection. Veronica Mishaan has revamped a penthouse apartment in Bogotá "We aimed to preserve the essence of the space and keep alive the memories amassed over 30 years, while refreshing the palette of colour and materials and reworking the layout for a new era," Veronica Mishaan told Dezeen. The apartment overlooks the city's greenery and mountainscape, so the design team worked to frame the views and bring the outdoors into the space with floral motifs, foliage tones and custom oak floors and finishes. The design showcases the family's art and antique collection "Material choices, colours and window-oriented planning all reinforce the connection between the home and its natural context," said Mishaan. "We prioritised natural, tactile materials to reinforce warmth, longevity and a strong connection to the surrounding landscape." Smooth marmorino plaster in the living room and circulation spaces serves as a soft backdrop for art. Grasscloth wallpaper carries through the dining room, primary bedroom and family room for a subtle texture. Guests enter the apartment via a double-height space Guests enter the apartment between an Elsa Foulon porcelain pendant and a staircase with a cast bronze railing that climbs like a tree branch through the apartment's multiple levels. In the first living area, an antique Aubusson rug pairs with a custom Lee Jofa wool bouclé sofa, mid-century armchairs from Donzella, the studio's signature hammed iron martini tables and artwork by Peter Halley. Bold colours and texture carry throughout the apartment In the office space, the studio lacquered the original built-in bookcases and panelling in deep blue to complement the blue-leopard Stark carpet. In the primary bedroom, Phillip Jeffries wallpaper envelops the room in rich indigo with pale blossoms that tie into the light pink of the patterned zellige travertine and marble tiles of the bathrooms. The team retained the original hand-painted sinks as a nod to the apartment's history. Phillip Jeffries wallpaper envelops the primary bedroom The mirrored walls of the dressing room add lightness to the space with a parchment vanity and a curved bench upholstered in Pierre Frey velvet. The dining room sets off an antique crystal and bronze chandelier with custom Schumacher light blue velvet dining chairs with leopard motifs and a soft coral wallpaper featuring tree branches. Read: Colombian designers transform Bogotá townhouse for furniture exhibition Animal-print drapery hangs in the family room, tying together the dark blue walls, terracotta-toned sofa and sand hues of the artwork. The team also created spaces that catered to the client's grandchildren with custom wooden bunks and a playroom with sage green millwork and bespoke children's furniture. "What makes this project unique is the confident, successful juxtaposition of multiple patterns, colours and furniture languages to create a cohesive, layered whole," she said. "That compositional balance, mixing antiques, contemporary art and locally made custom pieces, recurs throughout the apartment." Custom wooden bunk beds are also available for family Mishaan said that the biggest lesson this project reinforced was not to follow trends. "By prioritising lasting design principles, client needs, craft and locally made custom work, we produced a creative, authentic and unique home that will age well, a reminder to trust conviction over fashion in future projects." Other recent interior projects in Colombia include an apartment with glass brick and velvet as an homage to the 1980s by 5 Sólidos and a furniture exhibition in a renovated townhouse by Gallery NC Diseño. The photography is by Max Burkhalter . The post Veronica Mishaan carries out "successful juxtaposition" of patterns in Bogotá penthouse appeared first on Dezeen .

title: Lee Broom evokes 1970s glamour with The Chant Chambers installation
summary: Designer Lee Broom has created an "atmospheric environment" in his Shoreditch showroom with The Chant Chambers, an installation showcasing his glass-block Chant lighting collection at London Design Festival. The Chant Chambers displays the modular light in a variety of forms – as a portable lamp, wall lamp, linear pendants and oversized chandeliers. All are presented inside The post Lee Broom evokes 1970s glamour with The Chant Chambers installat

content.source_text: Designer Lee Broom has created an "atmospheric environment" in his Shoreditch showroom with The Chant Chambers, an installation showcasing his glass-block Chant lighting collection at London Design Festival . The Chant Chambers displays the modular light in a variety of forms – as a portable lamp, wall lamp, linear pendants and oversized chandeliers. Lee Broom added plinths and sculptures to his showroom All are presented inside Broom 's showroom, where textured vertical screens create a series of interconnected spaces designed to have a cinematic atmosphere. The Chant Chambers, which Broom described as "an elegant yet surreal lounge," has wood-panelled walls and tactile wall-to-wall carpeting and features stone plinths and a number of sculptures. Wood panels and textured screens divide the space "I wanted the Chant Chambers to feel like an atmospheric environment rather than a display of individual lights," Broom told Dezeen. "The installation explores how the same cubic form can be transformed as it is repeated across a space, using different configurations to create a sense of discovery," he continued. "It also reflects the way our clients are looking for lighting that can be adapted specifically to their interiors rather than choosing a single fixed object." Glass-cube pendants were hung in lines to create an architectural feel Broom also used Chant lights in linear arrangements as geometric ceiling designs with an architectural feel. The moody, smoky colour palette of the installation was inspired by Chant's latest iteration – a smoked-glass finish in a darker tone than the previous design. Read: Lee Broom displays "sculptural tableau of light" for Mexico City art week debut "The new smoked glass finish was a starting point for the concept," Broom said. "It has a depth and warmth that works particularly well with the design of Chant and it nods to the late 1970s, early 80s period when glass blocks were very prevalent in modern architecture." "The palette was developed around those darker, richer tones to create a space that feels alluring and atmospheric, while still allowing the geometry of the lighting to stand out," he continued. Broom drew on 1970s interiors for the installation Glamorous 1970s interiors have been making a comeback, with a number of designers looking to the decade for their interiors, as seen recently in a Marseille wine bar . Broom believes that his Chant light has played a part in this trend, especially when it comes to bringing geometric forms and glass blocks back into contemporary interiors. "Since I first introduced the original Chant Chandelier in 2022, those references have gained real momentum," he said. "What interests me is reinterpreting them rather than simply recreating the 1970s, giving those nostalgic materials a more contemporary expression." Wall sconces also decorate the space He argues that these types of interiors also help put the focus on the lighting. "This kind of aesthetic really allows lighting to take centre stage, not just through the fixtures themselves, but through the ambience they create," Broom said. At the end of The Chant Chambers installation, Broom placed a three-tier Chant chandelier to fully showcase the lighting collection. A three-tiered chandelier completes the installation The designer has previously created a "sculptural tableau of light" for Mexico Design Week and a chandelier installation for last year's London Design Festival . The photography is by Luke Hayes. The Chant Chamber is on show at 95 Rivington Street, EC2A 3AY, from 15 to 20 September. See our London Design Festival 2026 guide on Dezeen Events Guide for information about the many other exhibitions, installations and talks that take place during the week. content.source_text: From bars and hotels to private homes , this lookbook explores interiors where billiard tables are on hand for spontaneous games. Billiard tables – comprising a cloth-covered surface surrounded by cushioned sides that are punctuated with netted pockets – are a type of table that cue sports can be played on, such as pool and snooker. While they are traditionally covered in dark green cloth, to recall the appearance of grass lawns, contemporary designs feature differently-coloured cloth, from blues and reds to neutrals. Brightly coloured balls make the tables instantly recognisable, standing out against the background cloth when contained in a triangular rack or strewn around the table mid-play. The following interiors all feature billiard tables, from traditional games rooms in hospitality venues to unconventional placements in residential kitchens and living rooms. This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen's archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring wooden staircases , picture windows and cottage living rooms . Photo by Christopher Sturman Soho House São Paulo, Brazil, by Soho House Sculptural legs, deep netted pockets and a navy top allow this monolithic billiard table to anchor a lofty games room in members' club Soho House 's São Paulo outpost. Its ornately inlayed base ties it in with pattern found elsewhere in the room, from wall hangings to lounge chairs. Find out more about Soho House São Paulo › Photo courtesy of Caceres + Tous House Kala, Indonesia, by Caceres + Tous When the panoramic jungle and sea views have been taken in, residents of this home on the Indonesian island of Lombok can retreat indoors for a game of pool. Within a black-painted room, a billiard table with a honey-coloured wooden base and a pale, sandy-coloured tabletop allows the multicoloured balls to stand out. Find out more about House Kala › Photo by Richard Chivers Watson House Annexe, UK, by Ström Architects A billiard table covered in sky blue cloth sits in the centre of this wood -lined bar and games room within a timber-clad annex, designed by British studio Ström Architects . The firm designed the annex to have the atmosphere of a "rustic boutique hotel", facilitating drinking, dancing and partying in addition to extra accommodation for overnight guests. Find out more about Watson House Annexe › Photo by Ema Peter The Bell, USA, by Ste Marie The glamorous atmosphere of mid-century offices has been reinstated during the renovation of this 1960s tower in Chicago , including chic games rooms, a library and lounges. A billiard table upholstered in a fawn-coloured cloth sits within one such games room, recalling a time during which "business and leisure once overlapped". Find out more about The Bell › Photo by Ernest Theofilus Mawi Garage, Indonesia, by Dhaniē & Sal A fleet of cars and motorbikes are housed within this renovated garage by local architecture practice Dhaniē & Sal, who added a similarly sleek apartment and office space to the building. Inside the apartment, a futuristic pool table with metal edges and feet, softened by a dusky rose-grey cloth top, sits in the living room. Find out more about Mawi Garage › Photo by Alison Gootee New Orleans renovation, USA, by Office La A billiard table with a wine-red top sits where a conventional dining table would in this residential kitchen of a pink-painted house in New Orleans . Elegant legs, leather pockets and the colourful pool balls add to the visually stimulating interior, which compiles a mosaic tiles floor, deep green cabinets, pink walls and framed artworks. Find out more about New Orleans renovation › Photo by William Jess Laird Jac's on Bond, USA, by Gachot Studios Local design studio Gachot Studios put a billiard table with a custom-designed camel-coloured top in the back of this snug New York neighbourhood bar. Its silvery metal-capped corners and black base ties in with the rest of the pared-back interior, populated with low mood lighting, contemporary art and black dining chairs. Find out more about Jac's on Bond › This is the latest in our lookbooks series, which provides visual inspiration from Dezeen's archive. For more inspiration, see previous lookbooks featuring wooden staircases , picture windows and cottage living rooms . title: Anam Design Studio adds club-like dining room to East Sussex home
summary: A red travertine kitchen and a dark dining room with rounded timber walls form the heart of this home in East Sussex by Irish interiors firm Anam Design Studio. Anam Design Studio overhauled the home interior with tactile stone surfaces and deep tones of wood and ceramic tiles, aiming to create a warm and inviting setting that The post Anam Design Studio adds club-like dining room to East Sussex home appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: A red travertine kitchen and a dark dining room with rounded timber walls form the heart of this home in East Sussex by Irish interiors firm Anam Design Studio. Anam Design Studio overhauled the home interior with tactile stone surfaces and deep tones of wood and ceramic tiles, aiming to create a warm and inviting setting that suited the client's love of craft. A kitchen with red travertine surfaces forms the heart of this home in East Sussex "We endeavour to use natural materials such as timber and stone in all our designs," Anam Design Studio director Liz Hughes told Dezeen. "We feel that as humans we are more akin to natural finishes in our environment and we also believe that they age better than man-made materials." "We find ourselves increasingly drawn to these materials in an age of technology and social media noise," she continued. The kitchen is connected to a round dining room lined with curved oak panels The kitchen was designed to be the heart of the home, with slabs of red travertine forming a kitchen island and countertops that wrap around the walls into a window bench. Bespoke dark oak cabinets and metallic accents add to the warm tones of the kitchen, and an existing black aga was re-enamelled in brown and bronze to fit the colour scheme. Anam Design Studio designed the dark dining area to have a club-like appearance Adjacent to the kitchen is a round dining room that Hughes described as "the most exciting but challenging part of the design". "The dining room had very little natural light, so we embraced this area by giving it the feel of a bar or club," she said. Read: DAB Studio lines kitchen of Dutch home with oak and Afromosia wood Two stone-lined openings puncture the curved oak walls on opposite sides of the dining room, which also has a hidden curved door leading to the lobby. Upholstered seating, shelving, and a stone-and-lacquer table were custom-made to fit the circular space, and a large rounded ceiling light illuminates the room from above. A stone-surround opening connects two reception spaces Elsewhere in the home are two connected reception spaces. The front room has a light and airy feel, while the adjacent reception and TV room has a deeper colour palette with lacquer-finished oak panels adorning the walls. Anam Design Studio added a stone surround to the opening between the light and dark rooms, aiming to highlight the difference between the spaces. The TV room has a dark material palette that contrasts the lightness of the adjacent room "The front reception is south-facing and has plenty of natural light," said Hughes. "In the rear reception we went moodier, as it was a place for quiet contemplation or nighttime entertainment." "We wanted to punctuate the opening between the two contrasting rooms," said Hughes. "In the rear reception, the stone [surround] marries beautifully with the dark timber panelling. In the front section, it contrasts with the off-white walls and complements the dark cardosa stone fireplace." Dark oak panelling also features in the bedrooms A similar mix of dark oak and stone surfaces was applied to the bedrooms and study, with natural wool and linen fabrics designed to add to the tactility of the interiors. A red-tiled bathroom in the home features a coordinating Rosso Levanto marble basin, and a green-tiled bathroom is complemented with Verde Alpi marble flooring. Other home interiors that used a rich mix of stone and wood include a family home in the Netherlands by DAB Studio and an energy-saving home in London by Architecture for London . The photography is by Daniëlle Siobhán . The post Anam Design Studio adds club-like dining room to East Sussex home appeared first on Dezeen .

title: Badweather converts derelict canal boat into London's first off-grid bathhouse
summary: Architecture collective Badweather has transformed a 17-metre canal boat into Soak, an off-grid bathhouse that moves to a new location along London's waterways every two weeks. Soak combines a wood-fired sauna, two cold plunge pools, showers, changing facilities and a small bar for up to 12 people. It operates without mains water, electricity or sewage connections, The post Badweather converts derelict canal boat into London's first off-grid bath

content.source_text: Architecture collective Badweather has transformed a 17-metre canal boat into Soak, an off-grid bathhouse that moves to a new location along London 's waterways every two weeks. Soak combines a wood-fired sauna , two cold plunge pools, showers, changing facilities and a small bar for up to 12 people. Soak is housed in a restored 56-foot widebeam canal boat It operates without mains water, electricity or sewage connections, instead drawing water directly from the canal and passing it through a six-stage filtration and UV treatment system before it is used for bathing. Electricity is generated by solar panels and stored in an onboard battery system, while a wood-fired stove provides heat for the sauna. The sauna is lined with timber and features a wood-burning stove The project was developed by Badweather co-founder Leo Sixsmith and chef and former restaurateur Riccardo Codacci-Pisanelli, who wanted to create a communal bathing space that could move through the city rather than occupy a permanent site. "The changing location of the boat means that the view through these windows is never the same," Sixsmith told Dezeen. Circular portholes bring views of the canalside vegetation into the sauna Soak began with a near-derelict 20-year-old canal boat, with rotten floors, water damage and a steel hull that required extensive restoration. Around 40 people worked on its conversion, with the existing hull dictating much of the interior layout. The exterior was painted cream with black and red detailing, while circular portholes puncture the sides of the boat. Read: Future Simple Studio creates "contemporary vocabulary" for Montreal bathhouse Inside, the original 11-inch openings have been enlarged to 18 and 32 inches, with fiery-red frames that make the windows stand out against the hull. At the bow, a large picture window replaces an original steel door, opening the narrow interior towards the water. Blue steps lead from the changing area towards the plunge room The interior follows the boat's long, narrow form. Visitors enter through a dark changing and reception area lined with stained marine plywood. They then pass into a brighter plunge and shower room, featuring pale green tiles, stainless-steel pools and a central skylight that brings daylight into the boat. "The wet room is intentionally kept completely free of timber," Sixsmith said. "Its harder, clinical finish allows for easier maintenance, while heightening the sensory contrast with the warmth of the sauna." Stainless-steel plunge pools sit beneath a central skylight in the wet room At the bow, the sauna is lined with thermally treated Aspen and Alder wood and is centred around a wood-burning stove. Two benches were suspended from aluminium beams rather than supported by legs, allowing them to overlap within the tapered hull. A large window frames the canal from one of the plunge pools The boat's cramped dimensions were a major constraint, but Badweather aimed to use them to shape the interior. "Every centimetre had to work exceptionally hard," Sixsmith said. Founded in London in 2019 by Oli Brenner, Sophie Mei Birkin and Sixsmith, Badweather is an experimental architecture, scenography and design collective working across installations, objects, lighting and buildings. A large window opens the sauna towards the surrounding canal landscape Its previous work includes temporary structures for nightclubs and festivals, including the ongoing Pipeline project, a floating communal hearth made from reused corrugated polycarbonate. Other bathhouses featured on Dezeen include a communal sauna and hydrotherapy bathhouse in Montreal and the turquoise-tiled Komaeyu public bathhouse in the suburbs of Tokyo. The photography is by Kaye Song. The post Badweather converts derelict canal boat into London's first off-grid bathhouse appeared first on Dezeen .

title: Merckx-Holvoet Architecten designs seaside penthouse to evoke North Sea coast
summary: The sandy tones of Belgium's North Sea shore informed the interiors of this penthouse, designed by Antwerp-based studio Merckx-Holvoet Architecten. The holiday home, named V Penthouse, occupies the ninth and tenth floors of a building in Duinbergen, a seaside village in the West Flanders region of Belgium. "[We] aimed for an interior that envelops without The post Merckx-Holvoet Architecten designs seaside penthouse to evoke North Sea coast appea

content.source_text: The sandy tones of Belgium's North Sea shore informed the interiors of this penthouse , designed by Antwerp-based studio Merckx-Holvoet Architecten. The holiday home, named V Penthouse, occupies the ninth and tenth floors of a building in Duinbergen, a seaside village in the West Flanders region of Belgium. Merckx-Holvoet Architecten has completed a penthouse in Belgium "[We] aimed for an interior that envelops without overwhelming, one that reveals itself slowly rather than all at once," Merckx-Holvoet Architecten co-founders Marc Merckx and Sebastien Holvoet told Dezeen. "The design centres on poetry and refinement, built around a reduced palette of materials and colours," the architects continued. Merckx-Holvoet Architecten filled the 150-square-metre penthouse with a pared-back material palette and neutral tones that echo the dunes of the beach it overlooks. "The starting point was the sand colour found along the coastline," project architect Jef De Saedeleer said. "Where the view stretches out over the sea, the material palette echoes this seamlessly." Sandy tones inform the interior scheme Throughout the residence, walls covered in sandblasted Travertino Noce stone are teamed with lime-based flooring and solid oakwood details. Across both floors, the penthouse follows a simple, rectangular layout, with an entrance foyer at the centre of the lower floor where Merckx-Holvoet Architecten installed a sculptural, solid oak staircase leading upstairs. V Penthouse features a pared-back material palette The foyer is flanked by a sea-view living room on one side and a kitchen-cum-dining area on the other – both opening into a verandah. The studio chose neutral-hued furnishings for the living room, which it paired with tactile, modernist furniture pieces including a coffee table clad in parchment leather. Read: Woonpioniers builds a house that "moves with the dunes" Floor-to-ceiling Travertino Noce shutters conceal built-in worktops and storage in the kitchen, complemented by an oak wood island topped with a chamfered block of Egyptian sandstone. Merckx-Holvoet Architecten custom-made an Italian lavastone-topped table and an L-shaped bench crafted with Egyptian sandstone and oak wood for the dining area. The studio also sourced woven dining chairs for this space. A solid oak staircase connects the two levels The homogeneous material palette continues in the primary bedroom and guest suites located upstairs. The primary bedroom features an ensuite topped with a sloping roof. Here, Merckx-Holvoet Architecten installed picture windows by the bathtub as well as the shower area, both providing endless views of the North Sea. Much of the furniture and lighting was custom-made by Merckx-Holvoet Architecten, including a mahogany table lamp and an outdoor aluminium stool for the verandah. Minimalist artwork is dotted across the walls, including pieces by artists Andy Warhol and Sol Lewitt. Picture windows provide endless views of the North Sea Merckx-Holvoet Architecten is an architecture and design practice founded in 2018 by Merckx and Holvoet. Elsewhere in Belgium, Atelier Vens Vanbelle referenced brick industrial buildings to create a family home and Studio Okami Architecten extended a residence by adding a pavilion-like volume clad in green marble . The photography is by Eric Petschek . The post Merckx-Holvoet Architecten designs seaside penthouse to evoke North Sea coast appeared first on Dezeen .

title: Ivy Studio creates "soothing" exotic animal clinic in brutalist Quebec bank
summary: Canada's Ivy Studio has transformed a 1970s bank into a veterinary clinic for exotic animals in Laval, Quebec, featuring minimalist interiors and soft lighting. The Fauna clinic occupies a standalone structure completed in a brutalist style near the waterfront, just over the Prairies River northwest of Montreal. Ivy Studio leaned into the building's existing style The post Ivy Studio creates "soothing" exotic animal clinic in brutalist Quebec ban

content.source_text: Canada's Ivy Studio has transformed a 1970s bank into a veterinary clinic for exotic animals in Laval, Quebec, featuring minimalist interiors and soft lighting. The Fauna clinic occupies a standalone structure completed in a brutalist style near the waterfront, just over the Prairies River northwest of Montreal. Consultation rooms at Fauna are offset from one another and fronted by sweeping walls Ivy Studio leaned into the building's existing style to inform the interiors, creating a calm, minimalist environment for the patients and their handlers. "By celebrating its historical shell, Fauna establishes a unique dialogue between imposing institutional architecture and the compassionate, soothing nature of veterinary care," the studio said. The staggered motif is also applied to the walnut reception counter The building spans 380 square metres over two levels, with the public areas and treatment facilities housed across the ground floor. Boasting 16-foot (4.9-metre) ceilings, the reception and waiting areas maximise natural light from the building's existing windows. The building's tall, coffered ceilings allow for dramatic architectural features The original concrete coffered ceiling is left exposed and painted a deep brown, contrasting concrete flooring and the warm grey of the textured plaster walls. Facing the waiting area, the four consultation rooms are arranged in an offset row through the centre of the plan. Fluted glass doors slide open to the consultation rooms Each is faced with a curved wall that sweeps up to the tall ceiling, mimicking the building's exterior, and is also denoted by vertical partitions with stepped end-profile details. "This dramatic gesture provides intimacy for the consultation rooms while serving as a sculptural focal point from the waiting area," said Ivy Studio. Walnut desks with chrome bases match the benches in the waiting ares Fluted glass doors slide open to access the consultation rooms, which feature walnut desks with chrome bases, matching the waiting room benches and the reception counter. The individual rooms all link to the treatment area behind, where a spiral staircase leads down to office, storage and research space in the basement. Read: Ivy Studio converts historic bank building into offices for Montreal ad agency Careful consideration was given to the lighting design, comprising diffused light boxes inside the consultation rooms along with the natural illumination in the other public spaces. "A soothing environment is paramount for an exotic animal clinic, where patients are easily stressed," Ivy Studio said. "The lighting strategy in the public zones is soft, dimmed, and strictly indirect." A spiral staircase leads down to a staff area in the basement In the treatment room and basement, the building's concrete bones are exposed, and the fluted concrete walls are painted soft cream. The bank's original vault is repurposed as a closed pharmacy and lab – the finishing touch in adapting the former financial institution into a contemporary medical facility. The original bank vault is repurposed as a closed pharmacy and lab Ivy Studio is perhaps best known for its hospitality projects across Canada, with completed restaurant projects ranging in style from Japanese minimalism to colourfully retro and bold and glamorous . The studio's commercial portfolio includes a dry cleaners modelled on a Parisian apartment , an all-black spinning studio and offices for a digital advertising agency also housed in a former bank. The photography is by Alex Lesage . title: Surrane Design uses "stages of the rice plant" to tone Thai restaurant in New York
summary: New York studio Surrane Design has outfitted Thai restaurant Hommali in New York with a terracotta floor, a central "courtyard" space and personal items of the founders to create a space that resembles a traditional Thai house. Hommali is located at the edges of New York's West Village neighbourhood and was founded by Bangkok natives The post Surrane Design uses "stages of the rice plant" to tone Thai restaurant in New York appeared first on Deze

content.source_text: New York studio Surrane Design has outfitted Thai restaurant Hommali in New York with a terracotta floor, a central "courtyard" space and personal items of the founders to create a space that resembles a traditional Thai house. Hommali is located at the edges of New York's West Village neighbourhood and was founded by Bangkok natives chef Chattchakorn "Benz" Khajornchaisan, general manager Kritayanee "Air" Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak "Picha" Srigungvarl after they moved to New York City and met in the hospitality scene. Surrane Design has completed a Thai restaurant in the West Village The restaurant contains an eight-seat bar, a 20-seat dining den, a semi-private mezzanine and auxiliary spaces such as a wine room and dry-age room where ducks and other ferments are on display. Surrane Design layered the space with a rich assortment of textures and patterns, such as dark wood millwork, a marbled bar top and artwork sourced from Bangkok's Chatuchak Weekend Market. It brings together a rich assortment of textures and colours informed by Thailand According to the team, its palette of browns and greens was informed by the life cycle of a rice plant. "The color palette is inspired by the stages of the rice plant: fresh green for young leaves, golden yellow for mature stalks, earthy brown for paddy soil, soft beige for rice husks, and warm cream white for polished rice," said the team. Personal items from the ownership team line a partition It was designed to resemble a traditional Thai house, where the central dining den and mezzanine above recall a courtyard, and the terracotta floor also calls to the vernacular architecture of the country. Visitors are greeted with a rice plant light installation at the doorway and enter by the bar, which is clad in a sandy fluted tile with seats upholstered in leather and velvet. Stairs lead to a mezzanine with additional seating Two booths sit in front of the main dining space, which is tucked beneath the mezzanine. Curtains and open shelving separate the two spaces. Personal items from the ownership team, such as vintage Thai cookbooks from the late 1960s and early 1970s and other objects "one would expect to find in a living room" line the shelves. Small bamboo sculptures by Thai artist Korakot Aromdee are also peppered throughout the space. Read: OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum is "hidden in plain sight" Wood-lined stairs lead to the mezzanine above, which contains additional seating concealed behind a frosted glass railing. A large skylight hangs above the space and sits over a large dining table. Banquets and an off-white white wallpaper embossed with 3D-printed plants also line the space. Like below, a curtain can be drawn across the length of the space to provide additional separation. A large skylight hangs above the space Hommali will serve contemporary takes on traditional Thai dishes created under Benz, such as a seafood cocktail with razor clams imbued with the hot and sour notes of tom yum and the Tomato, "a michelada-meets-spritz with a Singaporean rice wine base accompanied by a Thai chile tincture." Surrane Design is an independent design studio based in Brooklyn by partners Bud Nitaya and Yoon Her. Other recently opened spaces in the West Village include Love Thy Neighbour next to The Stonewall Inn and The Cherry Lane Theatre The photography is by Hommali The post Surrane Design uses "stages of the rice plant" to tone Thai restaurant in New York appeared first on Dezeen .

title: Studio Cadena fills Medellín cafe with 31 towering wooden columns
summary: Architecture firm Studio Cadena has designed a forest-like interior for the Masa cafe in Medellín, Colombia, where over 30 plywood columns stretch to a concrete ceiling to create an "atmosphere without walls or enclosure". For the design of the spacious cafe in Colombia's second largest city, the studio focused on two main materials: concrete and The post Studio Cadena fills Medellín cafe with 31 towering wooden columns appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Architecture firm Studio Cadena has designed a forest-like interior for the Masa cafe in Medellín , Colombia, where over 30 plywood columns stretch to a concrete ceiling to create an "atmosphere without walls or enclosure". For the design of the spacious cafe in Colombia's second largest city, the studio focused on two main materials: concrete and wood. The eatery's main area, a six-metre-tall room where guests can enjoy Masa's coffees, smoothies and food, is defined by two large concrete slabs that appear to be held up by numerous slender columns. The Masa cafe in Medellín has towering wooden pillars However, the columns aren't load-bearing, but were introduced to create a striking interior that resembles a stylised forest. "They do not carry the building; they carry the room," Studio Cadena said. "Freed from load-bearing duty, they are multiplied across the interior to structure movement, filter light, and create a layered space, without the use of walls or partitions." Studio Cadena combined concrete and wood for the interior To Studio Cadena founder Benjamin Cadena, the repetitive design is what defines the architecture of the space. "The concept was to shape the space's atmosphere without walls or enclosure," he told Dezeen. "31 wooden columns sit within a six-metre-tall volume between two slabs. One move, repeated, does all the architectural work." The cafe connects with the outdoors The architect carefully considered what material would have the most impact, landing on plywood due to its ability to subtly reflect the light in the space. "Untreated pine-faced plywood was used to form the six-meter-tall columns," Cadena said. "Light bouncing off their surface is what gives the space its particular quality by introducing a diffused warmth." Read: Jagged windows pierce Studio Cadena's Masa bakery in Bogotá His studio left the concrete structure exposed throughout the cafe to show the "raw shell" of the building, and refrained from adding too many materials to the pared-back space. "Few materials were used," Cadena explained. "Wood, a marble counter, stainless steel for smaller pieces, with the structural shell left untouched." "It was an intentional choice to be resourceful, and reflects a recurring interest in reducing the design to the essential elements that shape how the space will be used and felt over time," Cadena continued. A circular opening gives a view into the production space One side of the large room opens up towards a green outdoor space, with the wooden columns leading out towards the exterior to underline the connection to nature. At the back of the room, a circular window gives visitors a view of the cafe's production area. The studio added a marble bar to the interior Throughout the space, Studio Cadena chose to let the materials speak for themselves, rather than using different colours. "More than colour, the idea was contrast between the existing structure and what was introduced," Cadena said. "Materials were left untreated, with more attention given to texture than hue. Colour enters the space indirectly, through natural materials, vegetation, and ultimately its occupants." Materials in the cafe were left untreated Other Medellín projects featured on Dezeen include a flat that "channels the 1980s" and a concrete office building on a steep hillsite . The photography is by Juan Camilo Roa . Project credits: Architect: Benjamin Cadena / Studio Cadena Project team: Benjamin Cadena, Thomas Gomez, Ospina, Alma Karlsson The post Studio Cadena fills Medellín cafe with 31 towering wooden columns appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Finnish firm Elementic has unveiled MO6, a wall-surfacing material produced from forestry industry offcuts that is almost pure carbon . Called MO6, the product takes the form of thick, lightweight tiles with a rough texture and an off-black colour. Materials technology company Elementic established MO6 as a brand in May, with the debut collection, MO6 Eternal, launched on Wednesday at trade fair Habitare . MO6 says its product can store carbon for thousands of years MO6 claims to be the most carbon-negative , or carbon-storing, building material in the world, with carbon molecules making up 90 per cent of its chemistry. It uses lignin as a raw material – a by-product of the forestry and timber industry that is considered difficult to use and is usually burned for energy. Through a patented process that remains highly secretive, impurities such as oxygen are removed from the lignin in a bioreactor to result in a material that is highly durable and fire-resistant with a dramatic aesthetic. The tiles are already being delivered to projects "It's quite a challenging material, but we love lignin because it's a very carbon-rich raw material," MO6 general manager Johanna Normiala told Dezeen. "In our process, the know-how is all about knowing how you transform lignin to make it something useful," she continued. "We take the lignin, we create a kind of dough that we bake like a cake, and in the end we get a hard, resistant, durable material but which is lightweight." MO6 is produced from lignin, which is usually burned MO6, which describes itself as a "premium interior design brand", is already delivering product to projects, including a spa under construction in Paris. "We are very much eager to help or support our customers whatever is the area of application, but I would say that the focused interest are in [the] area of hotels, restaurants – I think that's that's something where this material goes very well," said Normiala. For the time being, MO6 is only being marketed as suitable for dry indoor spaces, but Elementic has ambitions for much wider applications and is currently developing bricks. Read: Tarkett achieves "world's first" carbon negative linoleum "There's a huge potential for that, not only interior part, which is now our first business, but in future in a much larger scale in building," said Normiala. MO6 Eternal tiles are available with a rougher or smoother finish, and can be coated. According to Normiala, its thermal and acoustic properties are comparable to wood, but MO6 is hopeful that improvements can be made with tweaks to the manufacturing process in future. MO6 parent Elementic hopes its innovation will soon be usable as a structural material Carbon negativity refers to something that removes more carbon dioxide equivalent from the atmosphere than it emits. In the case of a material, emissions are generally produced during manufacture and end-of-life. The issue of carbon storage has attracted major focus among architects in recent years, driven by concern about the vast carbon emissions associated with constructing buildings. Read: The Dezeen guide to carbon Timber has been the subject of renewed interest as a building material as a result, thanks to the carbon sequestered by trees. According to MO6, one kilogram of its material stores approximately 2.4 kilograms of atmospheric carbon dioxide – roughly double the amount stored by wood . MO6 says its material can keep carbon locked up for potentially thousands of years, because it does not decay and is easy to recycle. For now, MO6 is only being marketed for use in dry interior spaces Dezeen previously explored innovations seeking to store and utilise atmospheric carbon through our Carbon revolution series. Other projects published on Dezeen that aim to put lignin to use include a bioplastic developed by German designer Basse Stittgen and a structural panel by Denmark's Natural Material Studio . The photography is courtesy of MO6. Habitare took place during Helsinki Design Week from 28 August to 6 September. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. summary: Chinese interior designer Bin Wu's book Timeless East explores the idea of a design language rooted in the philosophical context of the East. content.source_text: Chinese interior designer Bin Wu 's book Timeless East explores the idea of a design language rooted in the philosophical context of the East. For this roundup, he picks six of his own favourite projects in China and abroad. The Design Language of Timeless East features 17 projects completed by Wu and his studio W Design , spanning interior design, art installations and design research. Wu's aim was to challenge the absence of Eastern voices from modern design narratives. Instead, he hoped to show Eastern design through a different lens that would be more true to its original roots and promote a spiritual connection. The new book features 17 projects completed by Bin Wu and his studio W Design "Whether it was the Japonisme of the nineteenth century or the Chinoiserie of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, these were projections of the Eastern imagination filtered through a Western lens – not distillations of Eastern culture and art articulated by the East itself," Wu told Dezeen. "Even in the wake of China's rapid economic ascent over the past two decades, this predicament remains unresolved," he continued. "The Design Language of Timeless East is a response issued from the Eastern subject itself." Here, Dezeen selects six projects from the book that explore the Timeless East design language: Photo by Wang Ting Hai Shang restaurant, Shanghai, 2023 At this fusion restaurant in Shanghai , Wu combined raw materials with a dark colour palette to create a subtle atmosphere with a mysterious feel. Sea reeds are stacked into a circular enclosure at the entrance, which leads to a narrow corridor paved with rustic stone. This was designed to be reminiscent of old Chinese water towns – historic towns known for their bridges and rivers – and opens up to an open kitchen. The studio kept the exposed beams to reveal the history of the building, while adding a countertop crafted from a massive ink stone. Photo by Wang Ting The Fame, Chengdu, 2024 Wu designed this visitor centre for a residential complex in Chengdu , using locally sourced materials to evoke the experience of wandering in a garden. The entrance hall was clad with bamboo strips that allow light to filter through the gaps, creating a constantly shifting interplay of light and shadow. Connecting corridors weave together various open spaces, creating a fluid and ever-changing atmosphere that aligns with the Chinese garden principle of "not revealing everything at once". The main social space features dark terracotta panels on the wall that were designed to resemble local roof tiles in a nod to the rustic mountain dwellings nearby. Photo by Wang Ting Deqin Meri Poodom Hotel, Deqin, 2024 Located at the foot of Meri Snow Mountain, a sacred place for the local Tibetan community, this hotel design aims to balance spirituality and everyday living. Wu designed its central staircase to evoke a white pagoda – a historic building of religious significance. He created its encased and overlapping stairs, each turning at a forty-five-degree angle, for visitors to feel like they are climbing towards the sky. Locally relevant objects were incorporated into the interiors, including yak bells and black pottery. All guest rooms frame part of the Meri Mountain, which has 13 sacred peaks in total, to make visitors feel closer to the heart of Tibetan faith. Photo by Zheng Hao Collector's Mansion, Shanghai, 2024 W Design completed the facade renovation, as well as a display apartment, for this luxury residential complex in Shanghai's former French Concession. Orderly arranged balconies add a sense of rhythm to the otherwise clean, minimalist facade. Inside the apartment, the living room opens up after a narrow foyer. The interiors have a restrained colour and material palette to create a tranquil atmosphere and include tactile furniture with rough surfaces designed to resemble old objects. Photo by Shi Dai Pan Yuan: Momentality Unfold, Milan, 2024 Wu revealed this paper installation during Milan Design Week 2024. Located in the central courtyard of the Cortile d'Onore at the University of Milan, the installation reflected the Eastern architectural emphasis on change, seeking eternity within impermanence. Based on the theme "momentality", it used large-scale paper scrolls, a material commonly found in Eastern architecture and painting, to form an Eastern garden experience that contrasted the surrounding historical architecture. The installation was made from lightweight and durable DuPont Tyvek paper, which has a texture that strongly resembles traditional Eastern Xuan paper. Photo by Zhu Di Arbour, Shanghai, 2025 W Design created a quietly elegant "indoor theatre" for this residence in Shanghai, where soft lighting, a spiral staircase, and refined vintage furnishings evoke a sense of nostalgia. Drapes were used across dining rooms and bedrooms to soften the spatial boundaries, while wood furniture and timber flooring add warmth to the space. content.source_text: London studio Piercy & Company has taken over an apartment in the north of the city and given it a new interior featuring custom timber joinery and a mysterious curved corridor. Apartment 21 was conceived by Piercy & Company as a space for hosting private events and exhibitions, or for accommodating guests. Piercy & Company plans to host dinners and events in the apartment The design brings complexity to what was previously a highly minimal, open-plan home. The new layout brings contrasts of dark and light, with spaces revealed gradually rather than all at once. Key interventions include the curved wall, directing focus to an artwork rather than to the bedroom, which is now hidden behind a concealed door. A circular window unites a wall and door crafted from ash wood Elsewhere, a floor-to-ceiling joinery element separates the main living space from a new study. This incorporates both a wall and a door, united by a large circular window cutout. Piercy & Company co-director Fiona Neil said she and the team found "a sense of play and a joy in subverting expectations", rather than sticking with the tried-and-tested open-plan approach. "We focused on changes in volume and spatial character, in the use of solid and natural materials, and in the human-to-human spark of art and crafted objects," she told Dezeen. A curved corridor is painted in a contrasting dark shade The apartment is located in a neo-Georgian 1920s building that was once part of North London Polytechnic but was converted into residential in the late 1990s. It was previously the home of a gallerist who would occasionally stage exhibitions inside. This was how Stuart Piercy, Piercy & Company's founding director, first discovered it. The curve directs focus to an artwork rather than to the bedroom When the owner decided to sell, Piercy was keen to build on this tradition by using the 103-square-metre space as a testing ground for the architecture studio's recently launched interior-design arm, led by Neil. The idea was to create a space where people can share meals and conversation, guided by the principles of neuroaesthetics. Read: EBBA founder's all-timber London apartment celebrates "alive and imperfect" wood "The psychological and physiological effects spaces have on us lie at the core of our interiors studio," Neil said. "Here, we had the opportunity to witness the effects of experimenting with the compression and expansion of volumes, and the response to natural materials and plays on spatial perception; that all feeds back into the studio's work." A wall opening connects the kitchen with the living space The importance of hosting is made clear as soon as you enter. One of the first things you see is a wall of integrated shelving made from British elm, filled with glasses, tableware and a selection of cookbooks. The kitchen is located opposite, with a wall cutaway that opens the space up to the adjacent living and dining room. The joinery and dining table were both custom-made by furniture maker Benchmark Piercy & Company collaborated with British furniture maker Benchmark on all the custom woodwork, including a 14-seat dining table crafted from British ash. Other elements in the living space include a doughnut-shaped mirror sculpture by Poland-based Zieta Studio, iconic mid-century chairs by Alvar Aalto, Poul Cadovius and Nanna Ditzel, and textile drapes that extend from ceiling to floor. The circular window cutout frames a view through to the study, which features a curated library wall and a mezzanine loft. Artworks are on display throughout the house The mood is notably different in the more private areas of the apartment, signalled by the dark tones of the connecting corridor. The bathroom incorporates a curved shower, lined with dark grey tiles made from compressed basalt chips, which Neil said "feels like showering in a cave". The bedroom is tucked away at the back and is currently set up to double as a drawing studio. The bedroom is currently styled as a drawing studio Current artworks on display include pieces by Flora Yukhnovich, Jess Allen, John Virtue, Antony Gormley, Peter Cook, Guan Lee and Fabine Verbier, but are likely to change over time. The studio also plans to introduce new furniture designs over time. "We intend to keep evolving the space and using it as a testing ground for both materials and objects," said Neil. Tableware is displayed on bespoke shelving in the hallway "We are currently developing a light fitting with Hand & Eye; we will use Apartment 21 as a testing space at prototype stage and then later showcase the fitting in the space on a more long-term basis," she added. "Hosting temporary curations of art and objects is something we also hope to develop." The bathroom features dark grey tiles made from compressed basalt chips Other interior projects completed by Piercy & Company in London include an apartment in the former BBC Television Centre and a refurbishment of an office building in Mayfair . Piercy sees these projects as equally important as the studio's architectural output. "I've never believed scale changes the intensity of the question," he said. "A tower has to meet the ground the way a handle has to meet a hand – with the same sense of connection, the same care for how a hand rests, a body turns, a pause." The photography is by Jasper Fry . content.source_text: US celebrity Gwyneth Paltrow has collaborated with Texas-based studio Michael Hsu Office of Architecture on the first sit-down restaurant for wellness company Goop, giving visitors "a new way to experience the brand". Goop Kitchen Del Mar opened on 31 August and is located at the One Paseo shopping complex in San Diego . It is the first location of a broader expansion for Goop subsidiary Goop Kitchen, which plans to open additional locations across the region and New York City. Goop Kitchen has opened its first brick-and-mortar location in San Diego The interior design is coastal, with a mix of walnut millwork, banquets with striped upholstery, and a slew of textured surfaces, including a tiled floor. A black-and-white colour palette was used throughout. According to the team, Paltrow worked closely with Michael Hsu Office of Architecture and "personally curated every detail" to make the space feel "elevated yet welcoming". "Gwyneth has a real design vocabulary, so we could go deeper with her than we usually can – down to the nuance of how a piece of stone meets a piece of wood," said studio founder Michael Hsu. "Her attention to detail made the spaces sharper and more considered." Visitors enter upon a large marble wall Visitors enter a "dramatically veined marble feature wall", where an ordering system rests on a large wooden desk. Banquet seating is lined up against large steel-framed windows and spreads out into the centre of the space. Details include brushed-metal pendant lights and two thin rows of black-and-white checked tiles on the floor. Walnut wood banquets fill the dining room The details were meant to align with San Diego's beach oceanside culture. "Designed to feel elevated yet welcoming, the interior is anchored by a dramatically veined marble feature wall and layered with warm, natural details," said the team. "The space works for everything from a weekday lunch or sunset dinner, capturing the sun-soaked essence of San Diego." Read: Michael Hsu designs Shake Shack's New York headquarters in industrial space On the outside patio, the restaurant is outfitted with mint green metal chairs, marble table-tops and the same striped upholstery. Scalloped pagoda umbrellas lined with a black edge also fill the outdoor space. Visitors can order dishes such as an assortment of salads and bowls. Goop Kitchen will also explore expanding the menu to "take full advantage of having its first sit-down restaurant", according to the team. "The 92-seat flagship gives guests a new way to experience the brand, marking its first dedicated dine-in location," said Goop. An outdoor patio is outfitted with cloth umbrellas and mint green chairs Goop Kitchen was launched in 2021 primarily as a takeout and delivery service and an "upscale fast-casual concept". According to the team, it plans to open locations in La Jolla, downtown San Diego and Manhattan next. The Goop brand has been controversial since its launch . Paltrow herself has drawn scrutiny on social media recently for reportedly planning a dinner party for AI CEO Sam Altman . The Michael Hsu office has worked on a number of restaurants, including a Houston seafood restaurant and an eatery in Austin housed in a building from the 1890s . The studio has also worked with larger chains before, such as designing the Shake Shack headquarters in New York . The photography is by Michael PH Clifford. title: H3O uses "playful and intelligent gestures" to update historic Barcelona home

content.source_text: Barcelona-based H3O architects has renovated a 19th-century house in the city's Gracia neighbourhood, taking care to preserve heritage elements while introducing quirky details like hidden windows. Casa Plató is a formerly rural house that was transformed into a grand residence by the ancestors of its current owner, who added a tower, galleries, mouldings and balustrades in the late 19th century. H3O architects has renovated a 19th-century house in the city's Gracia neighbourhood The house was in need of restoration, but H3O was asked to retain the authenticity of its interiors and gardens, which have featured in numerous period film productions. "Casa Plató synthesises a double condition: it is both stage and dwelling," the architects explained. "A house that keeps a story alive, but that also allows fiction. A house that embraces what has been and what could exist in other cinematic realities." The house was in need of restoration H3O's project focused on the ground floor and adjacent outdoor areas, with interventions including expanding the kitchen, adding a bathroom and introducing new openings to brighten the house's central areas. The architects analysed films shot in the house to help determine a strategy for preserving its identity by carefully restoring heritage elements such as the mosaic floors, radiators, mouldings and colour palette. The existing kitchen was subtly enlarged "We greatly enjoyed thinking about the project as a dialogue or continuation with the pre-existing building, but from absolute respect and with playful and intelligent gestures," the studio added. "We did not want to create an intervention based on contrast or rupture, but rather an improvement through understanding what already existed." Dark tiles echo the tone of the original flooring The existing kitchen was subtly updated by enlarging the space and introducing elements that complement the original wooden cabinetry and marble sink. Dark tiles echo the tone of the previous floor, while a white geometric cooker hood, a wooden shelf and a wavy wooden table enhance the room's practicality. A circular shower forms the centrepiece of the bathroom A new terrace adjoining the kitchen strengthens the relationship between the interior and exterior spaces, with deep-blue tiles used on the steps evoking those found in the existing courtyard garden. The original bathroom was entirely preserved, and the studio also added a new bathroom that features clean lines and a minimalist palette that references its predecessor's modernist style. A circular shower enclosed by a matching curtain forms the centrepiece of the room, which features white mosaic tiles, a dark floor and stainless-steel washbasins with a marble countertop. Rounded shapes used throughout the bathroom also evoke the forms found in modernist architecture, including a circular mirror, curved taps and orb-shaped wall lamps. Read: H3O creates "unpredictable" zigzagging interiors for lightning-struck home "Modernism recovered these geometries that are marine, part of nature and more organic," explained the architects, who also added a porthole-like pivoting window in one of the bedrooms. "We found it playful to introduce these forms in elements such as the pivoting circular window, which works like an eye that opens and closes, allowing visual connections between rooms." Rounded shapes feature throughout The house's most distinctive heritage spaces were preserved largely as they were found, including the dining room with its decorative wallpaper, plaster mouldings, tiled floor and cast-iron radiators. Elsewhere, existing fixtures and fittings were repurposed to maintain a connection with the past, such as the salvaged marble surfaces in the kitchen and existing doors that were carefully relocated. The architects preserved the generously sized garden Previously dingy circulation spaces at the centre of the floor plan are brightened by the addition of three strategically placed windows, one of which is concealed behind a painting. The generously sized garden was preserved as one of the few remaining green spaces in an increasingly densified neighbourhood, providing a link back to the house's rural roots. H3O was founded in 2017 by Adrià Orriols, Joan Gener and Miquel Ruiz. The studio approaches architecture through a critical and experimental lens, with each project engaging directly with its physical, social and cultural context. Previous projects have included a converted barn with zigzagging interiors and a communal blue tile-clad barbecue . The photography is by Simone Marcolin . content.source_text: This waterfront residence overlooking Michigan 's Grand Traverse Bay has been reimagined to include a "mosh pit" lounge by California-based Lauri Design Studio. Willow Point was originally built in 2005 in a contemporary style, which lacked the warmth that its new owners envisioned for their quiet lakeside life. Willow Point's original steel staircase was refaced in a metallic plaster to add depth and texture They called upon Lauri Design Studio founder Jenni Lauri to bring out the softer side of the architecture, using natural materials and handcrafted details. "For this project, every decision – from reworking the architecture to layering natural materials – was guided by how the home would be lived in, creating spaces that feel calm, connected, and meant for gathering," said Lauri. A new window provides the kitchen with a view of the surrounding forest The floor plan was completely reimagined to strengthen the relationship between the interior and the surrounding landscape. Staircases were relocated, sight lines were cleared and views were framed – all while improving the overall spatial flow. A Kelly Farley sculpture creates a focal point in the living and dining area The glass-wrapped lower floor's interconnected areas include the kitchen, dining room, living room and family room, intended to be used as a large gathering space. A new picture window created through a concrete wall provides the kitchen with a view of the forest, while textured Ceppo stone was chosen for countertops and surfaces due to its resemblance to Lake Michigan's sandy shores. The home's main entry stair was relocated and reimagined in travertine and ash In the living and dining area, a beaded Kelly Farley sculpture is suspended from the ceiling beside a reimagined fireplace, and surrounded by a mix of soft and metallic furniture. "Layered textures and sculptural furnishings create an atmosphere that feels both refined and welcoming, encouraging long conversations and quiet evenings overlooking the water," said the studio. Read: Wheeler Kearns wraps Michigan lake house with two tones of wood The original steel switchback staircase in the centre of the dwelling connects all three floors, and was refinished in a metallic plaster to add texture and depth. The main entry staircase was relocated and reconstructed with solid travertine, ash treads and a curved plaster handrail. A large lounge area named the "mosh pit" offers a comfy spot for the whole family Upstairs, a family "mosh pit" was formed in a newly created loft space, providing a cushioned area for relaxing together with views across the lake. "Inspired by the nostalgia of a sunken living room, it has become the family's favorite gathering place, hosting everything from card games and movie nights to afternoon naps and grandchildren playing after long days on the lake," the studio said. A travertine vanity in the primary suite has a prime lake view The primary suite was modelled after a private apartment, featuring its own lounge and kitchenette, as well as an integrated Travertino Rizzi stone bathroom vanity overlooking Grand Traverse Bay. "More than any individual room, the home was designed around the family's evolving traditions, creating spaces where multiple generations can gather, reconnect, and build memories for years to come," Lauri Design Studio said. The residence was originally built in 2005 on the shore of Lake Michigan's Grand Traverse Bay Michigan's extensive shorelines along three of North America's Great Lakes offer countless potential for waterfront dwellings. Other examples in the state include a wood-wrapped house comprising three separate structures by Wheeler Kearns Architects, a multi-level home for "people of all ages and mobilities" by DMAC Architecture & Interiors and a residence with two wings that intersect at irregular angles by Snow Kreilich. title: Leroy Street Studio renovates historic New York City theatre for A24
summary: For its first brick-and-mortar venue, production company A24 worked with New York design office Leroy Street Studio to overhaul the city's oldest Off-Broadway theatre to host live productions and screen movies. A24 purchased the Cherry Lane Theatre in 2023 with plans to maintain its historic name and status as a live-theatre venue. Working with Leroy The post Leroy Street Studio renovates historic New York City theatre for A24 appeared first on D

content.source_text: For its first brick-and-mortar venue, production company A24 worked with New York design office Leroy Street Studio to overhaul the city's oldest Off-Broadway theatre to host live productions and screen movies. A24 purchased the Cherry Lane Theatre in 2023 with plans to maintain its historic name and status as a live-theatre venue. Working with Leroy Street Studio (LSS), the studio's construction affiliate BLDG and restaurateur Zeb Stewart, the production house then renovated the building's main theatre and overhauled the interior. Leroy Street Studio acted as a design-build studio for the renovation of Cherry Lane Theatre The project also included adding Wild Cherry , a speakeasy-like restaurant run by the group behind the city's popular Frenchette bistro, with interior design by Stewart. The theatre links two brick buildings along a tight curve on Commerce Street in New York City's West Village neighbourhood. The buildings date back to the 1830s, when they were used for manufacturing before becoming a theatre in 1924 – the taller of the two once operated as a grain silo. The studio focused on revealing the building's original character while modernising the spaces For the A24 update, Leroy Street Studio focused on synthesising the layers of bygone renovations the building had gone through, while paying respects to its history, such as colour-matching and repainting the theatre's bright red doors by working with the original painter. "When we arrived, it had a very early 2000s renovation in place," LSS senior interiors associate Leslie Bailey told Dezeen. "We wanted to strip that back, celebrate some of the original features, and be mindful about what we were putting over it." The main stage converts into a small movie theatre via a giant screening rig that descends from the ceiling "A lot of our work was about peeling back," added LSS senior associate Alex Witko. One of the larger projects was renovating the original main stage into a dual-purpose theatre for live performances and film. This required the addition of a giant screening rig, outfitted with speakers, that descends from the stage's upper canopy. The ticket booth is clad in a deep blue tile Updates in the space included exposing the original brick walls and replacing the seating with lush mossy green seats. It also required the studio to consider the vastly different audio conditions needed for the entertainment styles. To accommodate a film screening, for instance, curtains are pulled across the walls, while they remain open for plays. The conversion can happen within minutes if needed, according to LSS, as the theatre switches between programming often. The same blue tile runs into the lobby Elsewhere throughout the building, the studio built a box office that flows from the street into a lobby concession stand clad with the same ocean blue brick tile. The lobby area is small, with a historic exposed brick wall and restrooms to one side and the entrance to Wild Cherry towards the other, which is concealed behind a deep red curtain. A restaurant is concealed behind a curtain For the restaurant, the studio developed a low, scalloped ceiling and then worked with Stewart to create a space with "texture upon-texture" to match an eccentric menu. According to LSS, the team shaped the ceiling to protect sound from carrying up to residential units above the space, as the room was also once a small theatre. Read: Lights glow through slatted teak facades of Hamptons home by Leroy Street Studio "Historically, when the black box theatre was here, and they would have to put on a show, they would call all the residents above and ask them to be quiet," said Witko. "There was no separation." "One of the things that we did that I think was very successful in the space was create a series of boxes within boxes. So above [the ceiling], there are actually two more ceilings that separate the restaurant from the residential floors." The speakeasy-like Wild Cherry contains "texture upon texture" The Cherry Lane Theatre and Wild Cherry opened last year, with the venue slowly rolling out performances and screenings such as the play Weer . It is A24's first brick-and-mortar location and joins other companies such as Amazon investing in live-performance venues . Leroy Street Studio previously designed a Hamptons home and also curated an exhibition at its Allen Street Gallery during this year's New York design week . The photography is by Brian Ferry Project credits: Architecture: Leroy Street Studio Interiors: Leroy Street Studio Wild Cherry interior: Zeb Stewart Construction: BLDG Inc The post Leroy Street Studio renovates historic New York City theatre for A24 appeared first on Dezeen .

title: Aethos London Shoreditch designed using an "East meets East" approach
summary: Boutique hotel brand Aethos has opened its first London outpost with interiors designed by Astet Studio in a Ron Arad Associates building that was formerly home to Nobu Hotel Shoreditch. Created by Astet Studio, the interiors of Aethos London Shoreditch were designed to blend the industrial design language of the original building with a softer Japanese-inspired The post Aethos London Shoreditch designed using an "East meets East" approach appear

content.source_text: Boutique hotel brand Aethos has opened its first London outpost with interiors designed by Astet Studio in a Ron Arad Associates building that was formerly home to Nobu Hotel Shoreditch. Created by Astet Studio , the interiors of Aethos London Shoreditch were designed to blend the industrial design language of the original building with a softer Japanese-inspired material palette. Astet Studio used earthy tones to introduced warmth into the industrial setting "When we first approached the project, we saw an opportunity to explore what we call East meets East," Astet Studio co-founder Oscar Engroba told Dezeen. "Rather than recreating Shoreditch's industrial past, we wanted to bring its existing character into conversation with the precision and craftsmanship of Japanese design traditions." Textured fabrics were used to absorb rather than reflect light in the breakfast room The Barcelona -based interiors studio was inspired by the Japanese concept of Utsuroi for the project, explaining to Dezeen that its employment meant "the architecture stays constant while the experience quietly evolves". Astet Studio used the Japanese concept of Utsuroi to evolve the hotel's lobby, bar, gym, members' lounge and Mitsu restaurant . The 164-room hotel, originally built in 2017, is defined by its striking industrial facade, featuring cantilevered balconies framed in glass, steel, and concrete. Aethos London Shoreditch is housed in a building designed by Ron Arad Associates Guests enter through this layered concrete facade into an open lobby characterised by earthy browns and muted natural tones, which was designed to introduce warmth into the industrial setting. "We wanted guests to feel welcome and connected to the rhythm of Shoreditch, while still offering moments of calm," said Engroba. "The colour palette draws from the Japanese Shin-Bijutsukai movement, using natural materials, planting and filtered light to soften the architecture without diminishing its character." Aethos London Shoreditch fuses East London's industrial design language with "the craftsmanship of Japanese design traditions" Contemporary, low-height seating was used throughout the space, while a series of large, textured rugs zone the space to create areas of relaxation. Vintage decorative pieces and furniture were used intentionally throughout the lobby alongside works by local artists and designers to connect the interior to its east London roots. Astet Studio brings warmth and tactility to the industrial spaces by using bespoke wood panelling across the lobby area, breakfast rooms and bedrooms. The timber detailing across the interiors of Aethos draws inspiration from traditional Japanese carpentry "The palette combines hand-finished timber, textured ceramics, woven fabrics and predominantly matte finishes," Engroba explained. "By favouring materials that absorb rather than reflect light, the interiors develop subtle changes throughout the day, giving the spaces a quieter, more tactile quality." Astet Studio designed the bedrooms to have a more refined and pared-back colour palette In the bedrooms, the studio shifted the material palette to be simpler and more refined, featuring muted tones of grey, burnt orange, and blackened wood. "In the bedrooms, the focus moves towards comfort, tactility and a quieter sensory experience," said Engroba. "Materials become softer, lighting more controlled and the overall atmosphere more intimate, creating a retreat within the city." Aethos London Shoreditch features 164 hotel rooms plus a restaurant and private members bar Other Japanese-style interiors recently featured on Dezeen include Mitsu restaurant in London and Genso restaurant by Joyce Wang Studio in Tokyo . The photography is Pion Studio . The post Aethos London Shoreditch designed using an "East meets East" approach appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: US studio IA has combined Craftsman-style detailing and a minimalist technical look with the details of a historic building for AI company Notion in San Francisco , California. IA designed the headquarters for Notion, an artificial intelligence (AI) company valued at $11 billion, through five floors of the 1907 Monadnock Building in downtown San Francisco. IA designed an office for Notion in San Francisco According to IA, Notion originally came to them with a brief for a "clean and light" approach that didn't involve traditional detailing. However, in its peeling back of remodels from past tenants, including Uber, IA discovered historic materials and details, shifting the goals of the design to accommodate the building's historic resource. This included Columbia Marble floors hidden under linoleum and wood sliding-sash windows. The office comprises five levels in the historic Monadnock Building The studio implemented the Craftsman style to bridge the gap, repairing the historical detailing in the process. "As this project progressed and more of the historic building revealed itself, the concept shifted to intentionally honor the property's history while remaining true to the spirit of the original design aesthetic," IA design director Kristoffer Tendall told Dezeen. "We proposed the Craftsman style to combine the two, using simple and timeless details with clean and square edges," he continued. "This maintained Notion's core aesthetic principles while acknowledging the building's roots." IA used a Craftsman-style scheme to bridge the historic building with the high-tech company The five floors of work and amenity spaces feature lounge areas, a training room and a library. Entrance to the building is through an adjacent alleyway, and the lobby features a burled-wood reception desk and a prominent Gerrit Rietveld chair. IA utilised curtains to create modular spaces Throughout, the studio used custom-stained cherry wood for the wainscoting, decorative ceiling panels and on the wrap-around staircase that descends into the private cafe. Its central lobby area features drapery that can be pulled to create private space between waist-height wood-clad dividers. The curtains are echoed in one of the primary work halls, which feature cafeteria-style seating and break-out areas. Read: Charlap Hyman & Herrero adds custom workstations to futuristic LA office IA's Craftsman references can be most seen in the library, which features a geometric decorative ceiling and a higher wainscoting profile with tiered capitals. Throughout, rich tapestry rugs are paired with mid-century modern furniture, much of it wooden as well. The whole of the interior is oriented around a central courtyard, which was also updated for use by the company. Cherry-wood detailing was used for wall and ceiling treatments Tendall also said that the windows were oriented to take in views of the surrounding historic district as well as opening up the space to highlight the historic details. "Little design moments were added to further honor the building's historic components, including a fire-rated window in the lounge that creates a featured view to the historic cast-bronze interior stair, and reclaimed bar tops found in basement storage that were repurposed standing bar rails," he said. "Several prohibition-era objects found during construction were preserved and displayed, as well as a framed original section of the blueprint, helping to honor and tell the unique story of the building." He added that the team subtly highlighted disjunctions between the historic layouts and the renovation. "For example, when the existing marble floors didn't perfectly match the office's new layout, the remaining infill was intentionally completed in wood rather than a traditional marble patch, helping to subtly feature the building's prior history." The offices wrap around a central courtyard The offices are one of many build outs happening in the Bay area as AI companies need more space and reach higher funding thresholds. Notion global head of real estate Michael McGinley said the office represents a shift in offices from individual-centric to more community oriented. "Office spaces across San Francisco became playgrounds, instead of thoughtfully designed spaces like the office we have here at Notion," McGinley told Dezeen. "At our offices, for instance, we designed our space for the company rather than the individual. That means no ping-pong tables, and instead an actual Tools and Crafts room, where employees can be physical tool makers, not just digital ones." Other recent projects from San Francisco includes OMA's first fully affordable housing block in the US . The photography is by Garret Rowland.
