title: Yarlington Lodge at The Newt in Somerset blends "little snippets of history with life today"
summary: British studio Richard Parr Associates has renovated a trio of 19th-century buildings at The Newt in Somerset hotel in England, restoring their interiors to nod to the site's past. Named Yarlington Lodge, the buildings are spread across five hectares of rural land at The Newt in Somerset, a luxury estate, hotel and working farm located The post Yarlington Lodge at The Newt in Somerset blends "little snippets of history with life today" appeared f

content.source_text: British studio Richard Parr Associates has renovated a trio of 19th-century buildings at The Newt in Somerset hotel in England , restoring their interiors to nod to the site's past. Named Yarlington Lodge , the buildings are spread across five hectares of rural land at The Newt in Somerset , a luxury estate, hotel and working farm located just outside of Bruton. Yarlington Lodge is a three-building holiday home at The Newt in Somerset Conceived by Richard Parr Associates as a 32-guest holiday home, the project comprises the main lodge, the Coach House and the Cottage in the Wall – three buildings that historically served as a rectory, its coach house and the gardener's cottage, respectively. "They were once a functioning trio and we wanted them to become so again," studio founder Richard Parr told Dezeen. Patterns and bright colours reference the Napoleonic era in the main lodge The architect worked with The Newt in Somerset's founders, Koos Bekker and Karen Roos, to restore each property. For the 1831 lodge, striking patterns and bright colours were selected to reference the high drama of the Napoleonic era . The Coach House was renovated to reflect its equestrian history Bedroom ceilings were clad with swooping textiles that give the impression of military tents, while classical paintings embellish the green-hued library. Despite these statement design features, Parr explained that interventions to the bones of each building were intentionally subtle. This included carefully restoring the lodge's old fireplaces, elm floorboards and stonework. "Deliberately pared-back" changes were made to the facades "Houses need to retain the spirit of their entire life and should reflect their many owners, hence the references to previous occupants through portraiture and furniture," said the architect. "The renovation is a mix of little snippets of history with life today," he added. A swimming pool also features within the grounds The Coach House was also adapted to reflect its equestrian history. Blackened steel and raw timber characterise the interior spaces, including the brick-clad living room with a low-slung, beam-lined ceiling. By contrast, Parr and his team renovated the Cottage in the Wall with sandy-hued walls and wooden accents, which complement the building's lofty ceilings. Read: Invisible Studio builds giant window in Somerset hotel garden "Deliberately pared-back" changes were also made to the facade of each building, Parr said, using local Hadspen stone as well as brick, slate, tile and lead. "Internally, these same materials were subtly reinterpreted to different levels of sophistication in the form of timber floors, local blue limestone, and a range of pastel colours lifted out of late Regency England," explained Parr. A greenhouse sits opposite the pool Alongside the three buildings, the Yarlington Lodge site is home to a rectilinear, tile-clad swimming pool opposite a lush plant-filled greenhouse . When revitalising the 19th-century properties, Parr described the main hurdle as subtly incorporating air conditioning into the rooms – something he said felt necessary in 2026. "As the summers get hotter, the need to air-condition all of the bedrooms was introduced into the project," he said. "Devising a way of discreetly housing ducts and grilles into a listed building was extremely challenging." The Newt in Somerset's sprawling grounds also include a lakeside apiary for honey bees and a rammed earth yoga studio , both designed by Invisible Studio. The photography is by Ollie Tomlinson . content.source_text: US architecture studio KTGY has revamped the interiors of the HOK -designed Fairmont Hotel off of Chicago 's Millennium Park. KTGY 's Interiors Studio was brought on to refresh the detailing and bring light into the dark spaces of the hotel, with a focus on the premium rooms and lounges. In total, the studio renovated 83 rooms, as well as meeting rooms and a terrace on the second level. KTGY has revamped the Fairmont Chicago Millennium Park hotel Originally designed by global studio HOK in the 1980s, the postmodern skyscraper hotel in Chicago's Millennium Park neighbourhood features a rationalised structure with neoclassical columns at the base. At the top, it's crowned by an oxidised copper turret that recalls the distinct châteauesque style of Fairmont hotels. However, the elongated body gives the building a sense of verticality more akin to a modern skyscraper, with the mix of the historical and industrial contributing to the "postmodern" descriptions of the building. The scope included lounges and premium rooms The studio said that the primary reason behind the renovation was reflecting aspects of the postmodern skyscraper's facade in the interior, bringing the details down to scale. "KTGY's interiors team reflected the building's postmodern architectural style by bringing that prominence down to a human scale," said the team. Read: Tatjana von Stein blends Jugendstil style with 1980s glamour for The Dean Munich This included the uncovering of previously concealed architectural details, such as in the Rouge meeting room, where KTGY revealed windows and raised a sunken floor. Here and throughout, the team integrated a visual palette that is modern while retaining some of the decadent detailing – such as an abstract chandelier and a textural sideboard, flanked by roped-LED sconces. The finishes and interior architecture were updated to lighten up the spaces In the 15th-floor lounge, the studio completely redid the finishes and flooring and placed a library area to make the space feel more homey. On the second-floor terrace, patterned wood flooring meets fluted wall details painted a matte green. KTGY wanted to reference the architecture of the 1980s postmodern skyscraper The rooms themselves were given lighter colours and bronze accents. Fairmont Chicago Millennium Park is among the dozens of architectural landmarks in central Chicago. Nearby is Edward Durell Stone's AON Tower and Studio Gang's Aqua . content.source_text: Brazil's Estúdio Campana has wrapped a pop-up Tiffany & Co store inside a São Paulo shopping mall in a woven wicker skin. The pop-up on the ground floor of the JK Iguatemi Mall is cloaked in an undulating facade in Tiffany & Co's signature blue, with streaks of tan running horizontally across. A woven wicker facade folds around the entrance to the Tiffany & Co pop-up The collaboration with Estúdio Campana follows the studio's design for the brand's flagship store at another Iguatemi mall in São Paulo last year. "After the success of the store at Shopping Iguatemi last year, we had the opportunity to reinterpret the original concept into a more intimate format, like a woven jewellery box that visitors can step into and immerse themselves in the brand's dreamlike universe," said Humberto Campana. The store's interior is predominantly beige to allow the brand's signature blue hue to pop The long storefront is covered almost entirely in the wicker-style material, which parts to reveal the brand's illuminated logo mounted on beige stone. Around an arched doorway that leads into the retail space, the blue wicker is folded over to house cove lighting that denotes the entrance. Blue hues are also applied to chairs and mirror frames available for customers to use The same facade treatment is also used at the back of the shop, forming another arch over a semi-private consultation area. Blue tones are applied in swirling patterns to the seats and backs of chairs for customers, and across frames for wall-mounted mirrors. Read: MVRDV drapes glass veil around Tiffany & Co flagship in Beijing Tiffany & Co products are presented in glass vitrines raised on metal-framed bases around tambour panelling. Soft neutral tones were chosen for the remaining walls and carpet to contrast the bold blue elements, which feature in the brand's stores worldwide. The studio created a chair and two mirrors from its Sushi Collection. It also fashioned a collection of custom synthetic-wicker stools, with manually woven elements that match the facade. The wicker facade treatment is also applied around the entrance to a semi-private consultation area Recently, Tiffany & Co has worked with several notable architects and designers to update the facades of some of its global locations. MVRDV draped a glass veil around the brand's Beijing flagship , while Jun Aoki cloaked a store in Ginza , Tokyo, in curving glass panels. Streaks of tan run horizontally through the undulated blue material Estúdio Campana was founded by Humberto and his brother Fernando, who died in 2022 . Humberto debuted his first design collection since his brother's passing at New York gallery Friedman Benda in 2024. The studio has since created a park near São Paulo that includes pavilions made with live plants on land once farmed by the founders' grandfather. The photography is courtesy of Iguatemi. content.source_text: AIM Architecture has designed Zara Huaihai Road, a flagship store for the Spanish fashion brand in Shanghai , with an amphitheatre-like brick podium that connects the building with the street. Located on Huaihai Road, a well-known commercial district in central Shanghai, the new flagship store took over an existing five-storey concrete building, which AIM Architecture aimed to transform into a space for discovery. The flagship store is located in central Shanghai's commercial district "Rather than imposing a new identity, the design embraces the building's existing concrete structure, proportions, and spatial logic, allowing the architecture itself to shape the experience," said AIM Architecture. "The project reflects Zara 's evolution towards more open, flexible, and immersive environments, where the journey is as meaningful as the destination," it added. Brick steps create an open plaza at the front of the store The studio opened up the facade on the ground level by creating a stepped brick podium that extends onto the street. Passersby are encouraged to sit down and rest at the amphitheatre-like structure, which is planted with green shrubs and sheltered by the building. A similar, smaller brick podium was created inside the store, near the entrance. This podium, which functions partially as stairs and seating and partially as product display, connects the visual language of the store interior with its exterior. Brick steps also feature inside the store entrance At the Zara Huaihai Road store, the fashion brand's collections are spread over the building's five floors, where they are presented in different interiors to suit the different styles. Zara's TRF collection sits within a space that resembles a contemporary warehouse, while the main women's fashion collection is shown in an art gallery-like environment. The space for Zara's TRF collection was designed as a contemporary warehouse The menswear floor was divided into two spaces: an atelier celebrating craftsmanship and a contemporary Shanghai loft that was designed to have a more domestic feel. AIM Architecture covered the fitting rooms in mirrors to create a more immersive feeling. Read: AIM Architecture transforms oil silos in China into community park Throughout the store, exposed structural columns, polished concrete floors and a concrete cassette ceiling were used to create a raw, industrial atmosphere, while timber and linen add warmth and tactility. Lightweight and adaptable furniture and display systems were introduced to allow for flexible seasonal display changes. Part of the menswear floor was designed like an atelier AIM Architecture kept the building's existing staircase , but redesigned it to have a more sculptural shape. It paired the staircase's concrete steps with a black textured-steel railing, which was wrapped in serrated concrete at the lower end. A thin lighting tube hangs at the centre of the stairwell, illuminating the otherwise dark space. The existing staircase of the building was given a sculptural redesign "Zara Huaihai Road reflects a broader vision for the future of physical retail," said AIM Architecture. "By embracing the existing architecture rather than replacing it, the project transforms a commercial building into a contemporary public interior rooted in the life of Shanghai, creating destinations where commerce, culture, and community converge." The changing rooms feature multiple mirrors and reflective surfaces Founded by Belgian and Dutch architects Wendy Saunders and Vincent de Graaf in 2005, AIM Architecture now has offices in Shanghai, Antwerp, Hong Kong and Chicago. It was awarded Interior Designer of the Year at Dezeen Awards China in 2023 . Previously in China, it has completed a resort in Chengdu featuring sweeping, tentacle-like canopies , as well as a community park repurposed from oil silos in Changzhou . The photography is by Seth Powers. title: "I find it icky to glibly invoke brain chemistry in the marketing of style"

content.source_text: The "dopamine decor" interiors trend is taking social media by storm, but it's just another disingenuous dressing-up of superficial style as life-improving experience, writes Julie Lasky . For some time now, the internet has labeled a maximalist decorating trend that embraces candy colors, fuzzy textures and whimsical furnishings "dopamine decor". The reference is, of course, to neuroscience, and supporters claim that the style, which, like many interiors ideas, has its roots in fashion, produces a genuine emotional uplift. The look is energetic and often charming. Seen on social media, it leaves a stubborn pink glow in the mind as one moves on to a cake-fail video. For every white-paint-loving minimalist, there has always been a Barbie with a hot-pink dream house Books celebrate it, too. In April, Rachel Varney, who has an Instagram called The Shoestring Home , published Dopamine Home (Mobius) . The publicist described it as "the ultimate mood-boosting guide filled with color know how, creative hacks and cost saving tips and tricks". The central image on the bubblegum-pink cover is of a squiggle-based glass coffee table supporting a ceramic fruit bowl shaped like a bunch of bananas. And now, Maitri Mody, a New York-based designer whose Instagram is called Honey I Dressed the Pug , is coming out in late August with Dopamine Design: Creating a Home That Makes You Happy (Ten Speed Press) . Her goal is to teach readers that they are not chained to conformity but can break away and pursue their own idiosyncratic, ecstatic visions. "For years, design trends worshiped minimalism ," Mody writes, in prose that has the rhythmic cadences and offbeat assertions associated with generative AI. (A detection tool backed me up on that suspicion, though Mody denies using AI to write the book.) Read: "True trends always answer a need" "White walls, neutral furniture, and barely-there decor dominated Instagram feeds and Pinterest boards. But let's be honest – minimalism isn't for everyone. It's a look, not a feeling. Dopamine design flips the script. It's not about following rules or trends. It's about creating a home that celebrates your quirks, your story, and your joy." Let me pause here to raise an eyebrow at the description of minimalism as "a look, not a feeling". Even its haters describe it as cold, which is most certainly a feeling. I also object to the use of the color white as a straw man. For every white-paint-loving minimalist like, say, John Pawson , there has always been a Barbie with a hot-pink dream house. Dopamine decor is said to have influenced the look of food packaging in real life Let me add that I met Mody in person a few years ago, while she was exhibiting a checkerboard-patterned kitchen with cabinet pulls that looked like carrots, and found her very nice. It is not my intention to whimsy-shame anyone. But given the commoditization of health in everything from peptides to bathing culture, I find it icky to glibly invoke brain chemistry in the marketing of style. Dopamine decor claims to celebrate individuality, though it's driven by repetitive social media images. It is aimed at adults, though its tutti-frutti, cutesy-naive examples look incontrovertibly juvenile. It purports to stimulate happy brain chemicals, at a time when, in the US, public health movements are being eviscerated by deranged officials. "'Dopamine decor' can boost your mood," the Washington Post declared last year , like a snake-oil salesman. Well, so can a bucket of tiramisu, until the sugar high lets you down. Read: "What to do with the TV is among the most challenging design problems in today's American home" The most disingenuous thing about this trend is the pretense that images on a screen or in a book represent plausible experience. The photos are filtered, cropped and disjointed. They whiz by, just like an endorphin rush. Dopamine decor is said to have influenced the look of food packaging in real life, but food packages are quickly thrown away. What are the long-term effects of living with frenetic decorating choices? Do they lose their happy juice over time? Do they get on one's nerves? Do they drive one insane? Yes, said Ashley Couto, who wrote an article for Business Insider magazine last year with the headline: "I redid my space with color and 'dopamine decor' designed to bring me joy. It worked at first, but I already hate it." A style touted as authentic and livable can't seem to shed its performative, Instagram-y nature This would not surprise Andréa de Paiva, a Brazilian architect who specializes in the relationship between neuroscience and building design. In a cautionary article about dopamine decor on the website of her organization, NeuroAU, she writes: "Instead of thoughtfully enhancing the environment to support well-being, these spaces risk overwhelming the senses, potentially leading to fatigue, distraction, or even stress rather than joy and motivation." De Paiva urges designers to be responsible with terminology, especially when it comes to applied science: "Titles like Dopamine Design or even NeuroArchitecture can be intriguing and marketable, but they should not be used as buzzwords to sell incomplete or oversimplified ideas." Still, you don't need to be a brain surgeon to recognize that a style touted as authentic and livable can't seem to shed its performative, Instagram-y nature. According to Marianne Plaisance , a graphic designer and photographer featured in Modi's book, some of her YouTube followers thought her space looked AI-generated. She took it as a compliment. Julie Lasky is New York-based a journalist and critic specialising in design, architecture and urbanism. She was previously deputy editor of The New York Times' weekly Home and Garden section, the editor of Change Observer, editor-in-chief of ID magazine and editor of Interiors magazine. She is also a part-time assistant professor at Parsons School of Design. The image is a screengrab taken from Instagram. Dezeen In Depth If you enjoy reading Dezeen's interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth . Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines. content.source_text: You can still feature in Dezeen Events Guide's digital guide to the 24th edition of London Design Festival , which takes place from 12 to 20 September. If you're hosting an event in London – including an exhibition, installation, talk, product launch, tour, open showroom or party – get in touch to be listed in the guide. This year, the nine-day festival takes place across 11 participating districts: Bankside Design District, Blackhorse Creates, Brompton Design District, Chelsea Design District, Dalston to Stokey Design District, EC1 Design District, Fleet St Quarter, Mayfair Design District, Park Royal Design District, Shoreditch Design Week and Soho Design District. Get listed in Dezeen's digital guide to London Design Festival If you're hosting an event, get in touch with the Dezeen Events Guide team at eventsguide@dezeen.com to book in your listing or to discuss a wider partnership with Dezeen. There are three types of listings: Standard listings cost £150 and include the event name, date and location details plus a website link. These listings will also feature up to 50 words of text about the event. Enhanced listings cost £200 and include all of the above, plus an image at the top of the listing's page and an image in the listing preview on the festival guide homepage. These listings will also feature up to 100 words of text about the event. Featured listings cost £400 and include all elements of an enhanced listing plus a post on Dezeen's Threads channel, inclusion in the featured events carousel on the right-hand side of the festival guide homepage for up to two weeks and 150 words of text about the event. This text can include commercial information such as ticket prices and offers and can feature additional links to website pages such as ticket sales, newsletter signups, et cetera. About Dezeen Events Guide Dezeen Events Guide is our guide to the best architecture and design events taking place across the world each year. The guide is updated weekly and includes virtual events, conferences, trade fairs, major exhibitions and design weeks. For more details on inclusion in Dezeen Events Guide, including our guide to London Design Festival, email eventsguide@dezeen.com . The illustration is by Ross Becker . title: Tatjana von Stein blends Jugendstil style with 1980s glamour for The Dean Munich
summary: French-German designer Tatjana von Stein designed hundreds of bespoke lights and furnishings for this hotel in Munich, drawing on the city's art nouveau style and its exuberant nightlife history. The Dean Munich is the latest offering from the Irish hotel chain, with 281 rooms and suites, three bars, and a signature Japanese restaurant named Ibasho. The post Tatjana von Stein blends Jugendstil style with 1980s glamour for The Dean Munich appeared

content.source_text: French-German designer Tatjana von Stein designed hundreds of bespoke lights and furnishings for this hotel in Munich, drawing on the city's art nouveau style and its exuberant nightlife history. The Dean Munich is the latest offering from the Irish hotel chain , with 281 rooms and suites, three bars, and a signature Japanese restaurant named Ibasho. The design blends influences from art nouveau and 1980s nightclubs The project saw von Stein revamp an existing hotel in the city's Westend neighbourhood, with a design where shades of gold and red extend across velvet furniture, floral carpets, stained-glass windows and ornamental lamps. The project allowed the interior designer to dig into the design history of the city where she was born. Her scheme blends the city's distinct Jugendstil style, the manifestation of art nouveau in Bavaria, with the decadent nightclubs that proliferated in the 1980s. The lobby features a restored floor of black stone chevron tiles "This is a city rooted in history but always drawn to reinvention," said von Stein. "I wanted to capture that tension, somewhere between elegance and exuberance, and let it guide every surface, object and gesture." "The design also brings to life a side of Munich only locals truly know – its rich musical and cultural spirit, quietly woven into the character of the city." On a raised platform, a wrap-around bar is set below a circular ceiling recess The most radical interventions are in the communal areas on the ground floor, which were completely reorganised. They begin with the lobby, a space with a rich sense of theatricality. At its centre is a stepped platform, where a wrap-around bar is set below a circular ceiling recess with a reflective surface and a decorative wallpaper frieze around its edges. A pair of sphinx table lights were among the vintage pieces sourced for the lobby This is the first of many playful ceilings that feature throughout the hotel. On either side of the bar, lounge areas are framed by tiered ceiling recesses with zigzagging corners, matching the edge details of the internal columns. Read: Traditional wooden townhouses inform interiors of Kengo Kuma-designed Capella Kyoto hotel "We're really interior architects, so we start with layout and hard finishes before slowly making our way into furniture and fixtures," von Stein told Dezeen. "I love to fully envelop people in a world, and that starts with the envelope. So ceilings certainly play a big part." Fluted ceilings and stained glass windows characterise Ibasho's interior Over the restored chevron-tiled stone flooring, the rest of the space is carefully layered with patterned rugs and gloss-backed sofas, while focal points include bell-shaped sconces, frilled stools and sculptural tables. Many of the objects here were custom-designed by von Stein, although she also sourced some vintage pieces, including original late-19th and early-20th century pieces by Austrian design icons Josef Hoffmann and Otto Wagner. She points to a pair of sphinx table lights as a personal favourite in this room, "somehow out of place, but fabulous". A conversation pit is set below a gridded mirror ceiling Japanese influences come into play in Ibasho, inspired by the cuisine of chef Alex Craciun. Below mirrored and fluted ceilings, von Stein created a series of "rooms within rooms". These include a conversation pit with gold velvet sofas and a horseshoe-shaped marble bar encircled by pink leather Verner Panton chairs. Pink leather Verner Panton chairs encircle a horseshoe-shaped bar The Jugendstil-inspired stained glass frames a series of windows between these spaces, offering glimpsed views between them. "For me, the most compelling hospitality spaces are those that reveal themselves gradually," said von Stein. Noren features a timber-panelled ceiling and tapestry-style upholstery "We wanted to create a space which engages the senses, influences mood and encourages a certain rhythm of experience and connection throughout the diner's experience." Tucked away behind Ibasho, Noren is a more exclusive and intimate cocktail bar. This 48-seat space features Friendly Pressure speakers, a geometric timber ceiling and tapestry-style seating. The timber-panelled bedrooms feature a palette of olive greens The style is more pared-back in the bedrooms, but no less stylish. Against a backdrop of panelled walls, olive-green and orange textiles sit alongside tubular shelving units, tiger-stripe tables and sculptural chairs. As with the communal areas, these rooms are embellished with works by Munich-based contemporary artists. These were curated by Christian Ganzenberg, the director of Munich's international art festival, Various Others. Furnishings include tubular shelving units, tiger-stripe tables and sculptural chairs For The Dean, the hotel is its largest to date and its second outside Ireland, following the Berlin hotel designed by Rachael Gowdridge , showcased on Dezeen earlier this year. It also marks the latest in a series of lavish hospitality spaces designed by von Stein, following members' club Làlia in Palma, Mallorca, and the Locke am Platz hotel in Zurich, Switzerland. Works by Munich-based artists feature throughout the hotel In a recent interview with Dezeen, the designer described her approach as both theatrical and precise. "Let's face it, the world is rather chaotic and can be quite a depressing place," she told Dezeen's deputy editor, Cajsa Carlson. "So these moments of theatre are important, and decadence to a certain extent." The photography is by Dean Hearne , courtesy of The Dean. title: Ome Dezin and Lumens outfit renovated Los Angeles residence
summary: Los Angeles studio Ome Dezin has partnered with design platform Lumens to renovate and furnish a 1990s home in the Hollywood Hills, adding iconic furniture and lighting from Frank Gehry, Ingo Maurer and more. Situated in middle of a mature forest on over an acre of land, the house was originally designed by architect Jeff The post Ome Dezin and Lumens outfit renovated Los Angeles residence appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Los Angeles studio Ome Dezin has partnered with design platform Lumens to renovate and furnish a 1990s home in the Hollywood Hills , adding iconic furniture and lighting from Frank Gehry , Ingo Maurer and more. Situated in middle of a mature forest on over an acre of land, the house was originally designed by architect Jeff Mills in a style that blends mid-century modern and brutalism. Furniture, including Frank Gehry's Wiggle Chair, adds character to the renovated Los Angeles home The residence was once home to an A-list actor, then later converted into an art gallery, leaving white-washed walls, tall ceilings, exposed beams and expansive spaces for Ome Dezin founders Jesse Rudolph and Joelle Kutner to build upon. "It was stripped of all personality," the duo told Dezeen. "There were no doors, bedrooms, full bathrooms, etc. It was hard for some to envision this house as a home." A striped Up chair by Gaetano Pesce anchors a lounge area They restored the original architecture, making minor alterations like adding a gym, converting an upstairs guest bedroom into the primary bathroom and erecting an exterior sauna and full bathroom. Limestone flooring in some of the rooms was saved, while all the other surfaces were altered or added to in order to transform the property into a livable home. Warmth is introduced through pieces like a sheepskin chair by Audo Copenhagen "The space felt sterile when we got into it, and our goal was to bring depth, layers, and warmth to the home," the pair said. With the surrounding forested landscape in mind, Rudolph and Kutner used wood to clad entire walls in the main living spaces and bathrooms. The kitchen island is clad in rust-toned stone with an aged, tactile finish They also introduced atypically tall wood baseboards to create a sense of continuity throughout the home, while stone such as richly veined marble in the bathrooms was also employed to embellish the natural aesthetic. The kitchen is enveloped in a distinctive blue stone, while the island is clad in a rust-toned variation with an aged, tactile finish. "Throughout the home, these earthy materials are punctuated by glimmers of jewel tones, silver, and gold — appearing in the lighting, decorative details, and custom stained-glass windows and doors we designed specifically for the space," said the team. Read: Willett and Ome Dezin renovate mid-century CM G1 House in LA When it came to furnishing the residence, Ome Dezin teamed up with Lumens – a platform they already used frequently to source furniture and lighting – to choose distinctive pieces to complete the spaces. They began with lighting, selecting favourites such as gold Ingo Maurer pendants for the kitchen, along with pieces from Foscarini and In Common With . "Lighting is so important to us as we think of it as functional art," said Rudolph and Kutner. "It adds warmth, character, depth and shadows into a space for layer and movement." A glass-topped table and foldable wooden chairs create an outdoor dining setup Furniture was then layered in, from Gubi dining chairs to statement pieces like a striped Up chair by Gaetano Pesce and Frank Gehry's Wiggle Chair . "What I love about the result is that you feel the individuality of each piece, but nothing feels overly coordinated," Lumens chief marketing officer Dana Gers told Dezeen. "There's a sense of discovery to it. It feels collected, personal and entirely at home within the architecture." The house was originally designed in the 1990s by Jeff Mills in a style that blends brutalism and mid-century modern As an interior design and development studio, Ome Dezin reimagined, renovated and sold multiple properties across the greater Los Angeles area. These include a 1960s A Quincy Jones house in Brentwood and a mid-century Laurel Hills residence for which they collaborated with furniture designer Willet. The photography is by William Jess Laird . content.source_text: Interior design practice Busta Studio has filled the Kimpton Ashbel hotel on Park Avenue with art and objects intended to make it feel like "a warm, elegantly curated home". Located in a 1928 beaux-arts building on New York City's famous Park Avenue, Kimpton Ashbel was designed to feel like a private residence. A neutral colour palette is juxtaposed with jewel tones at Kimpton Ashbel "Park Avenue is one of New York City's most iconic streets, instantly evoking the elegance of its heritage townhouses," Busta Studio founder Anna Busta told Dezeen. "Drawing from this distinctive spirit, we envisioned a conceptual townhouse experience – welcoming guests into a warm, elegantly curated home." Artworks decorate both guestrooms and communal areas Anna and her husband Jonathan Busta, who run Busta Studio together, used hand-brushed blonde limed oak panelling and arches juxtaposed with Bianco Dolomiti and Pietra marbles to create the right feel for the interior. The studio also combined hand-cast bronze, glass, inlaid bronze and hand-cut mosaic stone with white plaster ceilings and mouldings for a deliberately simple yet elegant look. "The New York townhouse concept itself is an endless source of inspiration: a place where one lingers, surrounded by bespoke millwork, refined finishes, stylish furnishings, and a curated mix of art and collected objects that feel personal and storied," Jonathan Busta told Dezeen. The hotel was designed to feel like a home To create privacy from the bustle of Park Avenue, custom louvres were added at street level. Guests are welcomed by a custom inlaid mosaic featuring the hotel's KA initials when entering the lobby, which Busta Studio filled with specially commissioned artworks and decorative objects. Read: A-nrd designs Arthouse Glasgow hotel to "feel like it belongs to the city" "We curated the art collection to create a nice, easy vibe for the interior, with a mixture of graphics, original paintings, photography and sculpture," Anna Busta said. "All pieces are specifically commissioned for the space, and the overall collection has a simple but sophisticated guiding aesthetic," she continued. "We didn't want to provoke with art, but instead we simply embraced beauty." Designers Busta Studio added tactile materials and brass details The designers wanted to tie the communal spaces and guestrooms at Kimpton Ashbel together by using a coherent colour palette for the hotel, which focuses on calming neutral hues juxtaposed with jewel colours. "Jewel tones inject vibrancy into accent pieces like arch chairs, side stools, headboards, and art chairs, striking a harmonious balance between subtle and bold statements that add warmth and approachability to the space," Jonathan Busta said. Velvet and linen fabrics were used throughout the Park Avenue hotel To create a homely feeling, Busta Studio used velvets, linens, naturally tanned leathers and boucle fabrics. The studio said it hoped that the mix of tactile materials, refined finishes and well-considered artworks would create a feeling that is reminiscent of a well-designed home. "We believe the guest experience is enhanced by this intimate approach," Anna Busta concluded. Other hotels recently featured on Dezeen include a Glasgow hotel in a 19th-century townhouse and a Tokyo boutique hotel designed to feel like staying at the home of a friend . The photography is courtesy of Kimpton Ashbel. The post Busta Studio evokes the elegance of New York townhouses for Kimpton Ashbel hotel appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: British eyewear brand Cubitts has unveiled its first shop in Manchester , designed by locally based studio Youth to reflect the city's industrial and musical history without resorting to the obvious. Youth co-founders Oliver Collinge and Liam McGroarty planned the interior to reflect the present and future of the British city, with subtle references to the past rather than cliches. Shelving combines tubular steel uprights with dapple-textured glass shelves It includes a shelving display combining tubular steel uprights with dapple-textured glass shelves, a faceted oak counter housing a till and record player, and a pair of figurative sandstone sculptures by artist Richard Perry. The designers aimed to create a space "that feels both familiar and distinctly contemporary". Dimpled mirrors offer slightly cloudy reflections "Inspired by the city itself, the space draws on Manchester's culture and historic character, reinterpreted through a contemporary lens," they said. The approach reflects the brief set by Cubitts founder Tom Broughton "to make the space feel distinctly Cubitts without resorting to the usual Manchester shorthand". A faceted oak counter houses a till and record player "It was important that Cubitts Manchester was designed in Manchester, and not just deposited here," Broughton said. "Manchester does not need another London brand telling it how interesting it is. We're simply pleased to finally be here, and hope to make ourselves useful." Artworks include a pair of figurative sandstone sculptures by Richard Perry The store is located in Smithfield Buildings in the Northern Quarter, a collection of buildings that once housed the Affleck & Brown department store, dubbed the 'Harrods of the North'. After more than a decade looking at locations, Broughton and his team chose this one for its history as a supplier of cloth and made-to-measure garments. Read: EBBA Architects transforms former jellied-eel restaurant into eyewear store This aligns with Cubitts' own approach, with facilities for eye examinations, spectacle repairs and customisation made visible in the store. "Smithfield Buildings felt immediately right: a spectacle shop inside a former draper's department store, in a neighbourhood shaped by making, music and independent trade," said Broughton. The designers sourced a vintage bookcase made with salvaged timber from the HMS Foudroyant Waxed cotton curtains softly divide different areas in tribute to Affleck & Brown's legacy, while other additions include a vintage revolving bookcase. Produced by Manchester cabinetmakers Goodall, Lamb and Heighway, this century-old piece was made with salvaged timber from the Royal Navy ship HMS Foudroyant. A wall of material samples celebrates Cubitts' customisation options Artworks also hint at industrial production; a seamstress is depicted in a painting by artist Francis Hoyland, while a cubist gouache by artist Marcel Gille depicts a forge worker. Completing the design are dimpled mirrors that offer slightly cloudy reflections and a collection of records spanning soul, jazz, punk and electronica. Cubitts Manchester is located in Smithfield Buildings in the Northern Quarter Cubitts Manchester is the brand's 21st location, following others that include the peep-show-inspired Cubitts Soho and the art-deco-style Cubitts Leeds . The company also just unveiled a new headquarters in London's King's Cross , in a historic building that began as a working stable for the Crosse & Blackwell Vinegar Works, before being converted into an office for a publishing house. The photography is courtesy of Cubitts. The post Youth avoids Manchester cliches for city's first Cubitts eyewear store appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Architecture studio Kii has designed an ice cream shop on Miyakojima Island, Japan , featuring a pink ceiling, a limestone counter and perforated concrete tiles. Called SR Ice Cream Miyakojima, the cafe and ice cream shop is located on an island in the southern part of Japan's Okinawa prefecture in the Pacific Ocean. Its ocean-side setting influenced the interior, which features local materials chosen for their weather resistance. SR Ice Cream Miyakojima has a pink curved ceiling "On Miyakojima Island, its local residents, new arrivals and tourists coexist and the goal was to create a welcoming environment where people of all backgrounds can simply drop by to enjoy a shared atmosphere over an ice cream or coffee," Kii co-founder Satoshi Arai told Dezeen. "To withstand Miyakojima's subtropical oceanic climate, materials were also carefully selected to ensure finishes which are both functional and enduring," Arai continued. The centrepiece of SR Ice Cream Miyakojima is a large, rounded counter made from limestone and with a lime plaster tabletop, around which customers can stand or sit. A small door in the counter was added to provide access for maintenance Kii worked with an Okinawan plaster specialist to design the counter. "Work to the counter involves applying rounded lumps of limestone clay – Ryukyu limestone, a local material in Miyakojima – to the counter surface one piece at a time," Kii co-founder Kei Nakatomi told Dezeen. Miyakojima Island's seaside setting informed the materials used "The process of applying this material repeatedly creates a layered finish, and allows its unique texture to truly stand out," Nakatomi continued. "The tabletop was also crafted using the same limestone clay and polished to reveal the material's unique texture." Perforated concrete bricks were used for walls and flooring Kii also inserted a playful arched door in the counter to create easy access for filter maintenance. Above the central counter, Kii added a curved ceiling designed to draw visitors' attention and make the counter an attraction in itself. Read: Funamachi Base cafe and sweet shop designed as "extension of the park" The studio chose a pale pink hue for the ceiling, in response to the natural light of the cafe's surroundings. "Considering the dramatic shifts in natural light throughout the day on Miyakojima, we tested several options on-site to determine the ideal colour – ultimately selecting this specific shade of pink – to ensure it harmonised with the environment at any time of day or night," Arai said. Stools were designed to look like melting ice cream The salt air and harsh sunlight on the island influenced Arai and Nakatomi's choice of materials, and the two designers also aimed to showcase artisanal craftsmanship from different regions of Japan. Apart from the limestone counter, one of the most noticeable materials in the SR ice cream shop is a specific type of concrete brick, which is perforated with holes for typhoon-struck areas. "In the Okinawa area, where typhoons frequently hit, concrete blocks with holes are in use for architecture," Nakatomi said. "When considering how to incorporate this unique characteristic of the region as an element that would blend seamlessly into the interior, custom tiles by Tajimi Tiles were selected." The cafe was designed to appeal to both locals and tourists The studio also added cushions woven from Cogon grass, which is native to the island, and colourful glazed stools by NOTA shop in Shigaraki – an old pottery area. These pastel stools were specially chosen for the ice cream store as they had to be easy to maintain and have a non-directional design to fit under low tables. "We picked the stool regularly produced by NOTA shop, with an original glazed colour on it," Arai said. "We designed these with the mindset of embracing the unpredictable results over its final appearance, and enjoyed the process of letting the results surprise us." Kii wanted the cafe to function as a community space Kii did have some input into the glazing, as the studio wanted the stools to resemble ice cream that had started to melt. "We did, however, go through a number of prototypes to fine-tune the glaze, aiming for a colour and texture that's reminiscent of melting ice cream," Arai added. Overall, the studio said the ice cream shop, which sits on the ground floor of an ocean-side commercial development, has become the type of place that it envisioned when coming up with the design. "We had heard that many guests would linger or stick around, whilst being engaged with guests inside or outside – just like a community, and as the type of space we had imagined while we had designed it," Nakatomi said. Other Japanese cafes recently covered on Dezeen include a cafe and brewery on Teshima Island and a Blue Bottle Coffee cafe informed by Osaka Castle . The photography is by Masanori Kaneshita . title: Uppercut unveils summer exhibition in the stately rooms of Chateau de Spycker
summary: Antwerp-based gallery Uppercut is presenting the works of six contemporary designers in the ornate halls and salons of a neo-gothic villa near Bruges. Elaborate glass vessels by Danish designer Alexander Kirkeby and melted polystyrene furniture by French designer Nicolas Zanoni are among the pieces on show inside the rooms of the 19th-century Chateau de Spycker The post Uppercut unveils summer exhibition in the stately rooms of Chateau de Spycker

content.source_text: Antwerp-based gallery Uppercut is presenting the works of six contemporary designers in the ornate halls and salons of a neo-gothic villa near Bruges . Elaborate glass vessels by Danish designer Alexander Kirkeby and melted polystyrene furniture by French designer Nicolas Zanoni are among the pieces on show inside the rooms of the 19th-century Chateau de Spycker in Sint-Kruis. The exhibition spans three rooms of the neo-gothic Chateau de Spycker The exhibition, titled God Speed, also features pieces by Belgian designer Linde Freya Tangelder, South Korean designer Yoon Shun , New York-based Greek designer Kiki Goti and LS Gomma , the studio of British designer Joel Muggleton. The is the fourth annual summer exhibition that Uppercut has staged at Chateau de Spycker since director Scott Lippens founded the gallery in 2023. LS Gomma's Drunken Vessels are on show in the dining room Originally the summer residence of an aristocratic family, the villa was bought by Lippens' family nearly 20 years ago and has been operating as guesthouse since a renovation by his mother, fashion buyer Caroline Grootaert. While previous shows were limited to a single room, this time Uppercut's exhibition extends through from the grand entry hall into the dining and drawing rooms. These metal mesh and rubber vessels are displayed alongside antique sculptures In each space, contemporary works are in dialogue with period details that include decorative wall mouldings, gilded furniture, marble fireplaces and antique artworks. Lippens said the approach was inspired by the newly inaugurated Fondazione Dries Van Noten in Venice, with which he had some involvement. "I realised I could leave a lot of the antiquities in here and embrace the way they clash with the contemporary design," he said. "They actually go really well together." Nicolas Zanoni's melted polystyrene furniture is the focal point in the drawing room The juxtaposition is particularly apparent in the dining room, where LS Gomma's Drunken Vessels, made from metal mesh and PU rubber, are displayed on the table alongside figurative sculptures. For the drawing room, a space dominated by green walls and colourful textiles, Zanoni's multitextural furniture is arranged over patterned rugs, while Goti's hand-blown glass vases adorn a marble-topped console table. Kikti Goti's hand-blown glass vases adorn a marble-topped console table The balance tips more towards contemporary in the entry hall, where most of the large works are on show. There are various pieces by Tangelder, founder of the studio Destroyers/Builders , including her folded aluminium Reworked bench and a coffee table on which Kirkeby's glassware is presented. Shun has also contributed various pieces, including both lighting and furniture, which demonstrate his particular methods of handcarving and charring oak. Yoon Shun's works demonstrate techniques of carving and charring wood Lippens said the gallery focuses on designers who specialise in material processes. "Maybe it comes from my fashion background, but I'm very material-driven," he told Dezeen. The gallerist originally studied fashion design, but moved into the world of collectible design when a side-hustle of buying and selling vintage mid-century furniture gained traction. Glassware by Alexander Kirkeby is displayed on a coffee table by Linde Freya Tangelder Uppercut evolved out of this, as Lippens became increasingly interested in working with young talent and staging his own exhibitions. Until recently, the gallery operated out of Lippens' home, a fifth-floor art-deco apartment in the south of Antwerp. But now, following acclaimed presentations at major shows including Matter and Shape in Paris and the Collectible fairs in New York and Brussels, Uppercut is opening a dedicated gallery nearby. Read: Lisbon's Estrela Basilica sets scene for Portuguese collectible design show Lippens said he is growing in confidence with every show, as he becomes more adept at layering different scenographies. "I've become more strict with myself, but I can also work quite fast," he said, revealing that the install of the summer show was worked out in under four hours. "There's a feeling within you; it either resonates or it doesn't." God Speed is Uppercut's fourth annual summer exhibition Other recent collectible design features on Dezeen include a show in Lisbon's Estrela Basilica and our favourite pieces from NYC x Design 2026 . God Speed is on show at Chateau de Spycker, Spijkersdreef 13, 8310 Brugge, from 30 July to 30 August 2026. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world The photography is by Jules Ange .
